subtitle.text: "I've found my champion." Hermes peered through the crack in the temple wall. "Finish creating the passage, my friend."
"Are you certain?" Caerus sounded bored. "These time passages aren't a simple matter, you know.
None of the other gods could even begin to—"
"I know," Hermes interrupted.
"That's why I asked you to help me. Trust me.
It will be worth the effort if we succeed." He smiled.
Caerus smiled back, looking more interested now. "True," he said.
"Zeus will never figure out where you found your champion!"
Hermes didn't respond. He was watching the mortal boy again.
It wasn't easy to see through the tiny crack in the wall—curse Caerus and his laziness!
But Hermes could see enough. The athlete was handsome and strong, his muscles rippling as he ran.
Other mortals were chasing the boy, but he outpaced them easily.
Suddenly the boy stopped. He threw something on the ground and then leaped around gracefully.
"Is he celebrating his victory in the footrace?" Hermes thought. Watching him, Hermes had no idea.
The ways of mortals were often strange, and usually not worth puzzling over.
But Hermes could tell that this mortal was something special.
"Finish the passage," he told Caerus again. "We don't have time to waste if we want to have him ready."
"Good game, Brody," Coach Smith said as Brody jogged off the field with the rest of the football team.
"Yeah, I know." Brody puffed out his chest. "Thanks, Coach. Do you think we'll win the championship this year?"
Another player glanced over. "If you keep making touchdowns, Brody? Definitely!" he said.
Several of Brody's other teammates agreed, though some remained quiet. A few looked unhappy.
Brody wasn't surprised. He was only a freshman, but he played better than any of the older kids.
That had to be embarrassing for them. Brody didn't care, though.
They should be glad he was on the team.
Everyone said he was the best player to attend the high school in years.
Maybe he was the best player ever.
Brody headed into the locker room. He showered, changed his clothes, and went back outside.
A teammate waved good-bye. "Are you ready for that science test tomorrow?" he called.
Brody frowned at him. "Who cares about science?"
The truth was, he hadn't studied for the test yet.
Science was hard for him—even harder than most of his other classes.
But so what? The coach was already saying that Brody was sure to win a college scholarship when the time came.
Brody didn't care much about going to college, but he loved the idea of playing college football.
After that he'd probably be drafted by the professional league, and then he'd be rich.
He wouldn't need to know about science to play football.
The only schooling he'd need was enough math to add up all his money!
As Brody was thinking about that, a girl stepped in front of him.
He almost crashed into her, but he stopped just in time.
"Watch it," he said. "I'm trying to walk here."
"I need to talk to you." The girl sounded annoyed.
Brody stared at her. She looked familiar. "Hey, don't you ride my bus?"
"Yes." The girl sounded even more annoyed now. "I sit in the front seat.
Every single day since school started. I'm Julia."
"Oh. Uh, I'm Brody."
"I know." Julia rolled her eyes. "I'm supposed to write an article about you for the school newspaper."
"Really?" Brody shrugged. "There was an article about me in there three weeks ago.
I guess it's time for another one." He laughed loudly.
Julia didn't laugh. "Just so you know, I don't care about football.
They're making me do this because the reporter who usually writes the sports stories is sick."
"Whatever." Brody started walking. "I'm on my way to the bus stop.
You can interview me if you can keep up."
Julia broke into a jog to match his pace. "Can't you hold still for a second?
This won't take long." She looked at her notebook.
"What's your favorite thing about playing on the football team?"
That got Brody's interest. He loved talking about himself.
He stopped and leaned against the brick wall of the gymnasium.
"Well . . . ," he said. "My favorite thing about playing football is that I'm so great at it.
It's fun being the star of the team." He flexed his biceps like a bodybuilder.
"Hmm." Julia didn't look impressed by that, or by his answer either, but she scribbled a few notes.
"What valuable lessons have you learned from your teammates so far?"
That question wasn't nearly as interesting as the first one, in Brody's opinion.
"What kind of article are you writing, anyway?" he said.
"Readers won't care about stuff like that.
Maybe you should wait until that sick reporter gets back and let him write the story."
He started to walk away. Then he felt Julia grab his arm.
She had a strong grip for such a nerdy girl.
"Stop," she said, sounding annoyed. "I told you, I need to—"
Whoosh!
A sudden blast of air and sound interrupted her.
The bricks of the gym wall seemed to crackle and melt.
They pulled apart, leaving a narrow opening just tall and wide enough for a person to step through.
Brody felt Julia's grip on him tighten.
As he looked through the crack, his eyes widened in shock.
There was no sign of the gym interior through that crack in the wall.
Instead he saw a strange, shadowy space with stone walls. Two tall figures stood there.
One of the figures leaned through the crack.
He had curly blond hair and looked a few years older than Brody. His eyes glowed bright green.
"Hey . . . Ow!" Brody yelped as the mysterious figure grabbed him by the hair and yanked him through the crack.
Julia had no idea what was happening. She couldn't hear anything but the rush of air around her.
Then she landed on a hard marble floor.
She stumbled forward, letting go of Brody's arm.
"What's going on?" Brody shouted. "Hey!"
Julia looked around, too frightened to speak.
They were in a square room with stone walls.
A skylight overhead let in a beam of bright sunshine.
Two young men stood in front of them.
Both were tall and handsome and dressed in short robes.
"Chitons," Julia thought. She remembered learning that word in social studies class.
Chitons were simple garments worn by men and women in the ancient world.
The classes about ancient Greece and Rome had been among Julia's favorite parts of social studies last year.
But why were these guys wearing chitons?
What had happened to the high school?
"Where did the girl come from?" one guy asked. "She wasn't part of the plan."
The young man's face was so beautiful that it took Julia a moment to notice something odd.
He had only a single lock of brown hair hanging over his forehead.
The rest of his head was completely bald.
The second young man had curly blond hair and was as handsome as a movie star.
He leaned forward and poked Julia. "You, girl," he said. "What are you doing here?"
"Ow!" Julia yanked her arm away. "Stop poking me."
"What's going on?" Brody demanded again. "Where are we?"
"Silence, mortal." The blond man frowned at his friend.
"The girl was a mistake. Let's toss her back through."
"Are you certain you want to do that?" the bald guy said.
"Remember, this passage will close forever as soon as anyone passes back through it."
"I forgot about that." The blond guy looked annoyed.
"In that case, she'll have to stay.
We might need the passage again if this doesn't work out."
He glanced at Brody and looked him up and down.
"Are we being kidnapped?" Julia blurted out, still trying to figure out what was happening. "Who are you?"
The blond guy chuckled. "Do not be frightened, mortal. We won't hurt you.
Don't you recognize me? I am Hermes, messenger of the gods and friend to mortals."
"Mortals? Gods?" Brody said. "Huh?"
Hermes held up a hand to silence him.
"And this is my friend Caerus, god of luck and opportunity.
He saw the opportunity to help me humiliate Zeus by seeking a mortal champion in an unusual way."
Hermes and Caerus both laughed heartily. Julia caught a glimpse of movement and looked down.
Her eyes widened when she saw little golden wings on Hermes' sandals.
They were flapping gently. Could it be . . . ?
"I do have some influence over time and seasons," Caerus said, puffing out his chest proudly.
"Not that Zeus would ever notice—he treats me like a demigod.
He'll never figure out that I helped Hermes defeat him with a champion from the future."
"What? This is stupid," Brody said loudly. "Look, I'm tired of your dumb stories.
Why did you really grab me and drag me in here?"
"It's quite simple, my simple mortal friend," Hermes said.
"You see, the next Olympic Games will begin soon."
"The Olympics?" Julia echoed.
Caerus nodded. "And as usual, Zeus is already bragging about how his champion will easily defeat all others."
"Yes." Hermes snorted. "He's being quite annoying.
Just because he's king of the gods, he thinks nobody else can ever beat his hand-picked champion."
Brody looked confused. "Zeus?" he muttered. "Wait, that sounds familiar.
Is he from a video game or something?"
"No way," Julia said, staring at the two men. "You're not real.
None of this is real. Hermes is just a myth.
So is Zeus—all the ancient Greek gods are from myths."
"Greek gods? Like from social studies class?" Brody said with a snort.
"Yeah, right. These two are probably just a couple of jerks from Southbridge High.
They're trying to scare me before next week's game."
Hermes traded a look with Caerus. "What are they blathering on about?"
"Who cares," Caerus answered. He sounded bored again. "Let's move this along. I'm hungry."
"All right." Hermes gestured to Brody. "Come, mortal. I've arranged for you to stay with a local family." He glanced at Julia.
"I'm sure they can make room for the girl as well."
"No." Julia's logical mind still refused to accept what Hermes and Caerus—or whatever their names might be—were telling her.
"This isn't happening," she insisted. "We're not really in some temple in ancient Athens."
Hermes sounded impatient. "Aren't you listening to a word I say, mortal girl?"
"'Julia,'" she said. "That's my name, not 'mortal girl.'"
Hermes ignored her. "Of course we're not in Athens. We're in Olympia.
If you don't believe me, I'll prove it to you."
He grabbed Julia's arm. Julia tried to shake him off, but his grip was as strong as iron.
"Stop it," she yelled as he dragged her outside. "Let me go or I'll—whoa!"
She stared in amazement at the sun-drenched scene spread out before her.
It looked nothing like her hometown. It looked nothing like anywhere she'd ever seen, except in the pages of her social studies textbook.
Large, gleaming marble buildings lined with columns dotted the landscape, along with many smaller structures. A mountain rose in the background.
The only roads she could see were dirt ones, and there were no cars on them,
just people in chitons walking or riding donkeys or driving carts pulled by oxen or horses.
There were no power lines or billboards or tall buildings anywhere in sight.
Julia's mind whirled with confusion as she realized what it looked like—an ancient Greek city!
The temple was high on a hill, and it was a clear day, so Brody could see far into the distance.
And yet nothing he saw looked familiar. What had happened to the school and playing fields?
Where were the houses and his favorite fast-food place?
"What's going on?" he blurted out. "Where are we? Where's the gym?"
"The gymnasium? It's right over there, of course." Hermes pointed to the left.
But Brody still didn't see anything that looked like the school gym.
"It can't be," Julia murmured. "Are we really in ancient Olympia?"
"What?" Brody said. "There's no way we traveled through time."
Julia was staring at the city below. "What other explanation is there?"
Brody rolled his eyes. People thought he was dumb, but he wasn't dumb enough to believe what Hermes and Caerus were saying.
Only a freak like Julia would believe such a ridiculous story. Ancient Greece? Yeah, right!
Still, there was definitely something weird going on.
How could Brody make Hermes and Caerus admit it?
"I've got it!" He pointed at Hermes. "You're lying, and I can prove it."
Hermes raised one eyebrow. "Is that so?"
"Yes. If we're in Greece, how come you guys are speaking English?" Brody was proud of himself.
He might not be a genius, but he could figure things out when he needed to.
"On the contrary, we're speaking proper Greek," Caerus said.
"Hermes has powers over language and communication.
He has enabled you two to speak and understand Greek as if you were natives."
Hermes smirked. "That's very important. After all, speaking Greek is a prerequisite for entering the Games."
"Huh?" Brody didn't know what "prerequisite" meant.
Before he could ask, Caerus glanced at Hermes and pantomimed eating.
"Yes, this conversation is becoming dull," Hermes said to his friend.
He turned to Brody and Julia. "If you're still confused, your mortal hosts can explain everything."
"You'll be staying with the family that tends my temple."
Caerus waved a hand to indicate the temple they had just exited.
"Let's go," Hermes ordered.
Brody was more confused than ever. And being confused made him mad.
"I'm not going anywhere with you!" He gave Hermes a shove.
"You're not gods. You're just jerks and fakers!"
Suddenly a loud, chilling cry seemed to rip the air in two.
At the same moment, Hermes transformed into an enormous hawk and dived at Brody.
The hawk's giant talons stopped a hair's breadth from Brody's face.
Brody fell back, gasping with fear. A second later Hermes looked normal again.
"Learn this lesson well, mortal!" Hermes said sternly.
"Do not defy me! I can be either your friend or your enemy.
Trust me, you'd rather have me as a friend."
"Come." Caerus headed down the steps of his temple. "Your hosts are waiting."
Brody opened his mouth to argue again, but Hermes was still glaring at him. "Fine," Brody muttered.
Caerus led the way to a modest home halfway down the hill.
A bearded man wearing a purple robe stood in front.
"Welcome, Caerus," the man said, bowing. "We are honored by your presence. Yours as well, Hermes."
"Thank you," Hermes said. "Caerus tells me you've agreed to look after my champion until the Games."
"Of course." The man bowed to Brody. "My name is Nikolaos. My eldest son will take care of your needs."
A boy around Brody's age stepped outside.
Like the men he wore one of those strange-looking chitons. "Hi," he said shyly. "I'm Markos."
"Hey." Brody nodded. "I'm Brody." Julia stepped forward. "I'm Julia."
"Oh, right," Caerus said. "We'll also need you to look after the champion's . . . companion."
"A girl?" Nikolaos stared at Julia, and then shrugged.
"As you wish, Caerus. We can always use help in the kitchen."
Julia frowned, but she didn't say anything. Soon the two gods left.
"Take care of our guests, Markos," Nikolaos said.
"I have important work to do at the temple."
"Yes, Father," Markos said as Nikolaos left.
Brody quickly glanced at Julia. "I'm going back to the temple.
Caerus and Hermes said we could get home through that crack in the wall, so that's what I'm doing."
"What?" Markos looked alarmed. "You can't leave! Hermes will be angry."
Brody shrugged. "So what?"
Markos shook his head. "Hermes may seem good-natured, but he is still a god.
As you know, gods aren't like mortals, and they think nothing of punishing us at their whim."
"How would I know that?" Brody said. "Up until a few minutes ago, I didn't know gods really existed."
Markos looked confused. "What do you mean?"
"Listen, Markos." Julia jumped in. "What's all this talk about Brody being Hermes' champion?
And are the Olympic Games really starting soon?"
Her questions tumbled out. "Is Hermes really a god? I mean, for real?"
Markos stared at her. "You ask many questions for a girl."
Julia looked annoyed. Brody almost laughed, but he wanted to know the answer to her questions too. "Just answer her," he told Markos.
"Yes, the Olympic Games begin soon," Markos said.
"Every four years all the gods compete to see who can find the best mortal athlete."
He shook his head. "But you must already know that."
"No, we don't," Julia said. "We came from the future."
"The future? I don't understand."
"Wait . . ." Brody had just realized what Markos meant.
"So Hermes thinks I'm the best athlete around?"
Markos shrugged. "I suppose so."
"And he wants me to be in the Olympics?" Brody liked the sound of that. "Cool!"
But Julia was clearly worried. "We can't stay here," she told Brody. "We have to find a way home!"
"Why the big rush?" Brody grinned. "If I get to be an Olympic champion, maybe I'll stick around!"
"Here, try this on," Markos' sister murmured.
Julia took the chiton that the older girl held out.
As soon as the kids had entered the house, Helene had taken Julia away.
First she'd brought Julia into the kitchen and given her some figs to eat.
Then she'd taken Julia to change clothes.
"Why can't I wear my own clothes?" Julia glanced down at her jeans and T-shirt.
"Father says we're supposed to help you and Brody blend in so Zeus doesn't notice you," Helene said.
"If you insist on wearing such strange garments, you won't be allowed out of the house."
Julia didn't like the sound of that. She put on the chiton and a pair of leather sandals.
When the girls returned to the courtyard, Brody and Markos were already there.
Brody was dressed in a short chiton, like the one Markos wore.
"This is stupid," Brody was saying loudly.
"If any of the guys on the football team saw me wearing a dress—"
"How are they going to see you?" Julia snapped at him.
"In case you forgot, Brody, we're in ancient Greece!"
Before Brody could respond, Hermes appeared in a blast of light.
"Good, they've found you some proper clothing," he said.
"Let's go. It's time to start your training."
"I'll come along, if you don't mind." Markos bowed to Hermes.
"My father ordered me not to let your champion out of my sight."
"Good, good. Come along then, boy," Hermes said.
Julia stepped forward. "I'm coming too."
Markos hesitated, but Hermes shrugged. "If having your companion along makes you run faster, Brody, she may come."
"I don't care if she comes or not," Brody said.
But Hermes was already striding toward the exit, the wings on his sandals fluttering with excitement.
"I'm coming," Julia whispered to Brody with a frown.
"We still need to figure out how to escape.
And we can't do that if I'm stuck in the house."
"Escape? Why would I want to escape?" Brody flexed his muscles. "I'm going to be an Olympic champion!"
He hurried after Hermes. With a sigh Julia followed.
Olympia's gymnasium was a long, low building with a huge, grassy courtyard.
At least a dozen men and boys were exercising in the courtyard, tossing spears, stretching, or racing down a marked track.
Several other gods were there too.
"Who's that?" Julia asked, staring at a god with flaming red hair.
Hermes followed her gaze. "Ares, of course.
Don't let him hear that you don't recognize him—he's quite vain."
"Ares, the god of war?" Julia couldn't help being impressed.
After learning about the gods in school, it was actually pretty cool to see them in real life.
Hermes wasn't paying attention to her anymore. He was focused on his new champion.
"Now, what is your best distance, my boy?" he asked Brody.
"Best distance for what?" Brody asked.
"Running, of course." Hermes sounded impatient. "Every mortal athlete is better at some events than others.
So, what's your specialty? The stadion, the diaulos? Perhaps the dolichos?"
Julia remembered that these were the names of different footraces, but Brody looked totally confused.
"Brody isn't really a runner," she told Hermes.
"I mean, he's not on the track team or anything like that."
"Track?" Brody made a face. "No way! Those guys are nerds. I play football."
"Foot?" Markos said, looking down. "Ball?"
"What?" Hermes frowned at Brody in confusion.
"But I saw you running like the wind.
I watched you outpace the other mortals.
Are you telling me that you are not a runner?"
"Sure, I run all the time," Brody said.
"I'm fast, like you said. That's why I make so many touchdowns."
"Touchdowns?" Markos echoed. "What are they?"
"Duh, it's how you score." Brody shrugged.
"Haven't you guys ever seen a football game?"
Julia poked him in the arm. "Duh, of course, they haven't," she said.
"Football wasn't invented back then. I mean now."
Hermes still looked a bit upset about Brody's lack of running experience.
"Let's stop wasting time," he said impatiently.
Under his breath he muttered, "We may have even more training to do than I expected."
Julia glanced at the athletes in the courtyard again. "So which event will Brody enter?"
"All of them, of course," Hermes said.
"But we'll begin with the simplest—the footraces."
He pointed to the track and told Brody to run to the far end and back.
Julia and Markos watched as Brody repeated the course again and again, until he was dripping with sweat.
"Is it time for a break yet?" Brody asked after his eleventh run.
"Hermes! There you are," a voice called out.
Julia looked up to see another god striding toward them.
"Dionysus, you rascal," Hermes exclaimed. "What are you doing here?
Have you decided to enter the Games this time?"
"Of course not. What would I know of athletics?"
Dionysus laughed heartily, patting his plump belly.
"I'm in search of some good food and drink, and for pleasant company to join me."
"You've found the pleasant company, my friend," Hermes responded.
"And I'm ready to take a break for some good food and drink. Training a champion is exhausting."
Dionysus eyed Brody. "So this is your champion, hmm?
I hear you found him in the most distant reaches of Greece."
"Something like that." Hermes winked at Brody.
"Now let's go find that food and drink."
Without another word to the kids, Hermes headed off with Dionysus.
"Whew!" Brody collapsed on the ground and mopped his brow.
"Hermes is worse than my football coach."
Markos nodded sympathetically. "It's difficult for the gods to remember the limits of human endurance.
I think Hermes was pleased with your performance, though, Brody."
"How could you tell?" Julia asked.
Markos shrugged. "Well, Hermes didn't kill him!"
The next morning Brody was eating breakfast when a hawk landed in the courtyard. It quickly transformed into Hermes.
"Come, my champion," Hermes said to Brody.
"I'm taking you to the agora to show you off."
"Show him off?" Julia said. "I thought we were supposed to blend in so Zeus doesn't notice Brody."
Hermes eyed her. "You talk a great deal for a mortal girl. But you're partly correct.
I don't want Zeus to know where I'm keeping my champion.
Zeus might decide to tamper with him when I'm not here."
"Huh?" Brody looked up from his bread and fruit.
"What do you mean, tamper with me?"
"Never mind that. You're under my protection, boy." Hermes patted him on the shoulder.
"I can keep you safe, and also show you off in public."
"Okay," Julia said. "But listen, I've been thinking about that time passage we came through.
It sounds like it could easily close up again. Could we end up trapped here forever?"
"Forever?" Brody echoed. He didn't like the sound of that.
Ancient Greece was pretty cool so far—he was looking forward to competing in the Games.
But he already missed TV and video games and playing football.
"You don't need to worry about the time passage," Hermes said.
"Caerus assures me the passage should remain stable at least through the Games.
After that, you're welcome to return home."
"Do you promise?" Julia asked. "You'll let us go right after the Games?"
"Of course." Hermes shrugged. "Now come to the agora."
The agora was Olympia's central square. Dozens of merchants and farmers were there selling goods like honey, fish, silk, and gems.
People and gods wandered around shopping and chatting.
"Is Zeus here?" Julia asked Hermes.
"I don't see him. But look." Hermes pointed to someone in the distance.
"There's his lovely wife. Let's go and say hello."
"Zeus has a wife?" Brody asked Julia.
She gave him a scornful look. "Didn't you pay attention in social studies?
Zeus' wife is Hera. She's a very powerful goddess."
"And a very scary one," Markos whispered.
"Be careful not to say anything that might insult her."
Hera was a tall, stately woman with a sharp chin and even sharper black eyes.
"Greetings, Hermes. Who are these young mortals?"
Hermes yanked Brody forward. "I'm pleased to introduce my champion for the Games.
Say hello to the queen of the gods, Brody."
"Hi," Brody said. "Nice to meet you."
"Brody . . . ," Hera repeated. "What sort of name is that? It doesn't sound Greek to me."
Hermes squeezed Brody's shoulder to stop him from responding.
"Perhaps it does not sound Greek," Hermes said quickly.
"But as you can hear, the boy speaks Greek as well as you and I do."
"Hmm." Hera stared at Brody, her eyes suspicious.
"So, Hera," Hermes said innocently, "I hear Zeus has found himself another impressive champion.
Do you know whether this mortal hero has yet arrived in Olympia?"
Hera stiffened. "I have better things to do than keep track of Zeus' business."
"Of course you do." Hermes smiled. "Still, you must be as curious as the rest of us. What's the fellow's name again? Alexandros?"
"Alcides," another goddess said, walking over to join them. "Zeus' hero is named Alcides."
"Greetings, Athena." Hermes bowed, and Hera nodded coolly.
"Athena?" Julia whispered, elbowing Brody. "Wow! She's the goddess of wisdom. She was always my favorite goddess."
"You're such a nerd!" he said, laughing.
The gods were all exchanging rumors about Alcides.
"He's said to be the strongest mortal of his generation," Hermes told Athena.
"It's hard to know what is true," Athena replied. She sounded disapproving.
"I'm afraid you all exaggerate your heroes' abilities so greatly.
The Games are meant to be an honest contest," she went on.
"Not some silly competition full of deception and cheating."
"Don't be a spoilsport, Athena," Hermes said.
"Our gossip and mischief are just good fun. And I will have even more fun when my champion defeats Zeus' hero!"
Brody grinned. "Don't worry, I'll do it," he bragged.
Hermes clapped him on the back. "That's the spirit, boy!"
Hera eyed Brody with scorn. "We'll see about that.
If you'll excuse me, I have things to do."
She stalked off. Athena wandered away too.
As soon as the goddesses were gone, two more gods rushed over.
One was a muscular young man with wavy dark hair and mischievous golden eyes.
The other was a pretty young woman with a bow slung over one slim shoulder.
She had the same wild, dark hair and golden eyes as the young man.
"Apollo, Artemis," Hermes greeted them. "How are you, my friends?"
"We heard you found your champion," Artemis said, staring curiously at Brody. "Why, he's very impressive."
"Thanks." Brody puffed up his chest.
"Hera seemed impressed too," Hermes said. "Though I suspect she's much more concerned about Zeus' champion."
"Ah, the mighty Alcides," Apollo said with a laugh. "Have you seen him yet?"
"No one has seen him yet," Artemis said.
"According to the rumors, Zeus is keeping him hidden in the hills until Zeus is ready to present him."
Hermes smirked. "You know Zeus. He likes to make a dramatic entrance."
"Yes," Apollo agreed. "He also must know that everyone will be looking for ways to beat him in the Games."
Brody spoke up. "Don't worry, I'll beat his hero.
I scored more touchdowns last season than anyone in the history of my middle school!"
The gods stared at him, looking amused and puzzled.
Then Hermes chuckled. "Perhaps the boy is right," he said.
"Perhaps Zeus failed to find a suitable hero this time.
That could be another reason Zeus is keeping Alcides hidden."
"Perhaps." Artemis sounded doubtful.
"But I won't believe it until I see you and your champion setting off on the victory tour of Greece after the Games."
Brody's eyes lit up. "There's a victory tour after the Games?" he said. "Cool!"
But Julia was horrified by the news. "What do you mean?" she asked Artemis.
The goddess shrugged. "Just what I said. The Olympic champion always travels with his sponsor afterward."
"The tour gets mortals quite excited," Hermes added with a grin.
He looked at Brody. "You'll enjoy seeing more of the world, won't you, boy?"
"Sure!" Brody said. "It sounds like the parade after the Super Bowl!"
Julia was staring at Hermes in alarm.
"But you said we could go home right after the Games."
"Of course you can," Hermes told Julia soothingly. "Don't worry so much, mortal girl."
Julia glanced away, trying to calm down.
What if Hermes had been lying about letting them go home? What if they got stuck here forever?
"This could be bad!" she whispered to Brody in a panic.
"What are you talking about?" Brody asked.
Julia kept her voice low. "What if Hermes is planning to keep us here?
He and Caerus made it sound like the passage will eventually close. We could be stuck here forever!"
"Whoa!" Brody said.
For a second Julia thought she'd finally made him realize how serious this situation was.
Then she saw that he was staring across the agora.
"Who's that?" he blurted out. Another goddess was approaching them.
She was blond and gorgeous, with big blue eyes.
"Greetings, Aphrodite," Hermes called. "Come and meet my champion!"
Aphrodite held out one pale, slim hand. "Hello, champion. It's a pleasure."
"Uh, guh . . . ," Brody said. "I mean, me too. I mean, hi! I'm Brody."
"Brody," Aphrodite said with a musical laugh. "What a charming name."
Julia moaned to herself. She could tell that Brody was already in love.
Why were boys so easily distracted by a pretty face?
"Have any of you seen Zeus' champion yet?" Aphrodite asked the other gods.
"I hear he's very handsome. And strong."
"Nobody has seen him," Artemis replied. "Zeus is hiding him in the hills."
"That reminds me." Hermes grabbed Brody by the shoulder. "It's time for training. Let's go."
"Are you sure we can't stay?" Brody was still staring at Aphrodite.
Hermes pulled Brody away so fast that Julia and Markos had to run to keep up.
Once again the gymnasium was filled with athletes. Hermes ordered Brody to start stretching.
Brody dropped to the ground and touched his toes.
"What are we working on today, Coach?" he asked.
"We need to build your endurance for the dolichos and the hoplite," Hermes replied.
"They are the longer and more difficult races, and I wasn't impressed with how quickly you became tired yesterday."
"Quickly?" Brody sounded wounded. "You made me run for two hours straight!"
"We should get out of the way," Markos said to Julia.
"It's strange enough to have a girl here.
We don't want anyone to think you're trying to compete or something."
He laughed as if that was the funniest thing he'd ever imagined.
Julia was getting tired of all the comments about girls.
"It's not as if I'm the only girl here," she said, pointing.
Markos shook his head. "That's not a girl—it's a goddess," he said. "It's Demeter training her champion."
"Whatever." Julia followed Markos to some benches. They sat and watched Brody's workout.
After a while Caerus arrived and waved to Hermes.
"Take a quick rest, boy," Hermes told Brody. "I'll be back soon."
He hurried off to talk to Caerus. Brody collapsed on the bench beside Julia, huffing and puffing.
As soon as Markos hurried off to get Brody some water, Julia turned to Brody.
"Listen, we need to talk," she said quickly.
"If Hermes isn't going to let us go after the Games, there's no reason to stick around.
We should try to escape as soon as possible."
Brody didn't respond. He was peering toward the entrance.
"Do you think Aphrodite has a champion?" he asked.
"Maybe she'll bring him here to train. Do you think she will?"
Just then Markos returned with the water. He saw Brody staring at Aphrodite.
"Forget her," he warned Brody. "She's beautiful. But she's a goddess."
Brody looked disappointed. "So I guess goddesses never, like, date mortals, huh?"
Markos blinked. "Of course they do. But it never turns out very well for the mortal."
He glanced around and lowered his voice.
"According to the latest local gossip, Hera is very eager to see Zeus' new hero humiliated at the Games.
Alcides is rumored to be Zeus' child born of a mortal woman.
And we all know how jealous and vengeful Hera can be."
"We do?" Brody looked confused. "Okay, whatever. Back to Aphrodite, I—"
At that moment Hermes rushed over, looking excited.
"Apollo just arrived with his champion," he said.
"He's challenged us to a javelin contest. Come—it'll be good training."
"Javelin? I've never done that before." Brody shrugged.
"But it's just throwing a stick, right? How hard can it be?"
He followed Hermes.
Julia watched them go. "I can't believe Brody's being so stupid about all this!" she complained to Markos.
Markos gave her an uneasy glance. "Perhaps we should watch the contest in silence."
Halfway across the gymnasium, Brody and Hermes met up with Apollo and a tall teenager with broad shoulders and dark hair.
The two boys picked up javelins. Apollo's champion handled his confidently.
Brody fumbled with his javelin at first, but within moments he looked almost as comfortable as the other boy.
Julia couldn't help being impressed. Brody really was a good athlete.
"Too bad he doesn't have much brainpower to go with his athletic abilities," she thought.
"Go!" Hermes called.
Both athletes tossed their javelins. Julia blinked as the javelins flew through the air. Something about them looked strange…
She gasped as both javelins transformed into enormous hissing snakes.
They spun around in midair and flew straight back toward the boys!
"Look out!" someone yelled.
The voice sounded like Julia's, but Brody wasn't sure.
He couldn't take his eyes off the huge snake flying toward his face.
Its mouth was wide open, and its fangs looked huge and razor-sharp.
A sickly yellow liquid dripped from the pointy ends.
Beside Brody, Apollo's champion stood frozen in place, staring at the snakes with a terrified look on his face.
Brody wasn't afraid of snakes. He'd even kept one as a pet for a while until he'd forgotten to put the lid back on the tank and it had escaped.
But he didn't like the look of these snakes.
Especially with that stuff dripping from the fangs.
"Duck!" he yelled, leaping sideways and tackling the other athlete, who was still just standing there like a dope.
Both boys tumbled to the ground. The snakes flew over them, hissing loudly.
Then came the sound of loud, cackling laughter.
As he sat up, Brody saw Ares striding toward them.
"It seems you did find a good champion, Hermes!" Ares declared.
"You're quick, boy." He bent down and clapped Brody on the back so hard that Brody almost fell over again.
Brody stared at him for a second and then laughed.
"Thanks, dude," he said. "That snake thing was cool. Can all you gods do stuff like that?"
By then Hermes and Apollo had run over to the boys, along with Julia and Markos.
"Are you all right, Brody?" Markos asked, his face pale and anxious. "That was close!"
"Yes." Hermes scowled at Ares. "A little too close."
"I'm fine." Brody jumped to his feet. "No big deal. It was just a joke."
"A joke that could have killed you," Julia said. "I'm guessing those snakes are venomous."
"Oh, they are," Ares said with a smirk. "Extremely venomous."
Brody shrugged. "Okay. But they didn't bite us. Like I said, no big deal."
Apollo was glaring at Ares too. "It might be a big deal if it happens again," he snapped.
"Is that a threat, sun god?" Suddenly Ares' smile disappeared.
He clenched his fists and stuck his face in the other god's face.
"I don't make threats," Apollo retorted, his eyes flashing with fury. "I take action."
"Boys, boys." Artemis strolled over, looking amused by the gods' bickering.
"You're taking this far too seriously," she said.
"Shouldn't we all be saving our best tricks for Zeus' champion?"
"Don't tell me what to do, sister," Apollo muttered.
But he took a step back from Ares and looked less angry.
As the gods continued bickering with each other, Julia pulled Brody away.
"No matter what the gods say, Alcides obviously isn't their only target," she whispered.
"Markos told me the gods constantly try to sabotage each others' champions.
Now are you ready to escape? It's not exactly safe for you."
Brody shook off her hand. "Don't be such a wimp," he said.
"Like I said, it was just a prank. My teammates and I do stuff like that all the time in the locker room."
"You throw deadly reptiles at each other?" Julia said sarcastically.
Brody shrugged. "Why is she making such a big deal about this?" he thought. He could handle a few pranks.
If he couldn't handle them, he'd never survive being on the football team back home!
Hermes hurried over, still looking annoyed. "Back to work, boy," he told Brody.
"We must show Ares that his ridiculous stunt hasn't rattled you. Grab another javelin and let's try again."
Hermes worked Brody hard for the next couple of hours.
Finally, after a particularly fast sprint, Hermes smiled.
"Well done," he said. "That's enough for today. I have other business to attend to.
Go wash up, and then Markos will take you home."
Markos pointed Brody toward a bathing chamber nearby.
Brody was dismayed to find only a bare room with a mosaic floor, a stone tub, and no warm water at all.
Still, it was a very hot day, and the cool water felt pretty good.
He rinsed off the sweat and wrapped a towel around himself.
As he reached for his grungy chiton, the door opened.
"Excuse me!" Brody started to call out a warning.
"I'm—oh!" Brody gulped as Aphrodite slipped into the room.
"Greetings, Brody," the goddess of beauty purred.
"I was very impressed with your training today."
"You . . . you were?" Brody said. His face flushed.
"I didn't even know you were watching."
Smiling, she came closer. "Oh, I was watching," she said.
"Would you do me the honor of taking a stroll with me and explaining how you came to be so fast and strong?"
"Sure!" Brody blurted out. "I mean, yeah, that sounds cool. Whatever."
"Wonderful." Aphrodite beamed at him. Then she pulled something from behind her back.
"Here's a fresh chiton. Why don't you put it on? I'll wait for you outside."
"Uh, thanks." Brody took the garment, hardly believing that this was happening.
Back home, he'd never even had a girlfriend yet.
But here in ancient Greece, an actual goddess was practically throwing herself at him!
Being an Olympic athlete was even more awesome than Brody had expected.
"Don't be long, mortal champion," Aphrodite said with a wink.
"I'm really looking forward to our stroll."
As she headed for the door, it opened again. This time Athena looked in.
"There you are," Athena said to Aphrodite. "I've been looking for you. I heard that you and Hera were seen—"
Her gray eyes suddenly went wide. "Drop that garment, boy!" she commanded.
"Huh?" Brody said. "Why?"
Athena reached him in three long strides and snatched the chiton out of his hands.
"I said drop it!" she shouted. "It's poisoned!"
"And then Athena started yelling at Aphrodite."
Brody's voice was shaky as he told his story.
"I just put on my old chiton and sandals and got out of there."
Julia had always seen Brody looking cocky and confident.
But right now he seemed upset and unsure of himself.
He'd come rushing out of the bath ten minutes earlier, babbling about almost being poisoned.
She and Markos had led him to a private spot outside the gymnasium, where he'd told them the whole story of Aphrodite's visit.
"Wow," Julia said. "And Athena mentioned Zeus' wife, Hera?"
"Yeah," Brody said. "She seemed to think Aphrodite and Hera were working together or something."
"That makes sense," Julia said, thinking back on the Greek myths she'd read.
"I mean, it sounds like something Hera might do.
It reminds me of the story about the Shirt of Nessus."
"The shirt of what?" Brody looked blank.
"Never mind, I'll tell you about it some other time," Julia said.
"But what about trying to escape? Are you ready now?"
Brody thought for a second. "Maybe," he said. "But how?"
"We need to find a way to sneak into the Temple of Caerus." Julia glanced at Markos. "Will you help us?"
She expected him to say no. To her surprise, however, Markos looked thoughtful.
"Did Athena truly say that Hera and Aphrodite were working together?" he asked. "Because that would be quite unusual."
"Why?" Brody said. "Wouldn't anyone want to work with Aphrodite?"
Julia looked at him in astonishment. "She just tried to kill you, dummy! You can't still have a crush on her!"
Looking unhappy, Brody shrugged.
Markos looked troubled now. "Both Hermes and my father have ordered me to keep you safe," he told Brody.
"But if Hera is after you, there is no safety for you in Olympia. Or anywhere in Greece, for that matter.
Once Hera develops a grudge against someone, she won't stop until she's destroyed him."
He shuddered. "Even Zeus himself is not always safe."
"That's why we need to get home," Julia said. "Back to our own time."
She looked at Markos. Would he help them? Or would he tell Hermes what they were planning?
She and Brody had told Markos about the time passage in the temple on their first night in Greece.
But Markos hadn't said much in response. Julia wasn't sure he believed they'd really come from the future.
Finally Markos nodded. "I will try to help," he said.
"In return, I ask only that you not tell Hermes that I did so.
If he learns of my help, he will be angry and could even take out that anger on my father or the rest of my family."
"Don't worry," Julia said. "Once we get out of here, we're planning never to see Hermes again.
Now listen, I've been thinking about this, and I have some ideas about how we could get away. . ."
The three of them spent the rest of the day concocting their plan. By dinnertime Julia was feeling confident.
Hermes and Caerus entered the courtyard and took their seats at the table, just as they'd done the evening before.
Julia watched from the doorway as Hermes started talking to Brody about his plans for training.
Finally he turned away to talk with Markos' father.
Julia hurried over to serve Brody a second helping of grilled fish.
"You know what to do, right?" she whispered, glad for once that the girls and women of the household waited on the men and boys.
Brody shoved some figs in his mouth. "You know, I'll miss some of this food," he mumbled.
"Shh!" Julia shot a worried look at Hermes.
But Markos' father was telling a joke, and Hermes and Caerus were chuckling and paying no attention to Brody.
Julia thought the meal would never end. But at last the two gods stood up from the table.
"We must go," Hermes announced. He looked at Brody.
"Be ready early tomorrow, my champion. We have much to do."
"Okay," Brody said.
Julia was relieved. Hermes and Caerus always went to the agora to hang out with their god friends after dinner.
She hoped they would stay away long enough for the kids' plan to work.
"Oops!" she said, intentionally spilling water on Brody.
"Hey!" Brody blustered. "Oh! I mean, um, I'd better change clothes."
Julia glared at him. It was a good thing he was talented at football, because he wasn't much of an actor!
Luckily Markos was much better. He turned to Julia. "Fetch us a dry chiton immediately."
"Of course," Julia said. She rushed off.
Moments later all three met outside the house.
"That was pretty slick," Brody said with a grin.
"Do you think we convinced your family, Markos?"
Markos cast an anxious look at the house. "We should hurry," he said.
"I'll be missed if I don't return soon."
"You don't have to come with us," Julia told him.
"It's not as if we'll get lost on the way to the temple."
She gestured to the pale stone building, which was glowing in the moonlight above them. "We can see it from here."
"It's all right," Markos said. "I should come along in case you run into any trouble."
The three of them started for the path to the temple.
Brody was in the lead as they rounded a turn.
"Almost there," he said over his shoulder. "I think there's—ah!"
He jumped back, startled, as something burst from a bush beside the trail.
There was a flapping of wings and a loud caw!
Brody laughed with relief. "Oh, man," he said. "It's just a bird."
"A raven," Markos said, smiling.
"Let's keep moving," Julia said, pushing ahead.
"With any luck we should be there in less than—"
She gasped as a tall form stepped out of the shadows just ahead.
"Good evening, young mortals," Hera said. "Going somewhere?"
Brody stared at Hera and froze. Markos looked nervous too, but he stepped forward and bowed deeply to her.
"Greetings, Queen of the Heights and Goddess of Cattle," he said.
"It's our good fortune that we've encountered you this evening.
We're searching for a calf that wandered away from the herd and got lost."
Brody was confused. Why was Markos blabbing about cows?
Hera was a goddess—the most powerful one around according to Julia, who seemed to know everything about that stuff.
Why would someone like Hera care about some lost calf?
Especially if she had truly been trying to poison Brody earlier.
To Brody's surprise, Hera's stern features relaxed into an expression of concern.
"I see," she said. "Our meeting is most fortunate indeed, young mortals.
Where did you last see the unfortunate creature?"
"That way." Markos pointed down the hillside.
"Perhaps I could show you while my friends continue to search in this direction?"
"Yes, of course." Hera barely glanced at Brody and Julia before turning her attention back to Markos. "Lead the way, boy."
Markos and Hera disappeared into the darkness.
Brody stared after them, still confused. "What was that all about?" he asked.
"Didn't you hear Markos? Hera is the goddess of cattle," Julia reminded Brody.
"That seemed strange to me when I read it in our textbook. But I guess it's true.
Markos must have guessed she'd want to help a lost calf."
"The goddess of cattle?" Brody scratched his head.
"I thought she was the queen of the gods."
"She is. Most of them are the gods of more than one thing. Like Hermes, for instance.
He's the messenger of the gods, but he's also the god of travelers and literature and I think sports . . . Oh, never mind."
Julia grabbed Brody's arm. "We've got to get to the temple before Hera comes back."
She bit her lip and glanced in the direction Hera had gone.
"I just hope she doesn't figure out that Markos was lying to her to help us escape. Otherwise . . ."
"Otherwise what?" Brody asked.
"Never mind. Just come on."
Brody was getting tired of Julia's "never minds," but she was already hurrying up the path, so all he could do was follow.
When they neared the temple, Julia stopped so abruptly that Brody almost bumped into her. "I'm walking here," he complained.
"Shh!" She pointed. "There's a guard."
Brody peered at the figure slumped at the top of the temple steps.
"Looks like he's asleep," he whispered. "We can just sneak past."
"Are you sure?" Julia asked. "What if he wakes up and catches us?"
Brody shrugged. "He won't if we're quiet."
Without waiting for an answer, he started forward.
He moved lightly but quickly, as if carrying a football through a tough defensive line of football players.
Julia's footsteps were louder, but the guard didn't wake up, and soon the kids were inside.
"I think the passage is back there," Julia whispered, pointing to an inner chamber.
Brody nodded and hurried in. He smiled when he caught a glimpse of sunshine through the crack in the wall.
A bird flew past, and Brody could see his school's playing fields and the familiar row of buildings on the far side.
"Awesome," he said. "What are we waiting for? Let's go home!"
When Brody neared the crack in the wall, it seemed to pull him forward.
He was almost close enough to step through it when he heard the clatter of footsteps behind him.
"Halt!" an angry voice shouted.
Brody spun around. It was Hermes!
Caerus entered the temple right behind him, dragging a frightened-looking Markos. Then Apollo sauntered in, smirking.
"I warned you, Hermes," Apollo said. "It seems your mighty champion isn't quite as loyal as you thought."
Julia gasped. "How did you find us?" she cried.
"Oh! It was the raven, wasn't it?"
Apollo nodded. "One of my minions. I've had the birds keep an eye on some of the competition.
When that raven saw what was going on, of course, it alerted me immediately."
"And Apollo alerted me immediately," Hermes said, his voice shaking with fury.
"We found the other boy on our way here."
He gestured briefly at Markos before turning his full fury back on Brody. "How could you betray me?"
Brody swallowed hard. Hermes seemed really angry. "Um . . . it was Julia's idea?"
Julia didn't say anything. She looked scared, which surprised Brody.
Usually she seemed pretty brave, especially for a nerd.
Hermes glared at Julia, and then spun to face the other gods.
"My sincere thanks for alerting me to this, Apollo," he said in a formal tone. "I appreciate the gesture of sportsmanship."
"Sportsmanship?" Caerus let out a snort.
"I would say it's more likely he just wanted to silence the bragging you were doing down at the agora, Hermes."
"Perhaps, perhaps." Apollo still looked amused by the whole situation.
"Or perhaps I don't want to lose a promising champion.
Better to listen to Hermes' bragging than Zeus' bragging." He shrugged.
"What your champion lacks in intelligence, Hermes, he makes up for in strength and speed."
"Thanks, dude," Brody said. Then he scowled. "Wait—you were insulting me!"
"Silence!" Hermes thundered. "Now get over here, boy. At once!"
Brody hesitated, glancing over his shoulder at the time passage. Then he looked at Julia.
The crack was so close—he and Julia might be able to jump through before Hermes could stop him. Should they try it?
Hermes seemed to guess what he was thinking. "Don't you dare," he warned.
He spun around, grabbed Markos, and dragged him forward.
"If you take one step toward that passage, I'll see to it that Markos and his entire family suffer the consequences!"
Julia was so terrified she could hardly breathe. Still, she didn't hesitate.
"Stop!" she cried, leaping away from the time passage. "It's not Markos' fault. We'll stay."
She glanced at Brody, but he appeared to be frozen in place. Julia couldn't believe it.
Was he thinking about stepping through the passage despite Hermes' threats against Markos and his family?
A second later she let out a sigh of relief as Brody stepped away from the passage too.
"It's cool," he said. "I didn't really want to go anyway.
I was totally looking forward to being in the Olympics."
"You have a funny way of showing it, boy," Hermes snarled, though he sounded slightly less angry already.
"Come. We need to have a talk about loyalty."
As Hermes dragged Brody out of the room, Julia glanced at Markos.
He'd taken a few steps forward and was staring through the passage.
Julia glanced through at her own world just in time to see a car drive by.
"Oh!" Markos exclaimed, pointing at it. "What was that?"
"It's a car," Julia said. "It's like a wagon, except you don't need a horse or ox to pull it."
Markos looked impressed.
"Never mind. Let's step away from the time passage, shall we?"
Caerus herded Markos and Julia into the outer room of the temple.
The guard, now awake, was waiting there.
"I'm so sorry, master," he said, cowering in front of Caerus.
"I swear upon my life, I've never fallen asleep on the job before.
It must have been some trick. Perhaps the mortals enlisted the aid of Hypnos or—"
"Silence!" Caerus ordered, sounding annoyed. "I might forgive your incompetence just this once, mortal fool.
But if you value your family and your sanity, you'll guard this chamber with your life from now on."
"Of course. Thank you, Caerus!" The guard said quickly, bowing.
"No mortal will get past me again!" As he turned away, he glared at the kids.
Julia's heart sank. It was obvious that nobody was going to be able to sneak into the temple again before the Games.
Besides, Hermes was aware of their plans now.
If she and Brody escaped, Markos and his family would certainly suffer.
"I guess we're stuck," she thought with a shiver.
"We'll just have to hope that Hermes will keep his word and let us go after the Games."
The next day Julia sat on the bench beside Markos.
They were watching Brody's training session. He had already spent a couple of hours running and tossing the javelin.
Now he was about to start practicing the long jump required for the pentathlon.
That was a competition in which athletes competed in five different events.
"Hermes is working Brody harder than ever today," Julia observed.
"Does that mean he's still mad at us for trying to escape?"
Markos looked thoughtful. "I doubt it," he said.
"I mean, of course he was angry at the time.
You're lucky he didn't turn us all into frogs or something." He shuddered.
"However, I'm sure he's mostly forgotten about it by now."
"Really?" Julia winced as Brody made his first attempt at the long jump and landed with a splat.
"But Hermes kept saying how Brody betrayed him."
"Yes," Markos said. "But remember, the gods view us as mortals view dogs.
Would you really bother to hold a grudge against a dog?"
Julia shrugged. She didn't like being compared to a dog, but she knew Markos didn't mean anything bad by it.
"Thanks again for distracting Hera," she said. "That was really brave."
Markos bowed his head. "You're welcome. Thanks for helping me in turn.
You two could have easily escaped and left me to my fate."
"We'd never do that. You're our friend." Julia smiled at him.
Just then Hermes let out a shout of annoyance.
Julia turned to look and saw that Brody had just attempted another jump.
He was sprawled on the ground, panting and looking frustrated.
"You're hopeless, boy!" Hermes cried. "How do you expect to win the pentathlon with that sort of performance?"
Artemis and Apollo were watching from nearby, where their own athletes were boxing.
Apollo snickered. "Do you really expect to beat Zeus' champion with that, Hermes?" he called.
Hermes scowled at him. "Nobody asked your opinion, Apollo," he snapped.
He spun around and pointed at Brody. "Again!"
Brody groaned and climbed to his feet. "Okay," he said.
"But we never had to do anything like this at football practice."
Markos turned to Julia. "Do you think he'll improve?" He sounded worried.
"Probably," Julia replied. "He's actually a very talented athlete.
I mean, he picked up javelin throwing in about five minutes, remember?
He beat Apollo's guy three times out of five." She grimaced.
"That's not counting the time the javelins turned into snakes."
Markos sighed. "I hope you're right." His gaze wandered around the field.
"Because some of the other champions are looking pretty good. Not to mention Alcides.
If that guy is even half as incredible as Zeus is claiming, none of the other athletes will have a chance."
"Yeah." Julia didn't like to think about that.
It was true that Brody was a good athlete. Maybe even a great one.
Not that she'd ever tell him that—his ego was already big enough.
But this was the Olympic Games, not a high school football game.
And Brody was just a kid. What if he couldn't live up to Hermes' expectations?
What if he couldn't beat a bunch of Greek champions who'd probably been training for this their whole lives?
What would happen then to Brody—and to Julia?
She cringed as Brody jumped again and Hermes let out a howl of dismay.
She muttered to Markos, "I just hope Brody gets better fast."
"Wow, today's training was intense." Brody collapsed onto a bench in Markos' courtyard that evening. Every muscle in his body ached.
"You did well, Brody." Markos sat beside him.
"Hermes seemed pleased with your speed by the end of the session. And your long jump was much improved."
"But not improved enough," Julia said. "Did you see Athena's champion?
He jumped much farther than you, Brody."
"Julia!" At that moment Markos' older sister hurried toward Julia.
"We need your help in the kitchen. The men are hungry."
"That's right." Brody smirked at Julia. "We're hungry. Go cook our food, woman."
Julia gritted her teeth. "I'm busy," she told Helene. "I'll be there in a minute."
Helene frowned. "Please hurry. We're expecting Hermes and Caerus for dinner again, and Father wants them to be pleased with our hospitality."
"You should go to the kitchen," Markos said to Julia as Helene disappeared.
"Hermes will be angry if you are not following the customs here."
"I'm going," Julia retorted. "But first we should talk about what to do."
"What do you mean?" Brody asked. "We already know what we're going to do.
I'm going to keep training until I'm stronger and faster than I already am.
Then, after I win the Olympics, we'll go on my victory tour before going home."
"Forget your victory tour," Julia said. "The passage could close at any moment, remember? We need to get home as soon as we can."
Brody shrugged. Julia worried too much. Hermes was a god, which meant Hermes could do anything.
That probably included opening a new passage if the first one closed.
Still, Brody was too tired to argue with Julia about it right now.
"Okay," he agreed. "So the plan is, I win the Olympics, and then we go home. Is that better?"
"Yes," she replied.
"Julia!" Helene yelled again.
Julia sighed loudly. "Coming!" she yelled back.
Then she stomped off into the house.
"She might be right, you know," Markos said after Julia was gone.
"Once the Games are over, you should take the first opportunity to return home."
"Why?" Brody stretched and yawned. He wondered what was for dinner.
"Because . . ." Markos hesitated, glancing around carefully, and then lowered his voice.
"The gods can't be trusted. If you delay, Hermes might forget his promise to let you go."
"Really?" Brody blinked in surprise.
"But don't worry too much," Markos said. "If you bring glory to Hermes through your performance in the Games, he might not forget.
In fact, if you beat Zeus' champion, Hermes will probably let you do anything you want, including leave."
Brody relaxed again. "Then I'll just have to win," he said. "No problem."
Over the next couple of days, Brody did his best to put the plan into action.
He trained as hard as he could, doing everything Hermes asked him to do.
Hermes was still focused on the running races in the Games, though he also made Brody practice wrestling and javelin throwing.
Then one day Hermes told Brody it was time to practice throwing the discus.
Brody had never done that before. "I'm really good at throwing a football," he told himself. "It's probably the same thing."
But Brody quickly learned that a discus was a lot heavier than a football.
His first few throws were a disaster; the discus landed near his feet with a thud.
"This is definitely not going well," he thought, casting a look at Hermes.
When Markos brought him some water, Brody stood watching Artemis' champion for a few minutes.
The other athlete was nearby, practicing his discus throw too.
"I get it!" Brody declared suddenly. The other athlete swung the discus a few times before releasing it.
"Here." Brody thrust the water back at Markos and then grabbed the discus again.
This time he swung the discus back and forth before throwing it, just like the other athlete had done.
"Excellent!" Hermes cried as the discus flew halfway down the marked course.
"Much better, my champion! Now try it again!"
An hour later Brody's arm muscles were aching.
But Hermes was beaming. "We're making progress, young mortal friend!
We might just turn you into an Olympic champion yet.
As soon as you've mastered the discus, we'll move on to boxing. Oh, and the chariot race, of course."
"Chariot race?" Brody echoed. "You mean with horses?"
"Of course." Hermes tapped his chin thoughtfully.
"Poseidon owes me a favor—perhaps I'll ask him if I can borrow a team of horses."
Brody was surprised. He didn't know much about horses. But he wasn't worried.
"I've done great at everything else so far," he thought.
"I'm sure I'll be great at chariot driving too!"
Just then Apollo hurried over with Artemis at his heels.
"You look happy, Hermes," Apollo declared. "I suppose that means you haven't heard the latest gossip about Zeus' champion."
"Gossip doesn't worry me, my friend," Hermes retorted.
"Not when I have the finest champion in Olympia."
Brody grinned proudly.
"The gossip should worry you," Artemis said.
"Zeus claims that the mighty Alcides is training by racing against the swiftest deer in the forest—and beating them every time!"
"That's right," Apollo added. "I hear that Alcides chases down wild boars and strangles them with his bare hands for his dinner.
And he once threw the javelin so far that Zeus himself couldn't see where it landed."
Hermes scoffed. "It's easy for Zeus to brag when nobody has seen his champion yet.
I'll believe Zeus' tales when I finally see Alcides with my own eyes."
After Apollo and Artemis left to share their gossip with Ares, Hermes looked less cheerful than he had a few minutes earlier.
"Blast Zeus and his bragging," he muttered. He glanced at Brody.
"But perhaps some of his tales are true. So you'd better keep training hard, boy!"
The next day Julia and Markos went to the gymnasium to watch Brody's training, as usual.
"Wow, there are lots of gods here today," Julia said.
Markos nodded. "As the Games draw closer, the gods become quite focused on the competition.
Only the most powerful gods have a real chance of winning, of course.
But the others don't want to make it easy for them!"
Julia looked at the field. She couldn't help worrying about whether Brody would be good enough to compete against all these other athletes.
Still, she could tell that he was doing his best to train hard.
She watched Hermes hand Brody a discus and then gesture toward the course.
As Julia followed the track of Brody's toss, she noticed Ares creeping along the edge of the field.
"What's Ares doing?" she said.
Markos glanced at the god of war. "Probably trying to sabotage another god's champion."
"You mean like what Hera and Aphrodite tried to do to Brody?" Julia asked.
"Do the gods do that kind of thing a lot?"
"Of course," Markos replied. "Ares has quite a rivalry with Apollo.
He's not eager to have his sister Athena beat him in the Games either.
Oh, and I heard he recently quarreled with Hephaestus."
Julia shivered. "The gods really can't be trusted, can they?" she said.
"What if they keep trying to sabotage Brody?"
"They probably will." Markos shrugged.
"Then we should do something to help him." Julia stood up.
She was tired of sitting around watching Brody run and jump and throw things.
"Let's go spy on the other gods and their champions.
Maybe we can figure out which ones are the biggest threat to Brody."
Markos looked surprised, but he stood up too.
"That's a good idea. The gods usually can't help bragging about their tricks and plans.
If we listen carefully, we might be able to help Brody stay safe—and even win."
"Where are you two going?" Brody called out as Julia and Markos headed for an exit.
Hermes looked over too.
"We're, uh, going to the agora." Markos flushed.
"My mother asked me to get some extra eels for tonight's dinner."
Hermes smacked his lips. "Eels, eh?" he said.
"My favorite! Make sure you get plenty, boy.
We'll meet you at the agora when we're finished here in case you need help carrying them."
"How many eels does Hermes expect you to get?" Julia whispered as she and Markos hurried out.
"It doesn't matter," Markos said. "I just made that up about my mother.
Let's go to the agora and see who's there."
A few minutes later, the two kids were wandering around the agora.
As usual, it was crowded. A fabric merchant was placing a bolt of silk in front of his tent.
Two farmers were arguing loudly over the price of a flock of honking geese.
Several small boys dodged through the crowd toward another stall.
There were only a few gods in view, including Hera.
"Let's go closer," Julia whispered, nodding at the queen of the gods.
Julia and Markos moved toward Hera, who was talking to her champion, a muscular young man with a scar on his cheek.
". . . and you'll have to do much better at the long jump," the goddess was saying when Julia got close enough to hear.
"Because my husband has been bragging that his champion once leaped across the Elpeus River at its widest point."
"Do you think that's true?" Julia whispered to Markos.
"I don't know," Markos whispered back. "Nobody in Olympia has seen Alcides."
Julia noticed a pair of gods striding into the agora.
"Look! Artemis and Apollo. Let's spy on them for a while!"
After eavesdropping on some of the gods, Julia was feeling more confident about Brody's chances in the Games.
She and Markos had also spoken to three or four mortal champions who happened to pass by.
"It sounds like Brody actually has a good chance of beating most of the athletes in most of the events," Julia said.
"But I'm worried about two things."
"Alcides?" Markos guessed.
"Of course," Julia replied. "As you said, nobody will know what he's like until he shows up.
I'm also worried about the chariot race."
"Why?" Markos asked. "That event doesn't usually require much athletic ability."
Julia frowned. "It requires skill. And as far as I know, Brody has never even seen a horse up close.
He might be terrible at driving them. I think I'll try to convince Hermes to—"
A loud shout suddenly interrupted her. Suddenly everyone in the agora was turning around, peering in the same direction.
"What's going on?" Julia asked.
Markos stood on tiptoes, trying to see what everyone was looking at. "Oh!" he said. "It's Zeus."
Just then an enormous figure leaped onto a dais in the center of the agora.
Julia would have known that it was Zeus even if Markos hadn't said so.
Zeus looked just as she had imagined the king of the gods to look.
He appeared huge and powerful, with a long gray beard.
"Attention, people of Olympia!" Zeus' voice boomed out over the agora. "I have a very important announcement."
The agora went silent except for the sounds of animals and birds.
Out of the corner of her eye, Julia suddenly saw movement.
Turning, she noticed Hermes pushing his way forward with Brody at his heels.
They were staring up at Zeus just like everyone else.
"What is it, Zeus?" Hermes called out. "Don't keep us in suspense."
Zeus smiled. "I know you've all been eagerly awaiting the chance to cast your eyes upon Alcides," he said.
"Soon your wait will be over. Alcides—the most impressive mortal champion in all of Greece—arrives in Olympia in just two more days!"
"Wow," Brody said to Hermes as the crowd murmured in reaction to Zeus' announcement.
"I guess we'll get to check out this Alcides guy for ourselves soon, huh?" He glanced around.
"Look, there are Markos and Julia. Let's see if they bought those eels for dinner. I'm hungry!"
Hermes didn't seem to hear him. He was still staring at Zeus.
Meanwhile Ares pushed forward. Brody gasped when he saw the god of war.
Ares' hair always looked as red as flames. But now it had turned into real flames!
The people near Ares shrank back, looking nervous as sparks flew from the god's head.
"We'll be ready for your champion, Zeus!" Ares called out. "I hope he's ready for us."
Zeus smirked. "Trust me when I say that you won't be ready, Ares.
Nobody in Greece has ever seen anything like Alcides before.
Now excuse me while I go prepare for my champion's arrival."
"Pay my husband no mind!" Hera's sharp voice cut through the noise of the crowd.
"I don't know why you're all making such a fuss over his mysterious champion.
Nobody in Olympia has seen Poseidon's champion yet, nor Hades' champion either."
"That's different," Ares snarled. "Poseidon and Hades aren't telling outrageous tales about their champions."
"Yes," a man in the crowd called out. "I heard Alcides can read people's minds!"
"Nonsense," Hera spat out. "No mortal can do that."
Zeus smiled at her. "We shall see, my dear wife. Now I really have to go."
Thunder boomed, and lightning sizzled on the dais, so brightly that Brody closed his eyes.
When he opened them again, Zeus was gone.
"Whoa!" Brody said. "How'd he do that?"
Instead of answering, Hermes grabbed Brody's arm and dragged him over to Apollo, Artemis, and Caerus, who were all standing nearby.
"What do you think?" Hermes asked the other gods.
"Will Zeus really show his champion soon?"
Brody didn't pay attention to the other gods' responses because Julia and Markos had just joined the group.
"Did you see Zeus' lightning trick?" Brody asked them. "Totally cool, huh? And Ares' hair—"
Julia cut him off. "Never mind that, Brody. We've been talking to some of the other champions, and—"
She stopped talking as Hermes suddenly yanked Brody forward.
"And my champion will beat Alcides at every event!" Hermes bragged loudly.
"He's the best mortal athlete Olympia has ever seen."
"So you keep saying." Artemis looked Brody up and down.
"I suppose we'll find out soon enough if it's true."
"Being the best athlete won't help your champion if Alcides is as sneaky and ruthless as everyone says," Apollo remarked.
"I heard he killed his music teacher as a boy, and . . ."
Just then Brody spotted Aphrodite approaching.
"Don't worry, I'll beat Alcides," he said loudly, hoping that the goddess of beauty would hear him.
"I'm going to win every event, like Hermes said—just watch!"
He ran forward and went into a bodybuilder pose right in front of Aphrodite.
"Oh, my," she said with a smile. "What an impressive display!"
"Thanks." Brody puffed his chest out. "But this is nothing. You should see me catch a football!"
Aphrodite tilted her head, looking confused. "Catch a football?" she echoed.
Julia darted over and pulled Brody away. "Forget about Aphrodite, Brody!" she whispered.
"We need to talk to Hermes about the chariot thing!"
"What chariot thing?" Brody asked, but Julia was yanking him toward Hermes.
Brody looked back over his shoulder at Aphrodite.
The beautiful goddess had already turned away to talk to another goddess.
"Excuse me, Hermes," Julia said when they reached the god.
"What is it, girl?" Hermes asked, sounding distracted. "I'm very busy right now."
"I thought you should know that Brody doesn't know anything about horses or chariot driving," Julia said.
"He's never done it before. Perhaps it would be best to work on that event next?"
"Are you telling me how to train my champion, mortal girl?" Hermes thundered. Then he blinked.
"Wait. Perhaps you're right. I've been meaning to practice for the chariot race."
He patted Julia on the head. "Thank you for the reminder, mortal. I'll contact Poseidon right now."
He hurried off.
Brody whirled toward Julia. "What was that about?" he demanded.
"You made me sound like an idiot. I can drive a chariot!"
"Have you ever driven one before?" Julia asked.
Brody shrugged. "No. But I'd never thrown a javelin before, and look how great I am at that!"
Just then Markos emerged from the crowd and hurried over.
"Listen," he said. "I was just talking to a friend.
His father is a guard at the Temple of Hera.
He says Hera already has a plan to humiliate Zeus."
"That doesn't seem like a big surprise," Julia said.
"I know, but listen," Markos went on. "Hera doesn't only want to beat Zeus' champion with her own.
She also plans to banish Alcides to Tartarus through some trickery!"
"Tartarus? Really?" Julia said.
"Tartarus? What's that?" Brody asked. "Is it where they make tartar sauce?" He laughed loudly at his own joke.
Markos looked confused, and Julia frowned.
"This isn't funny, Brody," she snapped at him.
"Tartarus is part of the underworld. It's the most terrible part, actually."
She glanced at Markos. "Can Hera really banish someone there?"
"I don't know," Markos said. "But one should never underestimate Hera."
"Right," Julia agreed. "Brody almost found that out the hard way."
"I did?" Brody said.
"Yes. You don't remember? She got Aphrodite to try to poison you with that chiton! But there's also some good news.
If Hera stays focused on Zeus and Alcides, maybe she won't try to sabotage Brody anymore."
"Maybe." But Markos looked troubled. "Still, I wouldn't bet my life on it."
"I haven't seen Poseidon yet," Julia whispered to Markos. "What's he like?"
The two of them were following Hermes and Brody toward the hippodrome.
That was the stadium where the chariot races would take place.
Hermes had arranged to meet Poseidon there.
"We don't see Poseidon as much as the other gods," Markos told Julia.
"As the god of the sea, he prefers to stay beneath the waters.
Well, except when he wants to spend time with horses, that is."
"I didn't even know Poseidon was the god of horses," Julia said. "We didn't learn that in class."
"He created the horse out of sea foam to impress the goddess Demeter," Markos said.
"Oh, cool."
Julia looked around as they entered the hippodrome.
The place was deserted. "So where's Poseidon?" she murmured.
Suddenly they heard a crack of thunder, and rain poured down on all of them.
Julia ducked and covered her head with her hands.
A second later the rain stopped as quickly as if someone had turned off a faucet.
Standing before them was Poseidon. He had a flowing beard tangled with seaweed, and he was holding a trident.
Behind him were two teams of snorting horses. Each team was hitched to a chariot.
"Poseidon, my friend!" Hermes greeted him. "You're right on time."
"You always deliver my messages quickly, Hermes," Poseidon replied with a nod.
"Of course I'm on time when you need a favor."
"This is the champion I told you about," Hermes said, gesturing at Brody.
"I'm sure he's destined to beat Zeus' mystery mortal."
"Hmm." Poseidon looked Brody up and down. "Allow me to introduce my own champion."
A man jumped out of one of the chariots.
He was very tall, with broad shoulders and curly dark hair.
"This is Drakon," Poseidon said. "I thought it would be interesting for our mortal heroes to train against each other."
"An excellent idea!" Hermes agreed.
Julia wasn't so sure. "Brody isn't ready to train against anyone yet," she whispered to Markos.
"First he needs to learn what he's supposed to be doing!"
But Brody was already striding toward the chariots. "Is this one mine?" he asked.
"Brody, look out!" Julia cried as a horse lunged toward him.
Brody jumped away just in time to avoid a bite on the shoulder. "Wow, this horse is pretty aggressive," he said.
"They don't like standing around," Poseidon said.
"They'll settle once they get moving. Won't you, my pets?"
He stepped over and stroked the nose of the horse that had tried to bite Brody. The animal nuzzled him happily.
Brody climbed into the chariot. "Giddyup!" he called, whipping the reins up and down so they slapped the horses' rumps.
The animals didn't seem to like that. All four horses leaped in place.
One of them reared, while another kicked at the chariot.
"Easy, boy," Hermes called to Brody. "We don't want the horses to dump you before you get started."
Julia was growing more and more worried.
"Is this safe?" she asked Markos as both teams sprang into a gallop.
"Of course not," Markos said. "It's the most dangerous event in the Games.
The crowd loves it, which is why it comes last." He shrugged.
"Well, that's one reason it comes last.
I imagine there's another reason—if an athlete gets killed, he's already finished all the other events!"
Julia gulped. Brody had no idea how much danger he was in.
He was grinning as his chariot sailed around a turn, chasing the one driven by Drakon.
"Faster, boy!" Hermes shouted.
Brody snapped the reins again. The horses surged forward, which made Brody lose his balance.
He grabbed the edge of the chariot to keep himself from falling out.
But at the same time, he dropped the reins.
"Steer, mortal!" Poseidon thundered at Brody. The sea god turned to Hermes.
"Your champion isn't much of a driver, eh?"
"Give him time," Hermes responded with a smile. "He's a fast learner."
"Fast learner?" Julia muttered. "I definitely never thought of Brody that way before."
Markos heard her. "What do you mean? Brody learned how to throw the javelin and discus almost immediately."
Julia didn't answer. She held her breath as the chariots sped along the straightaway.
The horses' nostrils were flaring, and Brody's team was gaining on Drakon's, even though Brody's reins were flapping free.
"Grab those reins, boy!" Hermes shouted. "Oh, never mind. I'll help you, just this once."
Hermes' winged sandals lifted him off the ground and carried him swiftly through the air.
He snatched the reins out of midair and tossed them to Brody.
"Thanks, dude!" Brody called breathlessly.
"Watch out!" Hermes warned him. "You're about to crash!"
The horses had felt Brody pulling on the reins again, and they didn't seem to like it.
Now they were heading straight toward the stands!
"Turn, boy! Turn!" Poseidon called.
Hermes landed beside Poseidon. "You were right, my friend," he said. "This is interesting!"
Julia couldn't believe the two gods were acting so casual. Brody could be killed!
She watched him pulling the reins in all different directions, but that only seemed to make the horses gallop faster.
"Use the reins to steer the horses, Brody!" Julia yelled.
"Pull the reins in the same direction!"
Usually Brody didn't pay attention to her advice.
But this time he did. He yanked the reins to the left.
It worked! The team veered left, just missing the stands.
Somehow Brody managed to steer the horses back on the track, where they spotted Drakon's team and took off after them.
Julia sighed with relief. "That was close!" she whispered.
Things didn't go much better after that.
Brody's horses mostly ignored him and chased the other team.
By the end of the day, Hermes was clearly displeased. "Well, you survived," he told Brody.
"But you'll have to get much better at this if you expect to beat anyone—especially the mighty Alcides."
"Delicious." Hermes dabbed his mouth with a cloth and stood up from the dinner table. He glanced at Markos and Julia.
"Too bad Markos and the girl forgot to get more eels, though. I would have liked a third helping."
"I'm so sorry, Hermes," Markos' father, Nikolaos, said. "I thought we had plenty of eels. It won't happen again."
"Come, my friend," Caerus told Hermes. "Let's find Dionysus and celebrate the fine evening."
"Yes." Hermes shot Brody a frown. "Although I'm not much in the mood for celebrating after today's chariot practice."
Without another word the two gods left.
Nikolaos frowned at his wife, who was helping Julia and the other girls clear the dishes.
"That was an embarrassment," he said. "You know that eels are Hermes' favorite!"
"How could I predict he'd eat twice as many as usual?" his wife retorted, sounding grumpy.
She snapped her fingers at Markos. "Markos! Go to the agora right now and tell the vendor that we'll want more eels this week.
We want only the freshest ones and plenty of them!"
"Yes, Mother." Markos stood up.
"We'll come along and help you, Markos," Julia said. "Right, Brody?"
"Huh?" Brody looked up from his meal. "I'm not finished eating."
"Come on," Julia said, yanking on his chiton so hard that Brody was afraid she was going to pull it right off.
He glared at her. Back home he had barely noticed that Julia existed.
She was just a nerd who never came to the football games or did anything else interesting.
It was a lot harder to ignore her here in ancient Greece. When had she become so assertive?
He sighed loudly and stood up. "Fine," he said.
"I'm exhausted after my long day of training for the Olympics, but whatever."
He grabbed one last olive and tossed it into his mouth.
Soon the three of them were walking toward the agora.
"What do you think?" Julia asked Markos.
"Is there any chance that Brody will get good enough at chariot racing in time to win at the Games?"
"Why don't you ask me?" Brody said.
"I'm the one who has to do it. And controlling a bunch of crazy wild horses isn't as easy as it looks."
"It didn't look easy at all," Julia said. "That's exactly my point.
What if you don't improve fast enough?
If you don't impress Hermes, he might break his promise to let us leave."
