Brody shrugged. "I have more than a week to practice. Besides, who cares what Hermes thinks of me right now?
If I look bad at chariot driving, he'll be even more impressed when I win on the big day!"
Julia still looked worried. "I don't want to get stuck here in ancient Greece forever."
She glanced over at Markos. "Sorry, Markos. I don't mean to offend you."
"Don't worry, I'll win," Brody said. "End of story."
By then they were entering the agora.
Several young men were gathered near a fabric vendor's stall.
Brody recognized most of them as other champions. A few waved to him.
"Did you hear the news?" Apollo's champion called. "The mighty Alcides arrives soon."
"We heard all about it," Brody replied.
"So what? I'm glad we'll finally get the chance to see this guy."
Artemis' champion shook his head. "I'm not so sure I want to see him," he said.
"I overheard Artemis talking with Ares and Hestia, the goddess of the hearth and home.
Zeus told them that Alcides strangled two enormous serpents with his bare hands when he was less than a year old!"
"Serpents? That's nothing," said Demeter's champion. "I heard that Alcides killed a dozen men before he was ten years old!"
"Well, I heard that Alcides eats human brains for breakfast," Artemis' champion added. "Zeus says it makes him smarter."
"That makes sense," put in Ares' champion.
"Because Ares told me that Alcides eats human muscles for lunch. It's supposed to make him stronger."
Brody listened, not sure what to think about what the athletes were saying.
All these rumors were getting pretty tiring though.
Just then a sleek deer raced toward them, dodging around the people in the agora.
"Whoa," Brody said. "Loose animal!"
The deer stopped in front of the group.
It seemed pretty tame, so Brody stepped toward it.
He was about to grab the deer when it suddenly transformed into Artemis.
"Whoa!" Brody said again. He couldn't get used to the way the gods could transform into animals!
Artemis crooked her finger at her champion. "Come, my boy," she ordered.
"You need to rest. We have much more training to do tomorrow."
"Coming," her champion said.
"I'd better go, too," one of the others said. "Ares will be looking for me."
Before long Brody, Julia, and Markos were alone again.
"Wow," Julia said. "This Alcides sounds really impressive. I'm surprised I've never heard of him.
Though that story about the serpents seemed familiar. I think—"
"You haven't heard of him?" Brody cut her off.
"That's cool. It means Zeus is probably exaggerating, right?
I mean, if Alcides was really that great, wouldn't we have studied him in social studies class?"
"Maybe." Julia looked troubled. "Then again, it's not as if we could possibly learn everything about ancient Greece.
Maybe Alcides really is a great hero, just not quite as great as the really famous ones like Heracles or Achilles."
She sighed. "I wish I had my phone so I could look him up on the Internet."
Markos looked uncomfortable. Brody had noticed that Markos looked that way whenever Brody and Julia discussed their lives in the future.
"It's getting dark," Markos said. "We should tell the vendor about the eels and get home.
Brody, you need to rest too. Tomorrow is likely to be a busy day."
"Why aren't we going to the hippodrome?" Julia asked Hermes as the group entered the gymnasium the next day.
"I thought you'd want Brody to work on his chariot driving some more."
"That can wait," Hermes replied. "I've had enough of watching chariot driving for a while.
Besides, if I ask Poseidon to borrow his horses again so soon, he'll think I'm worried about Brody's chances in the event."
Julia didn't respond. She was pretty sure Poseidon had already figured out that Brody wasn't an expert chariot driver!
Athena and her champion spotted Hermes and Brody and came over.
"My champion is training for the hoplitodromos," Athena told Hermes.
"We've reached the point where he would benefit from running against an opponent. Can we train with you?"
"The hoplitodromos." Hermes snapped his fingers. "I knew there was something I meant to do today!"
"The hoplitodromos," Julia said to Markos. "That's the race where the runners have to wear armor, right?"
"Yes," Markos said. "It's quite a test of an athlete's strength and endurance."
Julia watched as Hermes snapped his fingers again and a pile of metal armor fell out of the sky with a clang.
It was so loud that it startled Ares, who instantly turned into a huge, growling dog.
"Sorry, my friend," Hermes called out with a smirk. "I didn't mean to scare you."
Ares returned to his normal form and scowled at Hermes.
"You didn't scare me, messenger," he snapped. "You merely distracted me!"
Julia watched Ares grab his champion and drag him off toward the javelin area.
She was glad to see the war god go.
After his trick with the javelins, Ares made Julia nervous when he was close.
"I guess it's a good thing Brody gets to practice with Athena's champion," Julia said.
"Athena probably won't turn Brody's shield into a hungry wolf or something."
Markos chuckled. "True. It's too bad we can't say the same for most of the other gods.
I hear they're already coming up with ways to sabotage Alcides as soon as he arrives."
Julia noticed Hermes staring at them.
"Well?" the god said. "Are you just going to sit there, or are you going to help my champion get ready?"
"Sorry, Hermes." Markos scurried over to Brody.
Julia went to help too. The armor consisted of a metal helmet, a large wooden shield covered in bronze, and a pair of metal leg coverings.
She picked up the helmet and almost dropped it.
"Wow," she said. "This stuff is heavy!"
"No kidding." Brody put on one of the leg coverings.
"This gear is a lot heavier than my football pads.
It's not going to be easy to run in all this stuff."
"Don't forget this." Markos picked up the shield.
"Be careful not to drop it while you're running, or you'll have to stop and retrieve it. That will slow you down."
"Okay. Hold the shield while I put on my helmet."
Brody adjusted the metal helmet on his head. Then he took the shield from Markos.
"Ready, boy?" Hermes stepped forward, looking impatient. "Athena's champion is waiting."
"I'm ready." Brody took a few steps toward the other athlete. His armor clanked with every step.
As soon as Brody neared Athena's champion, the goddess waved her hand. "Go!"
Athena's champion started running.
Brody looked startled. "Hey!" he exclaimed. "I wasn't ready!"
He lurched forward. The armor on one of his legs caught on the armor on the other leg.
"Brody, look out!" Julia cried.
It was too late. Brody tripped and fell.
His shield went flying as he hit the ground with a clank and a loud "oof!"
"Stop!" Athena called to her champion. "We need to start over."
Julia and Markos ran over to help Brody to his feet.
"Are you all right?" Markos asked. "Did you hurt yourself?"
"I don't think so." Brody took a few steps and then made a face.
"But this is ridiculous. How am I supposed to run like this? Especially here, in this crowded space."
Julia was surprised. She'd never heard Brody express doubt before.
Usually he acted so confident—too confident!
Then he looked over at her. "Sorry," he said.
"I mean, I know you're counting on me to get us home. I just hope I can really do it."
"You will," Julia said. "You can do this, Brody.
You learned how to throw the javelin and the discus, remember?"
"That's different." Brody frowned and kicked at the shield on the ground.
"It will be easier when you're running in the Olympic stadium," Julia said.
"For now, you just have to focus, and you'll be fine. You have lots of natural athletic ability."
"Do you really think so?" Brody blinked at her. Then slowly he smiled.
"Maybe you're right. I'm the best football player on my team. Coach says I can do anything!"
He grabbed his shield again. By then Athena's champion had returned to the starting line.
"Ready, boy?" Hermes asked.
Brody smacked his shield with his free hand, making it clang. "Ready!" he cried.
"Do you really think he can do this?" Markos asked Julia quietly as the two athletes lined up again.
Julia shrugged. "I guess we're about to find out."
"Go!" Athena said.
This time Brody and the other champion leaped forward together.
After a few steps, Athena's champion pulled ahead.
"Go, Brody!" Julia yelled. "You can do it!"
After another few steps, Brody surged forward, catching up to, and then passing, the other runner.
"Why is he holding his shield like that?" Markos asked. "He's cradling it like a baby."
For a second Julia couldn't figure it out either. Then she realized what Brody was doing.
"He's pretending it's a football!" she said with a smile. "That probably makes him feel more confident."
Hermes' cheers suddenly filled the air. Julia cheered too as Brody crossed the line well ahead of the other runner. He'd done it!
Two hours later Brody had moved on from practicing for the hoplitodromos race to practicing for the wrestling event again.
Brody hadn't wrestled much, but he wasn't worried.
Today he was practicing against Demeter's champion, a tall, thin youth with a big nose.
"Got you!" Brody cried as he pinned the other athlete for the third time in a row.
Demeter's champion gritted his teeth. "Never mind," he said.
"I may not be the best at wrestling.But I'll beat you at boxing every time!"
Brody let him go and stood up. "Boxing?" he said to Hermes. "Do I have to do that?"
"Of course," Hermes said. "We'll practice that tomorrow.
I've already started setting up some sparring partners for you."
Before Brody could say anything else, a loud buzzing sound filled the gymnasium.
"What's that?" Julia exclaimed.
Markos covered his head. "Look out above!"
Brody glanced up just in time to see a huge black cloud descending on the gymnasium.
When it got closer, he saw that it was actually a swarm of large insects.
"Gross!" Brody covered his head as the first insects hit him. "What are those things?"
"Cicadas." Hermes sounded disgusted. "Apollo! Did you have something to do with this?"
Apollo was standing nearby, grinning as the other gods' champions raced for cover from the rain of singing insects.
Meanwhile Apollo's own champion continued to jog around the track, untouched by the cicadas.
"What makes you think I had anything to do with this?" Apollo asked, still grinning.
Cicadas were pelting every inch of Brody's head and body. One even crawled into his mouth.
"Yuck!" he exclaimed, spitting it out and then running to join Julia and Markos, who were huddled beneath the shelter of an overhang.
"Enough, brother!" Artemis stepped forward, frowning. Ignoring the insects raining down on her, she lifted her bow. "Feathered friends, help us!"
A loud, piercing shriek seemed to tear the sky in two.
A moment later something scurried into the gymnasium.
"What's that?" Brody asked, peering through the veil of cicadas.
"It looks like a bird," Markos said. "It's eating the cicadas!"
"It's a guinea fowl," Julia explained. "My neighbors used to raise them.
They're really noisy. And they'll eat anything."
"Look!" Markos pointed. "Here come more of them!"
Dozens of guinea fowl were running or flying into view.
They immediately began gobbling up the cicadas. Some of them let out sharp cries as they fed.
"This is ridiculous!" Ares marched over to Apollo and Artemis, cicadas crunching beneath his feet.
"How can any of us train under these conditions?"
"Sorry." Apollo shrugged, not looking sorry at all.
"I was just testing out a little trick I might try on the mighty Alcides."
"Hmm." Ares suddenly looked much less angry.
"Now that you mention it, I have a few things in mind for Zeus' mighty champion as well."
He raised his spear to his own head just as his red hair burst into flame.
He lit his spear, and then twirled it, shooting fire at the cicadas.
A guinea fowl let out a squawk as a spark just missed its head.
"Maybe we should get out of here." Julia sounded nervous. "Things are getting a little dangerous."
Hermes sighed. "I suppose we won't get anything done until the others have had their fun," he said. "Besides, it's almost dinnertime. Let's go."
They headed back to Markos' house.
"Are the other gods really going to sabotage Alcides, like they said?" Julia asked Hermes.
He looked surprised. "Of course! What a silly question, girl."
Brody frowned. "But the Olympics are supposed to be about who's the best athlete," he said.
"How can you figure that out when you're all trying to cheat all the time?"
He was afraid that Hermes might get mad at his question.
Instead, the god laughed. "Oh, you mortals! You're always getting worked up about things like that."
He patted Brody on the head. "Don't worry about it. It's not as if any of this matters, after all."
"What do you mean?" Julia asked. "I thought the Olympic Games were super important.
Don't the games help to keep peace among all the Greek cities? And honor Zeus and the other gods?"
Hermes pointed to a dog chasing a rat along a path.
"To those creatures, their game is important," he said.
"To you mortals, the Games are important. To us?" He shrugged again.
"The Games are amusing, yes. They bring us pride and a chance to brag, certainly. But important?" He laughed loudly.
Brody was still thinking about what Hermes had said when the family finished dinner that evening.
He waited until he, Julia, and Markos were alone in the courtyard.
"So what did Hermes mean earlier?" he asked Julia and Markos. "Doesn't he care about the Olympics?"
"I told you before," Markos said. "The gods are different from mortals. We are playthings to them—pets, like that dog we saw."
Julia frowned. "I don't even think they see us the way we see dogs or other pets," she said.
"We're more like ants to them. They make us race each other, and then they pull our legs off or stomp on us for fun!"
"You're lucky you're Hermes' champion, Brody," Markos said.
"What are you talking about?" Julia blurted out.
"Hermes might not ever let us ever return home!"
"That's true," Markos admitted with a grim expression.
"But I hate to think of what might happen to Hera's hero if he fails to defeat Alcides.
Or what could happen to Alcides himself if he disappoints Zeus."
"Hmm . . ." Brody hadn't realized that some of the gods could be so cruel.
"Well, it sounds as if Alcides might not even make it to the Olympics," he pointed out.
"I mean, every god out there is going to try to take him down, right?"
"Except Athena and Zeus," Julia said. "Okay, maybe you're right, Markos. Maybe it could be worse."
"Hermes must have annoyed the other gods last night," Julia murmured to Markos.
It was the following day. Julia and Markos were in the gymnasium, sitting on their usual bench watching Brody's training.
Today Brody was practicing boxing. He'd spent the past few minutes sparring against Hermes himself.
Markos gasped as Hermes landed yet another jab on Brody's shoulder, and Brody fell back with a grunt.
"And now Brody is paying the price.
None of the other gods would agree to train with us today, so Hermes had no choice but to serve as Brody's opponent himself."
Julia watched as Hermes danced around, jabbing at Brody every chance he got. She winced.
The messenger god seemed to be enjoying himself.
He flitted back and forth, taking advantage of his greater height, speed, and strength, as well as his winged sandals.
So far Brody hadn't landed a single punch, although he'd received plenty from Hermes.
"Ugh," Julia said. "I hate boxing. It's so violent!"
"Good one, Brody!" Markos shouted as Brody swung at Hermes' chin, barely missing as the god spun out of the way. "Er, I mean, nicely dodged, Hermes."
Hermes grinned. "Don't hesitate to cheer for your mortal friend, boy," he called to Markos good-naturedly.
"He needs all the help he can get!"
"Urgh!" Brody grunted, lunging at Hermes.
But once again his punch missed the mark.
Hermes sidestepped easily and hit Brody on the ear as Brody went by.
"I don't want to watch anymore," Julia told Markos with a shudder.
She glanced around for something else to do, but the gymnasium was nearly deserted.
"Let's go to the agora and find out if Alcides has arrived yet.
Today is the day he's supposed to arrive, right?"
Markos was leaning forward, watching the fight with interest.
"Alcides is not in Olympia yet," he said.
"If he were here, we'd have heard about it."
Julia sighed and sat back. She looked away as Hermes punched Brody in the nose, sending sweat and a little blood flying.
Now she could see that Apollo was wandering toward them.
"Nice moves, Hermes," Apollo said. "It's a good thing you're getting your champion used to losing.
He'll be doing a lot of it once the Games start!"
Hermes frowned at the other god. But before he could say a word, the ground beneath the gymnasium let out an ominous rumble.
"What was that?" Julia exclaimed. "An earthquake?"
Suddenly the ground split open. Dirt and sand sprayed everywhere.
Hermes and Apollo jumped back as a chasm appeared in the spot where they'd been standing.
Brody just stood there staring, and Hermes had to fly in and grab him so he didn't fall into the chasm.
"What's going on?" Julia cried, grabbing Markos by the arm.
Markos' face had gone pale. He pointed. "Hades is here."
The chasm belched out black smoke, and then a god stepped out.
"Hades," Julia whispered, impressed and a little scared. "The god of the underworld!"
Hades' chest and shoulders were broad, and he had pale skin, sleek dark hair, and a craggy, ugly face.
He was holding a chain in one strong hand.
The other end of the chain was fastened to the collar of the largest dog Julia had ever seen.
But this was no ordinary dog. It had three heads and a serpent for a tail.
"Is that . . . is that Cerberus?" Julia asked Markos in a shaky voice.
"The three-headed dog that guards the gates of the underworld?"
"Of course!" Markos said.
Brody hurried over to his friends, staying far away from the edge of the chasm.
"What's going on?" he asked. He spit out a mouthful of saliva mixed with blood. "Who is that?"
"Hades," Julia told him with a shiver. "He's the god of the underworld."
"The underworld?" Brody echoed.
Markos nodded. "It's where the dead go after their lives are over. It's known as Hades."
Brody shook his head and looked at Markos in confusion.
"Okay, Hermes hit me pretty hard a few times," he said.
"But did you really just say that guy's name is Hades—and the place he comes from is also called Hades?"
"That's right," Julia said, wondering if Brody had paid any attention at all in social studies class.
Brody snorted with laughter. "Hades from Hades! Good one!"
Julia rolled her eyes and turned to watch as Hades looped Cerberus' chain around a column.
"Guard this entrance," Hades commanded the three-headed dog, pointing to the chasm. "Do not let the dead escape!"
Julia's eyes widened. "Can the dead really escape from the underworld?" she whispered to Markos.
"They can try. That's why Hades usually visits the surface through the entrance that lies across the river Acheron," Markos whispered back.
"He must be in a hurry if he decided to open a portal here in Olympia."
Hermes and Apollo looked perfectly relaxed as Hades stepped toward them.
"Greetings, Hades," Apollo said. "What brings you to this side of the Earth's surface?"
Hades greeted them. "It is good to see you.
I am here to see the champion my brother Zeus claims is the best he's ever seen.
I hear this amazing mortal has just arrived in Olympia."
"What?" Hermes exclaimed. "Why didn't we know of this?"
Apollo smirked. "Ah, so the messenger of the gods is the last to receive this particular message, huh? Too bad, Hermes."
Hades laughed loudly. "Never mind," Hades went on.
"If Zeus isn't here, perhaps he is bringing his hero to the agora first."
Hermes' scowl disappeared, replaced by an eager expression.
"What are we waiting for?" he cried. "Let's go to the agora at once!"
The agora was crowded when Brody and the others arrived.
Humans and gods gathered in small groups, most of them chattering about Alcides.
"Is he here yet?" Hermes called out.
His winged sandals fluttered, and he flew up and away, over the crowd. "Where's the mighty champion Alcides?"
"Hey!" Brody called. "Where are you going? Don't forget about us!"
"Never mind," Julia said. "We'll never catch up to him in this crowd."
She stood on tiptoes. "We'll never see anything either."
Markos pointed to the wooden roof of a nearby stall.
"Let's climb up there. Then we'll be able to see everything."
"Good idea." Brody jumped up and grabbed the edge of the roof, preparing to swing himself up.
But looking back at Julia, he hesitated.
She was shorter than he was; she'd probably never be able to reach the tall roof.
"Here," he said, letting go of the roof. "I'll give you a lift."
He made a step with his hands.
Julia hesitated for a second. "Thanks," she said at last.
She stepped onto Brody's cupped hands. He hoisted her up until she could grab the edge of the roof and pull herself onto it.
Then he scrambled up and pulled Markos up after him.
Markos was right. Brody could see the entire agora from the roof.
"Look, there's Hermes," Julia said, pointing. "Over there with Apollo and Artemis."
Markos shaded his eyes. "I see Aphrodite and Ares too.
I wonder if Hera is here. Maybe she decided to stay away—to annoy Zeus."
"Never mind them," Brody said. "I want to see Alcides."
He flexed his muscles. "I have to beat this guy."
At that moment a hush fell over the crowd.
Then Zeus stepped onto the dais at one end of the agora. Behind him were two teenage boys.
"Is that Alcides?" Brody peered at the taller and more muscular of the boys.
"Hey, he doesn't look much older than me."
"Who's the other kid?" Julia asked.
Brody glanced at the second youth. He was hanging back behind Zeus and the larger boy.
"He's kind of scrawny. I doubt he's an athlete."
"Greetings, visitors and citizens of Olympia!" Zeus' deep voice boomed out over the crowd.
"The moment you've awaited is here. I present to you my mortal champion—Alcides!"
The larger youth stepped forward. Most of the humans in the agora cheered, while the gods murmured or jeered.
Brody leaned forward, trying to get a good look at Alcides.
Zeus' champion was built like a football player.
But Brody knew that most of his teammates back home would probably make fun of Alcides' long, flowing brown hair.
"This is the mighty Alcides?" Apollo called out.
"He doesn't look very mighty to me!"
Zeus smiled. "Fear not, sun god.
Alcides might look mild-mannered, but he has the heart of a lion and the strength of an ox. Show them, my boy."
Alcides nodded and looked around. A large wooden wagon stacked high with logs was parked near the dais.
Hopping down gracefully, Alcides bent—and lifted the wagon over his head in one easy motion.
"Whoa!" Brody said. "How'd he do that?"
"So he's strong," Artemis called out. "Very impressive.
But strength won't help him win a footrace."
Zeus smirked. "Clear a path, and fetch me a fast horse. We're going to have a race."
Soon a sleek black horse was dancing beside Alcides at the starting line.
A nervous-looking young boy sat on the horse's back.
Zeus yelled, "Go!" and both the horse and Alcides took off.
The horse broke into a gallop, but Alcides stayed right beside it.
Just before the finish line, Alcides passed the animal.
The crowd cheered wildly. Even a few of the gods joined in this time.
Brody didn't make a sound, though. He could hardly believe what he'd just seen.
Zeus looked pleased. "Well?" he said. "Does anyone have any doubts about my hero now?"
A goddess stepped forward. She had brown hair and a motherly look.
In her hand was a sheaf of wheat.
"Who's that?" Brody blurted out.
"That's Demeter," Julia murmured. "The goddess of the harvest."
"I have a challenge for your champion," Demeter announced.
She pointed a sheaf of wheat at Alcides.
Vines sprouted out of the ground all around him.
They snaked around his body and head, completely hiding him from sight.
Demeter stepped back. "Let's see if your hero can free himself from the bounds of nature!"
Zeus looked slightly annoyed. "Fine," he said. "Alcides, go ahead."
For a moment nothing happened.
"Do you think he's okay?" Julia asked. "What if those vines are suffocating him?"
"Who cares!" Brody replied. "Then I won't have to run against him in the Olympics!"
Julia shot him a look. "He's the fastest and strongest person I've ever seen. Are you getting nervous?"
Trying to ignore his doubts, Brody swallowed hard.
"No way," he said quickly. "I . . . I can beat him."
Just then the first vine snapped. Then another. A few seconds later, Alcides wiggled one arm free.
Within a few more seconds, he'd squirmed free of the vines.
Zeus grabbed Alcides' arm and held it above the youth's head. "My champion!" he shouted.
The crowd cheered. Brody glanced at Hermes, wondering what the god was thinking now.
As he did, he saw movement nearby. Ares was pushing his way to the front of the crowd.
"Think fast, mortal," the war god said with a sneer.
Then he shot a flaming arrow directly at Alcides!
Brody barely had time to gasp.
Alcides reacted fast, clapping his hands together in front of him—and stopping the arrow just before it struck his chest.
The crowd cheered again.
"Uh-oh," Julia murmured.
Suddenly the cheering stopped. People in the crowd began whispering, staring off to one side of the dais.
"What's going on?" Julia asked.
Brody turned to look. The crowd parted beside the dais—and Hera stepped into view.
The sun shining down over the agora was hot, but Julia felt a chill run through her as Hera stepped up to Alcides.
"Well, well, well," Hera said, walking in a circle around Zeus' champion.
"I see your champion has finally arrived, Zeus."
"Alcides, may I present my lovely wife, Hera," Zeus said.
"Hera, this is the champion you've heard so much about:
Alcides of Thebes, the greatest mortal athlete of his generation. Possibly the greatest of any generation."
"It is my honor to be in the presence of the queen of the gods," Alcides said, bowing low.
Hera looked unimpressed as she studied Alcides from head to toe.
At last she turned to sneer at Zeus.
"He's just another ordinary mortal after all."
"You won't say that when he beats your champion in the Games," Zeus said.
Hera sniffed in disdain and returned her attention to Alcides.
She stared at the young man with pure hatred in her eyes.
Alcides gazed back, his expression calm and untroubled.
Julia, though, thought she could see his hands trembling slightly.
"It's not surprising that Alcides looks nervous," she thought with a shiver.
"Hera is scary all the time—but when she's angry, she's terrifying!"
Finally Hera turned away again. "I see that I've wasted my time coming here today.
My champion and I have nothing to worry about."
Zeus clenched his jaw in anger. "Is that so?" His voice boomed.
"Perhaps Alcides and I can show you otherwise."
Zeus leaped off the dais. In three huge strides, he reached a stall containing live chickens and sheep.
A large ram stood in a pen in front of the stall.
Zeus kicked the pen apart as easily as Julia might kick away some twigs, sending wood flying in all directions.
Then he grabbed the ram by the horns and dragged it over to Alcides.
"Here you go, my boy," Zeus said through gritted teeth.
"Please show my wife how you choked those serpents in your crib."
"So that tale is true!" Markos whispered in amazement.
Julia nodded slowly. "I knew that story sounded familiar.
So do some of the other stories we've heard about Alcides."
"Shh," Brody said. "He's going to strangle the ram!"
"Oh no!" Julia exclaimed. "The poor ram didn't do anything to him—or to Zeus, either."
The crowd murmured and pressed forward as Zeus stepped back, leaving Alcides facing off against the ram.
The ram lowered its head, snorted, and pawed at the dusty ground.
"Go on, boy," Zeus urged Alcides. He turned to the crowd.
"As you may have heard, Alcides strangled not one, but two deadly serpents when he was just a baby in his crib.
By doing so, he saved not only his own life, but also that of his twin brother. Isn't that right, Iphicles, my boy?"
Julia had almost forgotten about the second youth. But now Zeus pulled him forward.
"This is Iphicles," Zeus announced. "He and Alcides have been together since birth.
They're as close as brothers can be despite their obvious differences."
He chuckled, poking Iphicles in his skinny arm. "Isn't that right, my boy?"
Iphicles nodded. Then he ducked his head, looking uncomfortable.
Julia knew how he felt. She didn't like being the center of attention, and she could tell that he didn't either.
Alcides seemed to see it too. "Look at me!" he called out, stepping forward and blocking his brother from view.
"This ram is no match for my strength." He struck a pose to show his biceps.
The ram charged him with its head lowered, but Alcides grabbed its horns and flung it to the ground.
Julia winced. "Is he really going to strangle it?" she cried.
The crowd shouted with excitement as the ram bleated in alarm.
Julia braced herself for a horrible sight.
But Alcides didn't strangle the ram. Instead he held it down and tied its legs together.
Then he lifted the animal above his head and carried it back to its owner.
"Here you go, sir," Alcides said to the livestock seller. "You have a fine, strong ram here."
"Thank you," the livestock seller said. He sounded relieved.
Alcides walked back over to Zeus.
The king of the gods was frowning slightly.
"I thought I told you to strangle the ram," he said.
"I'm sorry, Zeus," Alcides said. "The crowd is so loud, I must not have heard you correctly. I meant no disrespect."
"Humph." Zeus hesitated, seeming unsure whether to get angry or not.
Finally he shrugged and turned toward the crowd.
"Behold Alcides, your next and greatest Olympic champion!"
The crowd went wild. Julia glanced at Hera.
The queen of the gods was watching her husband through narrowed eyes.
"Even the king of the gods cannot know the future," Hera said coolly.
"Anything might happen to your champion between now and the Games."
She smirked. "After all, he is mortal. Isn't he?"
Zeus stepped closer, his smile fading. "Is that supposed to be a threat, wife?"
"Of course not, husband." Hera raised one eyebrow. "It's merely an observation."
"Wow," Brody commented to Julia and Markos.
"For a husband and wife, they sure argue a lot."
Suddenly Zeus spun to face the crowd again.
"I just had a wonderful idea," he announced. "Come here, my champion."
Alcides stepped closer. Zeus pulled him over to stand between himself and Hera.
"I've decided to give my champion a new name," Zeus continued.
"One befitting the great champion he will soon become.
A grand name worthy of the grand feats he will soon perform."
Hera scowled at him. "We get the picture," she said. "Get on with it."
Zeus smiled broadly, his eyes twinkling mischievously.
"My champion's new name will also honor my beautiful wife, Hera," he went on.
"From this moment on, he will be known by the name . . . Heracles."
"Zeus' champion is named Heracles?" Brody said as the crowd in the agora cheered.
"That's weird. His name sounds almost like 'Hercules.'"
"He is Hercules, you dummy!" Julia slapped herself on the forehead.
"I knew all those stories about Alcides sounded familiar.
They were about Heracles! I forgot that Zeus renamed him to honor Hera."
"Honor her, or annoy her?" Markos asked.
A shiver went through Brody as he glanced at Hera.
She was glaring at Zeus with fury.
Brody almost expected real fire to shoot out of her eyes—sort of like Ares' hair.
"I still don't understand." Brody turned to face Julia.
"If that's Hercules, why did Zeus just call him Heracles? Did Alcides change his name again later?"
"No. 'Heracles' is the way the Greeks say the name," Julia explained.
"'Hercules' is the way the ancient Romans said it."
"Everyone on TV says 'Hercules' too," Brody said.
"Why can't they all call him the same thing?"
Markos looked troubled. "So you know of Zeus' champion?" he asked slowly. "From the future?"
"Of course." Julia paced back and forth on the tiny roof.
"He's the most famous ancient hero of all time! This changes everything!"
"What do you mean?" Brody was still watching Heracles.
The muscular youth was moving through the crowd, shaking hands and smiling at people.
He was only a few yards away now, so Brody could get a good look at him.
And what he saw made his heart sink.
Heracles seemed to have more muscles than Brody's entire football team put together!
"I mean . . ." Julia stopped pacing. She glanced around to make sure nobody was looking up at them, and then stepped closer to the two boys.
When she spoke again, her voice was low and urgent.
"I mean, Heracles isn't really a mortal. He's half god!
There's no way any true mortal will be able to beat him in the Games."
Markos gasped. "He's half god? So the rumors are true! He's Zeus' son?"
"Yes," Julia said grimly. "And I bet Hera knows it too. Maybe she's jealous of the other woman."
"You up there!" a voice interrupted from below. "Mortal children! Where is Hermes?"
Brody glanced over the edge of the roof.
Apollo and Artemis were looking up at them.
"We don't know where he is," Brody told the two gods.
"He flew off when we got here."
"Well, we need to find him." Apollo vaulted up onto the roof, landing lightly beside Brody. He peered out at the crowd.
"Yes, and quickly," Artemis added, joining her brother.
"This Heracles is much more impressive than we expected.
Perhaps Hermes can help us figure out how to defeat him."
Brody was glad that the gods also seemed worried about Heracles.
At least they realized it would be nearly impossible to beat Zeus' mighty-looking champion.
"I see Hermes!" Artemis pointed with her bow.
Brody caught a glimpse of Hermes hovering above the crowd, halfway across the agora.
Then the messenger god dropped down into the crowd and was lost from view.
"Hurry, sister. Let's catch him before he disappears."
Apollo leaped down from the roof as if it were no higher than a step.
Artemis followed. As she did, the end of her bow hit Julia on the shoulder.
"Oh!" Julia cried, losing her balance.
Brody gasped. Julia was falling off the roof!
"Julia!" He leaped forward, but he was too far away to grab her.
He looked down, expecting to see Julia sprawled on the ground below.
Instead he saw Heracles holding her in his strong arms.
"There you go, miss." Heracles carefully set Julia on her feet.
"Thanks," Julia said breathlessly. She gazed up at Heracles.
"How did you catch me so fast? You probably saved me from a broken leg or something even worse."
"You're welcome." Heracles smiled. "I was happy to help.
This crowd is quite something, isn't it? Zeus loves a big spectacle."
Brody swung down from the roof and landed beside Julia.
"Okay, thanks, dude," he said loudly to Heracles.
"We should probably be going now." He grabbed Julia's arm and tried to drag her away.
But she snatched her arm back. "Do you mind, Brody?" she said. "I'm trying to have a conversation here."
Markos had jumped off the roof too. He was staring at Heracles and looking almost as dazed as Julia.
Brody didn't like the way his friends were acting.
Didn't they realize that Heracles was the enemy? Heracles could ruin everything.
"You must be one of the other athletes," Heracles said to Brody with a friendly smile.
"That's right," Markos put in before Brody could answer.
"He's Hermes' hero. His name is Brody."
"Nice to meet you, Brody," Heracles said.
"What's your favorite event in the Games?
I can't decide, but I think the pentathlon—"
"Heracles, my boy!" Zeus suddenly swooped over and took his champion by the arm.
"Come with me. Hades is dying to meet you." He chuckled.
"Understand my little joke? Hades is the god of the dead, and he's dying to meet you?"
He dragged Heracles away, and they quickly disappeared into the crowd.
Brody glared after Heracles. "I don't like that guy," he muttered.
Julia looked thoughtful. "I don't know," she said slowly. "He actually seems . . . normal."
"Yes," Markos agreed. "Well, except for the huge muscles and amazing speed, of course."
Brody scowled. "Whatever. I just hope Hermes and the other gods come up with a way to get rid of Heracles before the Games."
"Me too," Julia said. "Otherwise he's going to beat everyone—including you, Brody.
And then Hermes might not let us leave." She was quiet for a second.
"I hope Hera doesn't actually send Heracles to Tartarus though.
Remember how she was threatening to do that?"
"She can send him to the moon, as far as I'm concerned," Brody retorted.
"It will make my life easier if I don't have to compete against him!"
Julia frowned at Brody. Heracles was definitely intimidating as an athlete.
But Heracles was a kid, just like them. And he seemed like a nice guy.
"Maybe we should talk to Hermes about a strategy," she suggested.
"Now that he's seen Heracles, he must realize that no mortal will ever beat him.
Maybe he'll even let us go home before the Games."
"Never," Markos stated. "The gods don't give up easily. Especially when it comes to the Games."
"Well, I don't give up either." Brody declared suddenly. He puffed out his chest.
"I'm going to beat Heracles, even if I have to train nonstop between now and the Games."
Julia stared at him. "Are you crazy? A minute ago you were worried about competing against him.
And you saw what Heracles did!" she added.
"He outran a horse! And picked up a giant ram!"
Brody looked stubborn. "I don't have a choice, Julia. And if I keep up the training, I can do it."
Julia shook her head. "This doesn't seem like a real plan, Brody."
"Yeah, well, until you come up with something better, this is what I'm going to do," he shot back.
Julia stomped off to get away from Brody for a few minutes.
This situation was bad, and he didn't even seem to realize it.
All this time she'd been hoping Brody could actually win at the Games.
But now that he was competing against Heracles, she was sure Brody—along with all the other athletes—was going to lose.
Unless the gods managed to sabotage Heracles. Then Brody might have a chance.
As she walked around, she could hear people talking about Heracles.
Everyone still seemed dazzled by Zeus' amazing hero.
Then there was a commotion somewhere near the dais.
Julia looked over there just in time to see Heracles lift Zeus by one ankle!
The king of the gods waved as the crowd cheered.
"Behold the greatest mortal athlete of all time!" Zeus called out.
Suddenly someone grabbed Julia's arm. "Let go," she snapped, yanking it back.
She turned around, expecting to see Brody. Instead Aphrodite was standing there!
Julia gasped. "I—I'm sorry," she babbled. "I thought my friends were . . ."
She was afraid that the goddess would be angry at the way Julia had spoken to her.
But Aphrodite just looked excited. She was staring at Heracles.
"Do you see Zeus' hero, mortal girl?" the goddess said. "I've never seen a mortal so handsome!"
"Um . . ." Julia wasn't sure what to say to that. "He's handsome, I guess."
Luckily Aphrodite didn't seem to care about Julia's reply. She grabbed a passing woman.
"Isn't this exciting?" Aphrodite said. "The Games should be quite interesting this year. Don't you agree, mortal woman?"
Julia slipped out of Aphrodite's view, relieved that she hadn't accidentally offended the goddess.
After Aphrodite's trick with the poisoned chiton, Julia didn't want to take any chances.
Hera and Aphrodite made her especially nervous.
A moment later she saw Brody and Markos coming toward her.
"You missed it!" Brody said. "We just heard Ares and Dionysus talking about Heracles."
"Oh?" Julia glanced at the dais. Heracles had lowered Zeus to the ground.
Now the hero was doing a one-handed handstand while he used his feet to balance a nervous-looking goat.
"Yes," Markos said. "The gods were trying to figure out a way to sabotage Heracles before the Games."
"And after that, we passed Hermes talking to Artemis and Apollo," Brody said.
"They were plotting too." He laughed, looking a bit more cheerful now.
"It sounds like all the gods are making plans to sabotage Heracles."
"That's good for you, for two reasons," Markos told him.
"One, the gods probably won't keep plotting against you, even though you're one of the best mortal athletes in the Games."
"Thanks, dude." Brody grinned broadly. "What's the second reason?"
"Duh." Julia rolled her eyes. "The second reason is they might actually succeed in getting Heracles out of the Games."
"Oh, right." Brody grinned. "Then I can definitely win!"
Suddenly they heard a loud gasp from the crowd. Julia glanced at the dais.
The goat on Heracles' feet had turned into white-hot flames!
"Hephaestus!" Zeus thundered. He pointed at the flames.
Twin lightning bolts shot out of his fingers, and a second later the flames sizzled and disappeared.
Heracles let his legs fall, and then he stood up.
"Thank you, Zeus," he said, bowing. His feet were blackened from the fire, but he didn't show any signs of pain.
Zeus was glaring at a god Julia hadn't seen before.
But based on the god's name—Hephaestus—Julia knew he was the god of fire and the forge.
"How dare you tamper with my hero?" Zeus thundered.
Just then Hera stepped into view behind Hephaestus.
"What's the matter, husband?" she asked in a voice that sent a chill through Julia.
"Are you afraid your hero isn't mighty enough to handle a few friendly pranks?"
"Friendly?" Zeus repeated, shifting his dark glare to her.
Hera took a few steps backward. "You'll soon see just how unfriendly I can be, wife!"
With a deafening thunderclap, he and Heracles both disappeared.
Julia shuddered. "Wow, things are getting serious."
"Yeah, did you see the way Zeus shot that fire right off Heracles' feet?" Brody exclaimed. "It was cool!"
"This isn't a video game, Brody!" Julia snapped.
"We're all in big danger here." She turned to Markos.
"Zeus is obviously guarding Heracles closely. What if the gods don't succeed in getting Heracles out of the Games?"
"Stop worrying, Julia. I'll beat him!" Brody declared. He flexed his muscles.
Julia ignored him as she waited for Markos' reply.
"Zeus is powerful," Markos answered. "But he's only one god.
The other gods can band together to outwit him. They will probably succeed."
"I hope you're right," Julia said slowly.
But as she watched Hera cross the dais, Julia felt a fresh wave of worry. What lay ahead for all of them?
"Grab it, boy!" Hermes shouted.
Brody grunted and pushed himself up on his hands and knees again.
An hour earlier Hermes had finished plotting with some other gods and dragged Brody away from the agora.
They'd returned to the gymnasium to continue Brody's training.
At the moment Hermes was making Brody practice wrestling.
But instead of wrestling another athlete, or Hermes, Brody was following Hermes' orders and wrestling a greased pig!
The creature was slippery and mean. It had already bitten Brody twice.
Plus it was nearly impossible for Brody to get a grip on its slick skin.
"Try grabbing its legs!" Markos shouted helpfully from the sidelines.
He stood there with Julia and Caerus, along with a small crowd.
"Every time I try that, the pig kicks me!" Brody complained.
Apollo roared with laughter. "Thanks for the show, Hermes," he said, clapping the messenger god on the shoulder.
"I was in a foul mood after getting a look at Zeus' impressive hero.
But watching your champion make a fool of himself has lightened my mood!"
"Don't get too happy, sun god," Hermes warned.
"You won't be laughing when my mortal beats yours in the Games."
"Neither mortal is likely to beat Heracles," Artemis chimed in.
"After what we saw today, I'm certain that Heracles cannot be defeated in the Games."
"Speak for your own champion, moon goddess," Hermes said.
Then he strode over and grabbed the pig. He placed the animal down.
"Get back to work, boy," he snapped at Brody.
Brody glanced at his audience with a frown. He didn't like being laughed at.
But he didn't dare disobey Hermes. So he wrapped his arms around the pig again.
It squealed and tried to bite him on the ear.
Brody's hands almost slipped again, but he finally managed to pin down the pig.
"There!" he yelled triumphantly. He let the pig go and jumped to his feet. "Now what?"
"Well done." Hermes sounded a little happier with Brody.
"Now we return to improving your running. Your times in the short races still aren't satisfactory."
"Brody's times will have to be better than satisfactory if he expects to beat Heracles," Julia muttered to Markos.
Hermes didn't seem to hear her, but Brody did.
He scowled as he walked past her, following Hermes.
For the next hour, Hermes kept Brody working hard, making him sprint and do various other exercises.
Just as Brody was about to ask for a break to catch his breath, Caerus hurried toward Hermes.
"Dionysus has invited us to dine with him," he said.
"Come. Let us see if he has new ideas about how to solve the Heracles problem."
Hermes nodded. "Dionysus is lazy, but he does have a creative mind."
He glanced at Brody. "I'll be back soon. Keep training while I'm gone."
"Okay," Brody said.
But as soon as the two gods were out of sight, Brody collapsed onto the ground near Julia and Markos.
"Wake me up when you see Hermes coming back," he said, closing his eyes.
"Are you sure you don't want to keep training?" Markos sounded nervous.
"Some of the other gods might tell Hermes you disobeyed him."
"Yeah," Julia added. "And I thought you were trying your hardest to beat Heracles."
"I am." Brody opened his eyes and then jumped to his feet.
"Thanks for the reminder, Julia. Back to training. I was just getting in the zone, anyway."
He did a few jumping jacks to get warmed up again, followed by some push-ups.
"Uh-oh!" Julia burst out. "Look who's here."
Brody glanced at the entrance. Heracles and his brother Iphicles had just walked into the gymnasium.
"Zeus isn't with them," Markos whispered. "I'm surprised Zeus would let Heracles out of his sight.
Especially with all the other gods eager to sabotage Heracles."
Brody squared his shoulders. "Hey, loser!" he called to Heracles. "What are you doing here?"
Iphicles frowned. "Who are you calling a loser?" he called back. "My brother is—"
"It's all right, Iphicles." Heracles put a hand on his brother's arm.
Then he nodded at Brody and his friends. "It's good to see you three again."
"Yes." Julia shot Brody a warning look. "It's good to see you too.
Sorry about Brody's outburst. He's kind of competitive."
Heracles smiled. "No hard feelings. We came to take a look at the gymnasium.
Zeus has kept me so deep in the hills, I thought I would never get to see any of Olympia!"
Julia and Markos chuckled, but Brody didn't. Why were the two of them acting so friendly to Heracles?
Brody couldn't imagine being friends with his football team's biggest rivals. In fact, whenever he saw those jerks from Southbridge High—
"I saw you warming up," Heracles suddenly remarked to Brody. "You have good form."
"Oh . . . uh, thanks," Brody said.
"You looked good racing that horse," Julia blurted out. "You can run so fast."
Heracles laughed and looked a little embarrassed. "That was Zeus' idea.
I wish he'd stop making me show off. I'd rather spend my time training."
"You'd better not let Zeus hear you say that, brother," Iphicles warned him.
"True." Heracles chuckled. "Zeus hates when anyone questions him."
"That sounds like Hermes," Brody chimed in. "He orders me around all the time."
Just then a cranky-looking god rushed in with a whoosh of wind.
"Heracles! Zeus wants you to join him in the hippodrome for some more chariot racing."
"Yes, Boreas," Heracles said. Brody thought he saw Heracles sigh.
"I'm coming." He looked at Brody and his friends. "See you later, everyone."
Julia and Markos smiled and waved good-bye, and to his surprise, Brody found himself lifting a hand too.
"See you," Brody said. "Good luck with the training."
Julia watched as Brody started doing more push-ups.
"It's hard to believe we were just talking to the real Heracles!" she said, thinking about all the stories she'd read about the mighty hero.
"I mean, he's really famous. Everyone has heard of Heracles."
Brody sat up and glared at her. "You sound like you're talking about a rock star or something, Julia," he snapped.
"The guy seems nice. But don't forget, he is the main thing standing between us and a trip home.
What did he do anyway that was so great?"
"Heracles did all sorts of interesting things," Julia answered.
"Some things were bad, but a lot of them were good.
For instance, he saved Prometheus from having an eagle peck out his liver over and over again."
"Prometheus? Who's that?" Brody asked.
"He was a Titan—that's a different kind of god," Julia explained.
"I'm pretty sure Prometheus is the one who created humans out of clay.
He also gave humans fire, which made Zeus mad.
So Zeus set up the pecking as punishment.
But eventually Heracles came along and set Prometheus free."
Markos looked confused. "When did this happen? Does Zeus know that Heracles did that?"
Julia shrugged. "I guess it hasn't happened yet," she replied.
"It probably happens later, when Heracles is an adult."
Ares rushed toward them. "Was that Heracles I saw leaving a little while ago?" he demanded.
"Yes, Ares," Markos said with a bow. "He came to see the gymnasium, but Zeus summoned him before he got to look around."
The war god's eyes widened. "You mean Heracles was here without Zeus?" he thundered. "I missed my chance to destroy him!"
The war god's hair burst into flames, and he gnashed his teeth in anger.
Julia jumped back to avoid being burned by the sparks flying off Ares' head.
Meanwhile Apollo wandered over. He smirked at the war god.
"Are you having a tantrum, Ares? " he asked. "And in front of mortals—tsk, tsk."
"Silence, sun god." Ares glared at Apollo. "You should be upset too.
Zeus' mighty champion was here alone just now, and we all missed him! It was our chance for sabotage!"
"He wasn't alone," Brody put in. "His brother was with him."
He turned to Julia. "What's the brother's name?"
"Iphicles." Julia wished Brody would stop talking to the gods.
Ares was another one who made her nervous, with his hot temper and fiery powers.
And Apollo wasn't much better. She knew he was supposed to be Hermes' friend, but he seemed pretty sneaky.
"Never mind," Apollo told Ares. "We'll put an end to Zeus' bragging one way or another."
With a toss of his head, he suddenly changed into a huge, strange-looking creature.
It had the head, wings, and talons of an eagle and the body of a lion.
It let out a terrifying scream while pawing the ground.
"Whoa!" Brody said.
"That's a griffin," Julia said, trying to hide her fear. "It's a legendary creature."
"Yes." Ares sounded bored. "It's one of Apollo's favorites.
I don't see how turning into one is going to help him get rid of Heracles though."
Apollo transformed back into his usual shape.
"Perhaps it won't help," he said with another smirk at Ares.
"But sooner or later, I'll find a way to sabotage Zeus' mighty hero. Just you watch."
"Only if I don't find a way to sabotage him first," Ares said.
Julia shivered as a creepy grin slid across the war god's face.
She definitely wouldn't want to be in Heracles' sandals right now.
All of the gods were conspiring against him.
Just then Artemis called Apollo's name from across the gymnasium.
Apollo hurried off to see what she wanted.
To Julia's relief Ares soon wandered away too.
"Wow," Brody said. "A griffin would make a really cool football team mascot.
Maybe I'll talk to the coach about changing our mascot to one when we get back."
"Don't you mean if we get back?" Julia muttered.
"I'm sure the gods will come up with something for Heracles," Markos said quickly.
"That reminds me, Brody. You should get back to training in case Hermes returns."
"Okay. It looks like there's nobody at the discus station right now," Brody said. "I'll practice throwing the discus next."
Julia and Markos followed him across the gymnasium.
A discus was lying on the grass. As Brody stooped to grab it, Julia's eyes widened.
"Stop!" she cried. "Don't touch that discus. It looks strange. See? The top is shiny, like a mirror."
"So what?" Brody sounded impatient. "I can throw it whether there's a mirror on it or not."
"Don't, Brody," she urged him. "I have a feeling something's wrong.
Maybe you should look for a different discus, just in case."
She could tell that Brody was about to start arguing with her again.
But at that moment, a large fly buzzed past the kids and landed on the mirrored discus.
Suddenly the mirror flickered—and the fly was sucked into it!
Brody gasped and leaned closer. "Did you see that? That fly is gone!"
"We should get away from here," Markos murmured. He looked nervous.
"That discus appears to be some trickery of the gods—probably Aphrodite."
"I think you're right," Julia agreed with a nod.
It made sense that the vain goddess of beauty would use a mirror for a prank.
Brody looked at Julia. "Thanks," he said, sounding a little sheepish. "You saved me."
"You're welcome," Julia replied. She turned away to hide her surprise.
As far as she could remember, that was the nicest thing Brody had ever said to her.
But before she could think any more about that, Hermes returned and put Brody back to work.
"Wow, it's crowded here today," Brody said.
It was the following morning. Brody was walking into the gymnasium with Hermes, Julia, and Markos.
Some gods were already there, along with their champions.
There were several gods Brody had never seen before, including a goddess with flowers sprouting in her hair and floating out of her mouth.
He also spotted a god with the legs and horns of a goat.
"The opening of the Games is drawing near," Markos reminded him.
"Naturally, everyone wants to be ready."
"Right. Including us," Hermes said. "We'll start with boxing today."
"Do you want me to spar with Brody, Hermes?" Markos asked, sounding nervous.
"No," Hermes replied. "I want you and the girl to wander around Olympia.
Find out everything you can about Heracles."
Markos bowed. "As you wish, Hermes. We'll return when we have news."
He and Julia hurried away. Brody felt disappointed.
To his surprise he liked having the two of them around while he worked out.
"I can't believe I actually like hanging around with a couple of nerds," he thought.
He forgot about that when Hermes dragged him over to a goddess wearing a veil and holding a staff.
She was watching her champion, a stout youth with long black hair.
"Greetings, Hestia," Hermes said. "My champion needs a sparring partner.
What do you say? Shall our champions box?"
The goddess eyed Brody. "I suppose that would be all right," she said.
"My champion hasn't had much chance to practice his boxing in Olympia.
Probably because his reputation as the best boxer in Greece has scared off the competition."
"We'll see about that," Hermes said with a chuckle.
He shoved Brody forward. "Get to it, boy!"
Brody nodded and lifted his fists. The other athlete did the same.
"Hi," Brody said as he sent off a jab with his left fist. "I'm Brody."
"Yes, I've seen you around the agora," the other boy said. "I'm Timon."
"Nice to meet you." Brody let his right fist fly.
"Oof!" Timon grunted as Brody's punch landed on his beefy shoulder.
"Pay attention, Timon!" Hestia called. "You'll need to do better than that if you wish to defeat Heracles."
Hestia and Hermes watched the two boys box for a while, calling out orders and encouragement.
But eventually they started to look bored.
Finally they wandered off to talk to Apollo, who was watching his champion run nearby.
Brody was pretty sure he heard Hermes ask Apollo if he'd seen Heracles that day.
"I wish they'd all stop talking about Heracles," Timon grumbled.
"I know what you mean." Brody dodged a punch.
Then he easily landed a punch on the other boy's chest.
"Ow!" Timon complained, rubbing the spot. "Look. Hera just arrived."
"Really?" Brody turned to look. Pain exploded in his chin as Timon's fist landed there. "Hey!"
"Sorry." Timon grinned. "I had to retaliate. Now we're even."
"Fine," Brody grumbled, rubbing his chin. He turned his attention back to Hera.
The queen of the gods was striding across the gymnasium. Her champion was jogging to keep up.
"Maybe she's here looking for Zeus and Heracles," Timon whispered.
Brody nodded. "I bet you're right. They're not here, are they?"
"No," Timon said. "Zeus knows everyone is out to get him.
He's probably only letting his champion out in public for short times."
Hermes and Hestia saw the boys watching Hera and hurried over.
"What are you two staring at?" Hermes demanded. "Get back to work.
No, wait," he added as Brody raised his fists.
"That's enough boxing for now. Come, boy."
Before Brody knew it, Hermes was dragging him away.
Brody soon realized why. Julia and Markos had just returned.
"Well?" Hermes demanded when he reached them.
"You were not gone very long. You must have learned something interesting."
"We did," Julia said. "Everyone is saying that Zeus has hidden Heracles in the hills again.
Zeus might not bring Heracles back to Olympia until just before the Games."
Hermes scowled. "Is that all the information you have?"
Markos looked nervous. "We thought you would want that news right away.
We can try to find out more if you wish."
Meanwhile Julia stared at Brody. "You look tired," she said.
"I do?" Brody was surprised. He didn't feel tired at all.
Boxing wasn't very strenuous compared to some of the things Hermes made him do.
"Yes." Julia faced Hermes. "Brody still seems quite easily winded, don't you think?"
"Does he?" Hermes turned to study Brody with interest.
"Definitely," Julia said. "We heard that Zeus is making Heracles run up and down the steepest hills he can find, so the champion can get fitter.
Maybe Brody should do that too."
"Huh?" Now Brody was annoyed. What was Julia doing?
The last thing he wanted was even more exercise!
But Hermes was nodding. "You know, I was thinking along those lines myself earlier," he said.
"Thank you for the reminder, mortal girl."
"Julia and I can accompany Brody while he runs," Markos suggested.
"We can keep track of his speed for you, Hermes.
I'm sure you have other important business to attend to."
"Indeed I do. I was about to suggest the same thing."
Hermes plucked a feather from the wing on his sandal.
He let it drift toward the ground—and halfway there, it turned into a chariot with wings sprouting out of its sides!
"Wow!" Brody said. "But where are the horses?"
"No horses required. Get in, mortals," Hermes said.
Markos and Julia climbed into the chariot.
When Brody started to follow, Hermes stopped him.
"You go on foot, boy," he said. "Now get moving!"
Brody sighed and jogged toward the nearest exit.
Out of the corner of his eye, he saw the chariot floating after him.
He couldn't wait to get out of Hermes' earshot.
He wanted to tell Julia exactly what he thought of her terrible idea to make him run up and down the steep hills outside of Olympia!
"Faster," Julia called to Brody. He was jogging slowly up a path leading out of the city and into the surrounding hills.
"We don't want Hermes to change his mind."
Brody stopped so suddenly that the winged chariot almost bumped into him.
"We don't?" he echoed, sounding grumpy. "Maybe you don't want Hermes to change his mind, Julia.
But I'm sure ready. It wasn't my idea to spend the day running up and down some stupid hills!"
"Shh!" Markos glanced over his shoulder. "Just keep going, Brody, please.
We'll explain when we're out of sight of the city."
Julia thought Brody was going to argue. But he turned and jogged away.
Finally they were on the other side of a hill.
Brody stopped running and sat down on a log. "Okay, it's time to explain.
Why did you convince Hermes to make me run out here?"
"We heard Heracles is training in these hills," Julia said. "Remember? We even told Hermes that."
"So what?" Brody still sounded grumpy.
"So don't you want to see what he's doing out here?" Julia said.
"Maybe we can figure out a way to beat him in the Games." She hesitated, not sure if she should admit the next part.
"Besides, if we find him, I want to warn him that all the other gods are plotting against him."
"What? Why?" Brody asked. Markos looked surprised too.
Julia shrugged. "Because he seems nice," she said.
"Because he saved me when I fell off the roof.
I just feel like it's the right thing to do."
But Brody was shaking his head. "Bad idea," he declared.
"Heracles already has enough advantages in the Games.
We should let the gods do whatever they're going to do, because it's none of our business."
"Brody is right," Markos agreed. "Besides, Julia, Zeus has surely warned Heracles of the dangers."
Julia frowned. "I hope so. But in case Zeus hasn't . . ."
"Look." Markos pointed to the next hill. "Smoke!"
"Do you think that's Heracles?" Julia asked.
Brody looked at her. "Would anybody else be hanging around out here in the middle of nowhere? Come on, let's go see."
He hurried off. Julia stared at the smoke twirling its way into the sky.
The magical chariot seemed to know which way she wanted it to go.
It stayed right beside Brody as he jogged in the direction of the smoke.
For a while it was easy to track the smoke over one hill and up another.
Then they reached a dense thicket of shrubs and vines.
The chariot stopped, hovering at the edge of the thicket.
"The chariot cannot travel through there," Markos said.
Julia nodded. "I guess we'll have to go on foot from here."
As soon as they climbed out of the chariot, it disappeared with a poof of smoke.
"Yikes!" Julia said.
Markos laughed at her surprised look. "I see you're still getting used to the ways of the gods, Julia."
The three of them pushed their way through the thicket.
Vines tangled around Julia's legs, threatening to trip her.
Thorny branches grabbed at her chiton and scratched her bare arms.
But finally the underbrush thinned out. The smell of smoke was stronger now.
Brody was in the lead when the group reached the other side of the thicket.
He pushed aside one last clump of thorny vines and then halted.
"What are you waiting for?" Julia poked him in the back. "Keep going!"
"Uh, I don't think so," Brody said quietly.
He moved aside so Julia could see what lay ahead.
She gasped. An enormous forge was built into a tall rock wall.
And standing in front of the fire were Hera and Hephaestus.
"Uh-oh," Markos muttered. "We'd better get out of here before they see us."
He spun around to lead the way back into the thicket.
But his foot caught on a vine, and he went sprawling with a loud "oof!"
"Who's there?" Hera's sharp voice rang out.
"Run!" Brody yelled.
Julia tried to do as he said. But she'd only taken a few steps when she was surrounded by a cloud of buzzing insects.
She heard Brody and Markos yelling in dismay nearby.
Julia tried to stop herself from screaming so the insects wouldn't fly into her mouth.
But she couldn't help crying out when she felt the flies lift her and carry her away.
A moment later the cloud of flies dropped Julia in front of the two gods. Brody and Markos landed beside her.
"Well, well. Who have we here?" Hephaestus' craggy face was curious but not unkind as he stared at them.
Hera, on the other hand, looked as unpleasant and scary as ever.
"I believe I recognize this mortal," she said, poking Brody in the chest with one long, thin finger. "You're Hermes' hero, aren't you, boy?"
"That's right," Brody said. "I'm Brody."
"I always knew that Hermes was foolish." Hera sneered.
"But I didn't know he was foolish enough to allow his mortal champion to wander these hills without his protection.
After all, it can be quite dangerous out here. Isn't that right, son?"
She turned and gave Hephaestus a meaningful look.
Hephaestus smiled. "You're right as usual, Mother," he said.
He grabbed an enormous pair of metal tongs and used them to reach into the fire.
When he drew the tongs out, they were gripping a large metal object.
The object was so bright and hot from the flames that Julia had trouble looking directly at it.
Hephaestus set the object down. Now Julia saw what it was—a giant metal statue of a bull with sharp, curved horns.
Then there was a snort, and black smoke puffed out of the statue's flared nostrils.
Julia gasped as the huge metal bull suddenly clanked into motion, pawing at the ground and tossing its massive head.
"Run!" Brody yelled.
"This way!" Brody shouted. He grabbed Julia, who seemed to be frozen with terror, and yanked her into motion.
Markos was already sprinting ahead of them, away from the charging metal bull.
"What is that thing?" Julia cried as she ran alongside Brody.
"The bull is made of metal, but it acts like it's alive! That's so weird!"
Brody shot her a surprised look. "Now you think things are weird?" he said.
"You didn't seem to think it was weird to ride in a flying chariot. Or to travel back in time either."
"Please," Markos called over his shoulder. "There is no time for talking right now!"
Brody saw that the sheer rock wall continued to their right for as far as he could see.
So did the thorny thicket on their left. Just ahead he spotted a forest.
"Keep going," Brody said. "Maybe the bull can't fit between the tree trunks."
Brody was right—sort of. The metal bull was still charging after them.
But when the kids darted into the forest, the bull halted, roaring with fury.
"Clever strategy, Brody!" Markos cried breathlessly. "We stopped him."
Julia gasped. "No, we didn't—keep running!"
The bull was already ramming its way forward.
Tree trunks cracked and fell in every direction.
Soon the kids found themselves running out of the far end of the forest.
Once again they were trapped in an open area between the high rock wall and the thorny thicket.
"What are we going to do?" Julia glanced over her shoulder at the bull.
"Run faster!" Brody yelled back.
"Easy for you to say, champion," Markos grumbled breathlessly.
Brody didn't answer. He'd just spotted something ahead. "Uh-oh."
The others looked ahead too. "Oh no!" Julia cried.
A short distance from them, the rock wall curved out, blocking their way completely!
"What are we going to do?" Julia cried again.
"We'll have to try going back through the thicket," Markos said. "Perhaps that will slow the bull."
"That won't work," Brody pointed out. "That metal bull won't feel any scratches.
It will charge through faster than we can go."
They reached the rock wall and skidded to a stop.
Julia stared up at the sheer cliff. "What other choice do we have?" she said.
Brody glanced at the bull, which was still coming at them. "I don't know," he said, feeling frantic.
The cliff didn't have a single handhold that he could see—they couldn't climb to safety that way.
He looked around for a sturdy branch or anything else he could use as a weapon.
Maybe he could fight off the bull long enough for Julia and Markos to crawl through the thicket to safety.
"Hello down there!" a voice called from overhead. "Look up! I'm throwing you a rope!"
Brody gasped and looked up. A face was peering down at them. It was Heracles!
"Hurry!" Another face appeared beside Heracles—his brother, Iphicles.
"The bull automaton will reach you in a moment!"
A thick rope dropped down near them. Heracles was holding the other end.
"Grab hold of it," Heracles called. "Now!"
"All of us?" Markos looked worried. "But how can you . . . you can't possibly—"
"Hurry!" Iphicles yelled. "It's coming!"
He was right. The bull was charging toward them.
"Oh well," Brody said. "Here goes nothing."
He grabbed the rope with both hands. So did Julia and Markos.
"We're ready!" Markos called.
"They can't do this, can they?" Julia's voice was shaking.
"They can't possibly lift all three of us at once. Not all the way up that cliff!"
"Heracles lifted that wagon by himself," Brody reminded her. He tried to sound confident.
But inside he was just as scared as Julia looked.
What if Heracles dropped them when they were halfway up that cliff? They could all be killed!
Then Brody would never get to be in the Olympic Games. He'd never return home.
He'd never play football again, or see his parents, or . . .
Brody was so busy worrying, he almost didn't notice when his feet left the ground.
He snapped back to reality when Markos shouted in his ear.
"Hurry!" Markos yelled, sounding terrified. "It's almost here!"
"Brody," Julia said. "Lift your feet! Quick!"
Brody did as she said. He felt something swish past under one sandal.
When he looked down, he gulped as he realized it was one of the bull's sharp metal horns.
Up above he could hear Heracles grunting with effort as he slowly, slowly pulled them up.
Finally Brody and the others were safe at the top of the cliff.
"Thanks, dude!" Brody said to Heracles. "Hera and Hephaestus tried to kill us with that bull statue!"
"It's an automaton—that's an animated statue.
Hephaestus frequently creates them." Iphicles peered down at the bull.
"We should get away from here," he added.
"If the automaton returns to Hera and Hephaestus, they could come looking for us."
"Good thinking, brother." Heracles smiled at the others.
"Are you strong enough to walk, or should I carry you?"
Brody blinked. Heracles might be even stronger than Brody had realized, but that didn't mean Brody was a wimp!
"No, we're fine," he said quickly, and his friends nodded.
Iphicles was already hurrying off. Brody and the others followed, not talking much until they'd walked for at least twenty minutes.
Finally Heracles stopped his brother with a hand on the shoulder. "Let's rest here."
Brody looked around. They were in a pleasant clearing with a babbling brook running through it.
He walked over and splashed cool water on his face.
The kids all sat down together. For a few moments, nobody seemed to know what to say. Brody felt awkward.
Heracles was supposed to be his enemy, but he'd just saved Brody's life.
Now what was Brody supposed to think of him?
Julia felt as if she were living in a story from her social studies textbook. Heracles' strength was amazing.
No wonder everyone was still talking about him thousands of years later.
Finally she couldn't hold her feelings in any longer.
"Wow," she blurted out. "I can't believe I'm sitting here with the real, live hero Heracles!"
Heracles looked surprised. "What do you mean?"
Iphicles rolled his eyes. "What do you think she means, brother? Everyone in Greece wants to meet you.
Thanks to Zeus' bragging, you're nearly as famous as the king of the gods himself."
"It's not that," Julia said, blushing. "It's just, I've heard so many of the Greek myths . . ."
She realized she was babbling, but she couldn't stop. "And you know . . ."
"Myths?" Heracles looked puzzled. "About me?"
"Trust me, someday you'll perform great feats," Julia replied.
"You'll be one of the most famous heroes ever."
Iphicles frowned at Julia. "It's bad enough that Zeus keeps filling Alcides' head with dreams of glory.
You don't have to make up even wilder tales."
Julia felt annoyed by his challenging tone. She didn't notice that Brody was also frowning at her.
"I'm not making up anything," she snapped. "It's all true."
"How could you possibly know that?" Iphicles shot back.
"Because we come from the future!" Julia retorted.
Then she gulped, realizing she'd said too much. "Um, I mean. . ."
Heracles looked stunned. "The future? You are oracles?"
"Not exactly." Julia finally noticed that Brody was making faces at her.
But it was too late to take back her words.
She took a deep breath. "Uh, you know Hermes' friend Caerus? I believe he's the god of time?"
"He's the god of opportunity and favorable moments," Iphicles said.
"I suppose he has something to do with time as well. What of him?"
Markos spoke up. "He created a crack in his temple.
He used the crack to bring Brody here from the future."
"Yeah," Brody put in. "Hermes wanted me to be his champion. And Julia came along by accident."
It took a little more explaining, but eventually Heracles and Iphicles seemed to believe their tale.
"So I will be a hero?" Heracles asked thoughtfully. "That's good.
I was beginning to think I might not even survive these Games."
Julia chuckled. "You'll survive. And you'll defeat horrible monsters and achieve great feats of strength."
"Good." Heracles nodded. "What else? Will I marry and have children?"
Julia hesitated. She didn't remember all the details of Heracles' personal life, but some of what she remembered wasn't very good.
"Uh, I think so," she said.
"What about me?" Iphicles' dark eyes were sharp and eager.
"Will I be famous as well? Perhaps for feats of horsemanship?"
Julia gulped. She'd barely remembered that Heracles had a brother, and she had no idea what became of him.
"Er, you like horses?" she asked, hoping to change the subject.
"Iphicles is the finest hand with horses this side of Sparta," Heracles said proudly. He clapped Iphicles on the back.
But Iphicles was still staring at Julia. "Well? What happens to me?"
Julia thought about making up a story, but she could tell that Iphicles was smart. He probably wouldn't fall for a lie.
"I don't know," she admitted. "I'm sorry. I'm sure you will have a fantastic life, though.
I mean, you're Heracles' brother, right? That's pretty awesome."
Iphicles frowned and turned away without a word.
Heracles shot him a worried look. "Never mind the distant future," he said.
"Right now I'm supposed to be training, and so are you, Brody. Should we practice together for the Games?"
"I guess we could do that," Brody said, sounding a little uncertain.
"Good." Heracles smiled at Julia and Markos.
"You can join in too, if you like. It'll be fun."
They started with a running race. At first Iphicles was going to sit out, but Heracles talked him into joining in.
"Ready . . . go!" Heracles shouted.
Julia didn't like running in gym class. But this was different.
She was out in the fresh air, in ancient Greece, with a real live hero beside her.
"Yeah!" she yelled as she sprinted with the others.
Brody soon pulled ahead, with Iphicles close behind him.
Julia was surprised that Heracles was just keeping pace with her and Markos.
She was certain that Heracles wasn't running as fast as he could, but she didn't mind.
"I win!" Brody yelled as he crossed the finish line.
He grabbed a rock and threw it at the ground, like a football player spiking a football.
Iphicles stared at him in confusion. "What are you doing?" he asked.
"Spiking the ball." Brody grinned. "Hey, that gives me a great idea—let's play football!"
"Football?" Heracles glanced down at his feet.
Julia groaned. "Football? Really?" But she couldn't help smiling.
For once, football actually sounded like fun.
Brody explained the rules of the game.
The others were confused at first, including Julia, who barely knew anything about football.
But finally they all understood enough to get started.
Brody pointed at Julia and Iphicles. "You're on my team. Markos, you get Heracles. He counts as two players."
Heracles chuckled. "Fair enough."
After several plays Julia was laughing so hard she could barely hold onto the piece of wood they were using as a ball.
Heracles kept running in the wrong direction.
And Markos liked to stop and spike the ball at random times.
But nobody seemed to mind the mistakes.
They were all having fun—for the first time since Julia had arrived in ancient Greece.
"Okay, that's a first down," Brody called as he tagged Markos. "Now we have to—"
Boom!
His words were drowned out by a deafening clap of thunder.
Lightning tore across the clear blue sky.
Heracles gasped. "Quick!" he yelled, shoving Julia and her friends toward the woods.
"You have to get out of sight—Zeus is coming!"
Brody dived behind a boulder and so did Julia.
Markos flattened himself on the ground nearby.
With another blast of thunder, Zeus appeared in the clearing.
"Heracles!" he exclaimed. "There you are. Come with me, boy.
Poseidon still doesn't believe you're as strong as I say you are.
Let's show him exactly how wrong he is. He's at the agora right now."
"Yes, Zeus." Heracles grabbed Iphicles, and then Zeus made the three of them disappear.
Brody stood up. "Okay, why did we have to hide?" he asked, his ears still ringing from all the loud thunder.
Markos stood too. "Because Zeus may not like Heracles mingling with the other athletes."
"Yes, and Zeus knows that everybody in Olympia is trying to sabotage Heracles," Julia added.
"He never would have believed we were just playing football together.
Maybe Heracles was trying to protect us." Julia's face suddenly turned gloomy.
"What's wrong?" Brody asked.
Julia bit her lip. "I didn't tell Heracles everything I know about his future."
Markos frowned. "I'm not sure it was wise to tell him your secret either."
"I know," Julia replied. "I didn't mean to say anything—the truth just came out.
But I don't think he or Iphicles will tell anyone else about us."
"I think you're right," Brody agreed.
Markos was watching Julia's face. "You said Heracles would become a great hero. What more is there to tell?"
"Yes, that part is true," Julia said.
She wandered back into the clearing and sat down beside the stream.
"He'll free Prometheus, as I said before.
He helps the Argonauts search for the Golden Fleece.
He defeats lots of bad guys, helps lots of ordinary people, kills some nasty monsters, and does many other things.
And of course there are the Labors of Heracles—12 very difficult tasks that he completes.
But I definitely didn't want to tell him the reason he must perform these Labors."
"What's the reason?" Brody asked.
Julia shook her head. "Brody, didn't you pay attention at all last year?"
He smiled sheepishly. "I had social studies class at the end of the day. I missed it a lot for football games."
"Right—football." Julia's tone was sarcastic. "Well, Heracles has to complete the 12 Labors as punishment for killing his own children."
Brody gasped. "Really? He kills his own children?"
Markos looked shocked too. "No wonder you didn't want to tell him that."
Julia nodded. "Yes. But he only kills his kids because Hera uses her powers to drive him insane," she added.
"That's no surprise," Brody said. "She already seems to hate him."
"Probably because she has guessed that Zeus is Heracles' father," Markos said. "She is very jealous."
Brody kicked a stone into the stream. "Then why doesn't Hera tell everyone that Heracles is half god?" he asked.
"Wouldn't he get kicked out of the Games then?
Having a half god compete against the rest of us would be like having a professional football player compete in a high school game!"
"That's actually a good analogy," Julia told him with a smile.
"Thanks." Brody wasn't sure what an analogy was, but he didn't want to admit that.
Julia rarely complimented him, and he didn't want to ruin the moment.
"It's a good question too." Markos looked thoughtful. "Maybe Hera isn't sure she's right yet."
"Or maybe she has a worse punishment in mind," Julia said grimly.
"Like the stuff we heard about her wanting to send Heracles to Tartarus."
Brody didn't like to think about that, especially now that he knew what a nice guy Heracles was.
"Let's go back to Olympia," he said. "I don't want to stay out here too long and make Hermes think we're trying to run away again."
"Okay." Julia stood up and looked around. "Which way is Olympia from here?"
She and Brody both looked at Markos.
"I'm not sure," Markos admitted. "I could probably find it if we could get back down that cliff."
"But we can't," Brody said.
"And we don't want to." Julia shuddered.
"We would have to go past Hephaestus' forge that way." She bit her lip.
"What if we can't find our way back before dark?"
That reminded Brody of something. He squinted up toward the sun. "I think I can find the way."
"You can?" Julia sounded surprised. "How?"
"I used to go camping with my cousins a lot before I got too busy with football."
Brody smiled, thinking back on those days. "It was a blast! My cousins are older, and they taught me a lot.
