One of the things they taught me was how to use the position of the sun to find my way around."
"Good idea!" Markos looked relieved.
Julia seemed skeptical, but she shrugged. "Okay, it's worth a try," she said. "Lead the way, Brody."
"I will." Brody remembered all the times the sun had made him squint while trying to follow the javelin or discus he'd just thrown.
He used those memories, combined with the sun's current position, to figure out which direction to start walking.
And it worked. Within half an hour, the kids found a wide dirt road.
"I recognize where we are," Markos said with relief.
"It's just a 15-minute walk to the agora from here."
"Wow." Julia looked impressed. "Good job, Brody."
Brody smiled. "Thanks." Before he could say anything else, there was a shout from behind.
Several young men were hurrying along the road.
Brody recognized one of them as Apollo's champion.
"Are you on your way to the agora to see Heracles?" Apollo's champion asked Brody.
"Um, I don't know," Brody said. "Why?"
"Haven't you heard?" One of the other youths grinned.
"Zeus is showing him off again. We can't wait to see what he does this time!"
"Yeah." Brody exchanged a look with his friends. "We can't wait either."
Julia was shocked at the size of the crowd gathered in the agora.
Once again she and the two boys had to climb onto a rooftop to see what was going on.
"Hey! Check it out!" Brody said, pointing to something in the ground. "What is that?"
"It looks like a huge pit," Julia said. "Where did that come from? It wasn't there before."
"I'm guessing it's Hades' work," Markos said. "Zeus probably asked him to create it.
See? Zeus is making Heracles carry cattle up from the bottom."
Julia squinted to see better. Sure enough, she soon spotted Heracles climbing the rough dirt wall of the pit.
He had a full-grown cow slung across his broad shoulders.
Several more cows were milling around at the bottom of the pit, looking confused.
The animal Heracles was holding was mooing with fear and kicking its hooves. But Heracles hardly seemed to notice.
Within moments he climbed out of the pit and set the cow in front of Zeus, who was standing on the dais.
"Behold my hero!" the king of the gods shouted.
The crowd cheered as Heracles returned to the pit and started climbing back down.
"Look, Iphicles is standing behind Zeus," Markos said.
"You're right." Julia peered at Heracles' brother.
"He doesn't look very happy about what's happening."
"Maybe he's worried that Zeus is making Heracles work too hard," Brody suggested.
"He might wear him out before the Games."
Julia shot Brody a questioning look. Was he still hoping he could beat Heracles at the Games?
But Brody just looked worried as he watched Heracles bring another cow out of the pit.
"Behold!" Zeus cried again. "And my champion is not even tired!
You might as well award me—I mean Heracles—the Olympic champion's laurel wreath right now!"
"No chance of that, Zeus," Apollo called from the crowd.
He was standing with Artemis and Hermes.
"The Games will proceed as planned, and we'll have to wait to see who emerges as champion."
"That's right." Hera stepped into view from behind Zeus.
Zeus jumped, clearly startled by his wife's sudden appearance.
"Oh, good," he said. "My lovely wife has arrived."
Hera stepped closer to Zeus. Iphicles sidled away, looking nervous. The crowd went silent.
"Did you come to cheer on my champion, my dear?" Zeus asked with a smirk.
"Hardly." Hera peered over the edge of the pit at Heracles.
He was climbing up with another cow across his shoulders.
Hera waved her hand.
A shimmer of amber light filled the agora, and suddenly all the cattle disappeared, including the one Heracles was carrying.
Heracles gasped, thrown off balance by the abrupt disappearance of his heavy burden.
"Oh no!" Julia exclaimed as the hero started to slip down the crumbling wall of the pit.
But Heracles caught himself a moment later.
The crowd sighed with relief as he climbed out of the pit.
"That was a nasty trick," Zeus said, glaring at Hera.
"I thought we all agreed not to tamper with one another's mortals."
"They did?" Brody said. He sounded surprised.
"Because they seem to tamper with us a lot."
"I know," Markos said. "But I think they all agree to . . . well, they agree to avoid killing one another's' mortals."
Julia grimaced, shocked once again by the way the gods sometimes acted. They could be really brutal.
"Save your blustering, husband," Hera was telling Zeus.
She walked around Heracles, studying him closely.
"I'm much more interested in hearing exactly where you found this champion of yours."
"What difference does it make where I found him?" Zeus retorted.
"The important thing is that he's going to defeat all others at the Games."
"Why the secrecy, husband?" Hera asked. "Is there something you're not telling us?
Because I sense a strange quality about this mortal hero of yours."
Julia traded looks with Markos. Had Hera put a little extra emphasis on the word mortal?
"Do you think she does suspect the truth?" Julia whispered.
Markos shrugged. "If she does, Heracles will be the one to pay the price."
Zeus didn't look worried. "Question me all you like, wife.
The answers will come at the Games when Heracles wins every event."
"Oh? How certain are you of that outcome?" Hera demanded. "Would you be willing to make a bet?"
Zeus looked suspicious. "A bet? Why would I do that?
I'm not greedy—the laurel wreath will be enough reward for me and my champion."
"Oh, come on, Zeus," Hermes called out.
"A friendly bet might make things more interesting."
"Yes," Ares added from elsewhere in the crowd.
"Your Heracles is impressive, but so are our champions."
"Unless you're afraid of the outcome, husband?" Hera said, sneering.
Zeus frowned. "I fear nothing, and neither does my champion."
He clapped Heracles on the back. "Isn't that right, boy?"
"Yes, Zeus," Heracles replied quietly.
"What was that?" Artemis called out. "I couldn't hear you.
Did you just tell Zeus you doubt you can beat all our champions at every event?"
"He said no such thing!" Zeus roared. His face was going red with annoyance.
"We'll beat you all, mark my words. To prove it, I'll accept any bet you're willing to make."
"Good," Hera said immediately. "Because here are my terms."
Julia held her breath. What would Hera say next?
"If Heracles wins every event, you may do as you wish with all the other champions," Hera said.
"Kill them, make them your slaves, anything."
"What?" Brody gulped. His eyes were wide as he turned to Julia. "Did you hear that?"
Julia nodded, and then glanced at the other gods in the crowd, expecting some of them to protest.
But they were all listening with interest.
"However," Hera went on, "if anyone beats your champion at just one contest, you must promise to throw Heracles into Tartarus with your own hands."
The crowd gasped, but Zeus didn't hesitate.
"It's a deal!" he agreed firmly.
"Whoa!" Brody said as gasps and exclamations rang out from all around.
Heracles was staring straight ahead, his expression stony.
Nearby, Iphicles was hiding his face in his hands and shaking his head.
"This is bad," Julia muttered. "This is really bad!"
"I know," Brody agreed. "The gods' bet makes the Olympics seem like a football game that nobody can win.
If I beat Heracles at even one event, he'll end up in that terrible Tartarus place."
Julia nodded. "If that happens, he might never become the great hero he's supposed to be!"
"But if Heracles wins everything, Zeus might kill me or make me his slave," Brody reminded her.
"I don't like the sound of that, either."
"Neither do I. So what are we going to do?" Julia said. "We need a plan."
"There's nothing we can do," Markos said. "Now that the stakes are higher, the other gods will work even harder to defeat Heracles.
We won't be able to stop them, and we will surely suffer if we try."
"But Heracles is our friend now," Julia argued. "We can't just—"
She stopped herself as Hermes flew over.
The wings on his sandals were fluttering so fast that Brody could hardly see them.
"Come, boy." Hermes' eyes flashed with excitement.
"This bet makes things much more interesting, does it not?
The champion who beats Heracles and sends him to Tartarus will become a legend.
And I wish that person to be my champion! Let's get back to training!"
Over the next couple of days, Brody's life got even busier than it had been before.
Hermes made him train for hours each day. In the evenings the messenger god lectured Brody on strategies to beat Heracles.
It was pretty boring. Besides that, it left Brody no time to talk privately with Julia and Markos.
One morning at breakfast, Julia set a platter of barley cakes in front of Brody.
Brody quickly looked around the table. Hermes had arrived, but he was busy talking to Caerus.
"Listen," Brody whispered to Julia. "What are we going to do about Heracles?"
"I don't know," Julia whispered back. She pretended to be serving more food so she could stand there for a minute.
"But Markos and I are thinking about a plan."
"You'd better think fast," Brody said. "The Olympics are only three days away!"
"Hurry and eat, my champion," Hermes called suddenly. "We have much work to do today."
Brody started eating as Julia moved away. He knew he'd better eat fast.
Hermes was impatient, and yesterday he hadn't even let Brody stop for lunch.
Training for the Olympics was hard enough without trying to do it on an empty stomach!
By the time Brody returned to Markos' house that evening, he was exhausted.
Hermes had made him practice every single event of the Games.
Brody's cheek was bruised where Athena's champion had hit him during their boxing match.
His leg throbbed where one of the chariot horses had kicked him.
Every muscle in his body ached from running and wrestling and throwing things.
"I hope dinner is ready soon," he said, collapsing onto a bench in the courtyard.
"I want to go to sleep before Hermes shows up again. He'll probably spend hours telling me about all the ways I can beat Heracles."
"I'm glad Hermes let us walk home from the gymnasium by ourselves tonight," Julia said, glancing from Brody to Markos.
"He's been hanging around so much that we've barely had a chance to talk.
We still need to figure out what we're going to do about Hera's bet."
Brody didn't respond. He was sniffing the air.
"Do you guys smell something weird?" he asked. "It definitely doesn't smell like dinner."
Julia pointed a short distance away. "Look!"
A thick cloud of white smoke was pouring into the courtyard.
Markos coughed. "It smells like incense. But where is it coming from?"
Brody coughed too. The smoke was twirling around him now, making it hard to breathe. His lungs burned.
"Let's get out of here!" He choked out the words.
Suddenly the smoke disappeared, leaving Hermes in its place.
"I have important news, my champion!" Hermes declared.
"I should have guessed the smoke was from Hermes," Markos muttered, his voice slightly hoarse. "He has a special love for incense."
Hermes waved a hand to silence Markos.
"Did you not hear me? I have news!
Hera has just announced that she'll host a banquet to honor all the athletes and their sponsors."
"A banquet?" Brody's stomach grumbled. A big meal sounded pretty good just then. "Is it tonight?"
Hermes chuckled. "I see that my champion is as eager to celebrate as I am."
He clapped Brody on the back. "The banquet is tomorrow evening."
"Why is Hera hosting a banquet?" Julia asked.
"Does that always happen before the Olympic Games?"
"No, this is the first time. I suspect she's trying to make Zeus look bad for not thinking of it first." Hermes smirked.
"But that won't stop everyone—even Zeus—from attending and having a splendid time."
Markos bowed to Hermes. "I am certain that you and Brody will enjoy the festivities, Hermes."
"I'm certain of that too," Hermes said with a smile.
"But you'll be able to see for yourself, my boy.
As Brody's companion, you shall attend as well."
"Really?" Markos' eyes lit up.
"Cool." Brody grinned at Markos. "This banquet sounds like fun."
"What about me?" Julia asked. "Can I come too?"
"You?" Hermes laughed. "Don't be silly. Of course not!"
Brody was surprised. "Why can't she come?"
"Oh, you mortals!" Hermes kept chuckling. "Excuse me, I want to see if dinner is ready.
Preparing my champion for Olympic glory is hungry work."
As soon as Hermes had disappeared into the house, Julia whirled to face Markos.
"Why did Hermes laugh at the idea of my coming to the banquet?" she demanded.
Markos looked surprised. "Females are never allowed at that sort of banquet.
And I think only unmarried females are allowed at the Games."
"What?" Julia frowned. She was getting tired of hearing about all the stuff that girls and women weren't allowed to do in ancient Greece.
"But Hera will be at both events, won't she?" Julia argued. "She's female!"
"She's a goddess," Markos replied. "That's different. All the goddesses will be there with their champions, of course."
Julia glanced at Brody. He didn't look upset at all.
"Aargh!" Julia exclaimed, stomping away from the courtyard.
"Hey!" Brody called after her. "Where are you going?"
Julia didn't answer him or slow down.
Right now she wished the boys would just ignore her, like everyone else in ancient Greece seemed to do.
But footsteps soon pounded behind her. A moment later Brody and Markos reached her.
"Are you all right?" Markos asked.
"She's just upset because of the whole girl thing," Brody told him.
"In our world girls can do all the same stuff boys can do." He paused.
"Well, most stuff, anyway. They don't usually play football."
Julia rolled her eyes, but she didn't respond.
She was staring up at the Temple of Caerus.
The moon had just risen, and the temple looked beautiful perched on the hillside in the silvery light. For a second she almost smiled.
Then she remembered that their only way home lay inside that temple. "Let's go up there," she said.
"To the temple?" Brody said. "Why?"
Markos looked worried. "You're not going to try to sneak through the rift again, are you?"
"We wouldn't do that," Julia said. "We know that would make Hermes punish your family."
"Yeah," Brody added. "Besides, dinner will be ready soon at your house, and I'm hungry."
"It will only take a few minutes," Julia said.
"I want to try to peek in, to make sure the rift is still open."
"Why wouldn't it be open?" Brody asked with a shrug.
"Hermes said it would stay that way until after the Olympics, at least."
Julia corrected him. "He said it probably would. Anyway I just want to see it."
She bit her lip, not wanting to admit that she was homesick.
Being in ancient Greece was fun and sometimes interesting.
But at other times it felt dangerous and hard; there were so many things she couldn't do.
"I wonder what our parents are thinking," she said to Brody.
"Do you think they called the police when we went missing?"
He looked startled. "I never really thought about that.
They probably did. They must be super worried about us, right?"
Julia nodded, glancing at the temple again.
"At least we'll be home soon. The Games are only three days away."
"Right." Brody stared at the temple. "Maybe it's not a bad idea to try to get a peek at the rift."
Julia smiled at him. He smiled back. Then he turned away and charged up the path.
"Be careful, Brody!" Markos called. "We don't want the guard to see us, or he might tell Hermes we were looking around the temple."
"Oh. Good point." Brody slowed down, and soon the three of them were sneaking toward one side of the temple.
The guard was standing on the steps.
"Too bad the temple doesn't have more windows," Brody whispered.
"I don't think we'll be able to see the rift from out here."
Julia realized he was right. "Oh well," she said.
"I guess we'll have to hope it stays open until . . ." She stopped herself. "Did you hear something?"
The sound of voices was drifting toward them from the path below.
Markos' face went pale. "That sounds like Hermes and Caerus," he whispered. "What are they doing here?"
"I guess dinner isn't ready yet," Brody commented, rubbing his stomach. "Maybe they're out for a walk too."
"We can't let them catch us here!" Markos darted away from the temple.
Brody followed. But Julia's chiton caught on a branch.
By the time she pulled it loose, Hermes and Caerus had come into sight.
Julia ducked behind a tree. She would have to meet up with the boys later.
Just then she heard Hermes mention Brody's name.
". . . and the boy is making progress," Hermes was saying.
"I truly believe he could beat even the mighty Heracles at boxing, or possibly in one of the shorter footraces."
"Yes." Caerus sounded amused. "Especially if some disaster happens to befall Heracles while he's running."
Julia winced. It sounded as if the gods were still planning to sabotage Heracles—even during the Games!
"I can't wait to see Zeus' face when his hero fails to win," Hermes said with glee.
"I plan to enjoy the victory tour—and to make sure Zeus hears all about it!"
"I'm sure that will be enjoyable indeed," Caerus agreed.
"But what will you do with your mortal champion if the rift closes before he can return to his own time?"
Julia almost gasped. She clapped her hand over her mouth just in time.
Then she leaned forward, listening more intently than ever.
"What do you mean?" Hermes asked. "The boy can return home if he wishes, as long as he does it after I've had my fun at Zeus' expense."
"But the rift is unstable, remember?" Caerus said.
"I can't guarantee how much longer it will stay open.
If the boy ends up trapped here, he might tell someone he isn't really from Greece and thus isn't qualified for the Games."
"Yes, I suppose that could be a problem." Hermes didn't sound very worried.
"If it happens, I'll deal with it somehow. But first, let's make sure he wins."
"Pin him, boy!" Hermes shouted. "That's the way to do it!"
"Settle down, Hermes." Athena sounded exasperated. "The mortals are only training.
Save your enthusiasm for the Games. Or at least try not to shout directly into my ear."
Brody stood up, brushed off his hands, and waited for Athena's champion, a dark-eyed youth named Leontis, to climb to his feet as well.
"Are you okay?" Brody asked. "I didn't twist your arm too hard, did I?"
"I'm fine." Leontis flexed his arm, checking it.
"But don't expect to pin me again so easily."
Brody grinned. "Oh, I do expect it!" he bragged.
The two of them started wrestling again.
Brody tried to stay focused on the match, but he was a lot stronger than Leontis, and his thoughts quickly wandered.
Last night Julia had told him what she'd heard Hermes and Caerus say about the rift.
What if it closed before they could return home?
"My family must already be worried about me," Brody thought.
"What will they think if I never come back?"
"Pay attention, boy!" Hermes' shout broke into Brody's thoughts. "He's beating you!"
Brody blinked and focused on the wrestling match again.
But it was too late. A few seconds later, Leontis pinned him.
"There." Leontis smirked as he let Brody go. "Now we're even."
Brody didn't answer. He'd just heard Zeus' booming voice.
The king of the gods swept past, cheerfully greeting Hermes and Athena.
Heracles and Iphicles were right behind Zeus.
As they passed, Heracles gave Brody a friendly nod. Brody nodded back.
Athena's champion noticed the two champions' interaction.
"Be careful that you don't seem too friendly with Zeus' champion, my friend," he said grimly.
"What do you mean?" Brody asked.
Leontis shrugged. "All the gods wish to defeat Zeus' hero," he replied.
"If they think you're his friend, they might decide to include you in their plans."
"I'm not scared of anybody," Brody declared.
"Perhaps you should be." Athena's champion flexed his hands as he prepared to grip Brody's shoulder.
"Hera appears to have stopped meddling with Heracles for now.
Everyone thinks she's waiting until the Games officially begin to return to her trickery."
"Why would she do that?" Brody asked.
"Her bet only counts if Heracles actually takes part in the Games," Leontis replied.
"If he's knocked out before the competition begins, the bet is off."
"Oh, I get it," Brody said. "Cool. Then we don't have anything to worry about, right? At least not for two more days."
"Not exactly," Leontis said. "The other gods might have different plans."
He cast a quick look around to make sure that Athena and Hermes weren't close enough to hear him.
"In fact, I heard that Ares was seen just this morning consulting with Hypnos."
"Hypnos?" Brody said. "Who's that?"
"The god of sleep," Leontis replied. "Everyone suspects Hypnos and Ares are plotting something against—"
He stopped talking abruptly. Brody saw that Athena had just stepped closer.
Leontis was watching her, and he seemed nervous.
Brody quickly decided to take advantage of the other champion's distraction.
"Yeaaaah!" he cried as he flipped Leontis onto his back and pinned him.
Hermes laughed. "Well done, my champion!" he exclaimed.
"Clearly this fellow is no match for you.
Why don't you take a break and drink some water?
I'll try to locate a more worthy opponent."
"Sure. Thanks, Hermes." Brody grinned and shook Leontis' hand. "See you later, dude."
Brody jogged over to join Markos and Julia. Markos handed him a jar of water.
"Did you see Heracles come in?" Markos asked.
"Yeah." Brody gulped some water. "Athena's champion was worried about him.
Leontis said he heard that Ares and some god called Hypnos might be plotting something against Heracles."
Julia looked alarmed. "Hypnos?" She turned to Markos.
"Is he the god with the wings sprouting out of his head?"
"Yes, that's Hypnos," Markos answered. "He's the god of sleep.
The other gods often cause mischief among us mortals with his help."
"Uh-oh," Julia said. "Leontis might be right.
I saw Hypnos and Ares talking when I came into the gymnasium."
"I hope Zeus is keeping a close eye on his champion," Markos said.
"Why?" Brody looked around. "Because at the moment Zeus isn't watching Heracles.
He's over there talking to Dionysus, and I don't even see Heracles right now." Suddenly Brody understood.
"Hey—do you think Ares is really trying to mess with Heracles?"
"Of course Ares is trying to mess with him!" Julia exclaimed.
"Let's go find Heracles and warn him."
Brody glanced at Hermes. The messenger god was halfway across the gymnasium talking with Artemis and Apollo.
"Okay," Brody said. "Hermes did say I could take a break."
He followed Julia and Markos as they rushed around the gymnasium looking for Heracles.
They didn't find him, but eventually they came across Iphicles.
He was lounging in the shade with a bored expression on his face, watching several athletes practicing the discus.
"Where's your brother?" Julia demanded.
Iphicles sat up straighter, looking startled. "Alcides? Uh, I mean Heracles. . . ." He made a face.
"I still can't get used to his new name.
Anyway, Zeus sent him to find a heavier discus. In there."
He pointed to a door leading into the gymnasium building.
"Come on," Julia said breathlessly.
"Wait, what's the matter?" Iphicles called as she, Brody, and Markos rushed off and shoved open the door.
Brody could hear Iphicles hurrying after them.
The door led into a medium-sized room with equipment stacked inside.
Brody had to squint to help his eyes adjust to the dimness after being outside in the bright sunlight.
When he could finally see clearly, he gasped.
Heracles was splayed out on the stone floor, sound asleep and snoring.
Slithering toward him from every direction were at least ten large snakes!
Julia heard Brody gasp loudly beside her.
But she didn't take her eyes off the snakes slithering toward Heracles from every direction.
All of them had the triangular heads of venomous serpents.
If she didn't do something, the fastest snake would reach Heracles within seconds!
Julia glanced around the room. A few feet away she spied a barrel with several javelins.
She grabbed a javelin and leaped forward.
"Be careful!" Brody cried.
Julia used the javelin to flick the fastest snake to the side.
The creature hissed, and then lunged toward the end of the javelin.
"Quick!" Julia called to Markos and Brody.
"Grab a javelin! Call Iphicles to help us!"
Markos dashed to the door, almost colliding with Iphicles, who was just walking in.
"Hurry!" Markos exclaimed. "The serpents are threatening your brother!"
"What?" Iphicles' jaw dropped. He froze in the doorway, staring at the sleeping Heracles.
"Grab a javelin!" Brody said. "If you guys can hold back the snakes, I'll drag Heracles outside."
Markos rushed over to the javelin barrel.
Julia glanced at Iphicles, but he was still standing there, as if he didn't know what to do. "Help us!" she exclaimed.
"Never mind him," Markos said. "I think he's stunned."
He leaped forward and flicked away the largest snake. "Got one!"
Julia forgot about Iphicles and knocked a smaller snake off to the side.
Working together, she and Markos soon cleared a path for Brody.
"Cover me—I'm going in!" Brody said.
He put his head down, charged toward Heracles, and grabbed the sleeping champion by his muscular shoulders.
Brody grunted as he dragged Heracles slowly toward the door.
Heracles mumbled and moved his hands, but he didn't wake up.
"Hurry!" Julia cried, flicking away a speedy little viper.
"I think we're making them angrier! They're coming back toward us!"
"Look out!" Markos yelled. "Behind you, Brody!"
Julia gasped when she saw a snake preparing to strike at Brody.
"That one must have been hidden behind Heracles!" she exclaimed. "Watch out, Brody!"
As the snake struck, Brody dodged to one side, almost dropping Heracles.
The snake missed, and Brody managed to kick it away.
"Whoa, that was close," he said. "I guess all that training Hermes is making me do is coming in handy!"
His voice sounded a little shaky. Julia didn't blame him. The snake had nearly bitten him.
At last Brody managed to drag Heracles to the door.
"Excuse me, dude," he said, shouldering his way past Iphicles.
Heracles' brother was still standing in the doorway.
As Brody dragged Heracles past his brother, Iphicles finally seemed to wake up.
He turned to Julia. "Where did all those snakes come from?" he asked.
"Where do you think?" Julia said grimly. Wasn't the answer obvious?
"The gods are still after your brother."
She hurried outside after the other boys.
Markos was already fetching water, which he then splashed in Heracles' face.
"Ugh," Heracles mumbled, one eye opening halfway. "Is it raining?"
"Wake up, brother!" Iphicles said loudly, leaning over and slapping Heracles on both cheeks.
"You picked a bad spot to take a nap."
"I'm sure it wasn't his idea," Julia said.
"We heard Hypnos was seen plotting with Ares."
"Ares?" Heracles mumbled. With a groan, he pushed himself into a sitting position.
"Yes, I was just talking to Ares. Where did he go?"
"What were you and Ares talking about?" Markos asked.
Heracles rubbed his face sleepily. "I . . . I don't remember."
His face stretched into a wide yawn.
"Ares approached me—another god was with him, I think."
Julia traded looks with Markos and Brody. "Was it Hypnos?" she asked.
"Hypnos!" Heracles nodded. "Yes, that's who it was.
The two of them said they were searching for someone. Or was it something?
I remember Hypnos touching my arm, and the next thing I know, I'm here with all of you."
Julia traded another look with the others. "They tricked you," she told Heracles.
With help from the boys, she told Heracles what had happened.
Heracles looked more awake by the end of the story.
"I suppose that's why Zeus warned me never to go anywhere alone," he said.
"You'd better take his advice from now on, dude," Brody said.
"Yes," Julia agreed. "Otherwise you might not survive until the Games!"
"Come, brother," Iphicles said suddenly. "Zeus will wonder what's keeping you."
Heracles smiled at Julia and the others.
"It seems I owe you my life," he said.
"Then we're even," Brody said. "You saved our lives when that bull automaton was chasing us, remember?"
Heracles nodded. "Still, I offer you many thanks."
"You're welcome," Julia said. She shivered, thinking about all those snakes again.
"I'm just glad we found you in time."
Heracles hurried off with his brother. Markos looked troubled.
"I didn't want to say this in front of those two," he said.
"But perhaps it would be better if Heracles doesn't survive until the Games."
"What?" Julia exclaimed.
"Dude!" Brody added, sounding horrified.
"No, listen," Markos said. "If he dies now, Heracles will go to the underworld like anyone else. But if he makes it to the Games . . ."
"Oh," Julia said, catching on. "If he competes and loses, he might end up in Tartarus instead."
"Is this Tartarus place really that bad?" Brody asked.
"I mean, I know you guys said it was terrible, but being dead sounds pretty terrible too."
Markos shuddered. "Tartarus is said to be a deep pit of pure torment.
The most evil people who ever lived are said to be there, where they are eternally punished for their wicked deeds."
"Wow," Brody said. "Okay, that does sound bad." He shrugged.
"But how can we keep Heracles from ending up there? I mean, there's not much the three of us can do, is there?"
Julia didn't have an answer for Brody's questions.
She was glad when Hermes interrupted and dragged Brody off to prepare for the banquet.
"Wow," Brody said as he stepped into the banquet room with Markos and Hermes.
"There are a lot of people here. It's like one of my football team's parties!"
The banquet room was large and full of people and gods.
Men and boys were lounging on the sofas that lined the walls, talking and laughing and drinking from goblets.
Servants bustled around, carrying trays of food and drink. Candles flickered inside clay lamps.
Brody spotted Zeus right away. The king of the gods was at the far end of the room, one hand on Heracles' shoulder.
Iphicles stood behind them. Zeus was talking to several other gods, including Hades and Poseidon.
Brody soon saw more familiar faces. Apollo was helping himself to food from a servant's platter.
Nearby, Athena was chatting with a pot-bellied god who had a bald head and a white beard.
"Hey, look, there's a donkey here!" Brody said, pointing to an animal standing next to the god.
"Yes," Markos said. "Silenus rarely travels without his donkey.
But I heard that many of the other gods also decided to bring their lucky creatures to this symposium."
He nodded toward Artemis, who was surrounded by several lean, amber-eyed hunting dogs as she talked with Hephaestus and Demeter.
"Symposium?" Brody blinked. "What's that? I thought this was supposed to be a banquet.
I hope they're going to serve more food!"
"A symposium is a type of banquet," Markos said, grinning at him.
"Don't worry, Brody, the food will be plentiful."
As if to prove Markos' point, a servant hurried up and offered them roasted meat and vegetables.
Brody helped himself to a piece of the meat.
He'd barely taken a bite when Hermes grabbed his arm and dragged him across the room.
"Nike, the goddess of victory, just arrived," Hermes said eagerly.
"I don't think she's seen you yet, has she, my boy?"
"Uh, I don't know." Brody glanced back to make sure that Markos was keeping up with them.
"Nike, my friend!" Hermes said when they reached a tall, broad-shouldered goddess with wings sprouting out of her back.
"I wish to introduce my champion, the finest mortal athlete in Greece!"
"Greetings, Hermes." Nike looked Brody up and down.
"I've heard that your champion is very talented." She smirked.
"Perhaps if Demeter's latest plot is successful, your champion might even win an event or two at the Games."
"Brody will win every event at the Games," Hermes bragged.
Then he blinked. "Wait—what plot are you talking about?"
Nike looked around, and then leaned closer.
"I've heard that Demeter plans to cause the grass beneath Heracles' feet to become as sticky as honey when he runs," she whispered loudly.
Brody looked at Markos to see if he had heard this news too.
But Brody quickly forgot about Heracles when Aphrodite walked into the room, followed by her champion.
"I see Aphrodite!" Brody exclaimed.
Hermes heard him and glanced toward the goddess of love.
"Stay away from her, boy," Hermes said sternly.
"She's been seen plotting with Hera. You don't want to get involved in that kind of trouble."
Brody waited until Hermes turned away again to talk to Nike.
Then Brody flashed a look at Markos. Brody and his friends had known about the goddesses' plotting days ago!
Hermes soon began dragging Brody around the room, introducing him to several other gods and goddesses.
But finally Hermes seemed to get bored.
"You may amuse yourselves for a while, my boys," he said to Brody and Markos.
"But stay together, just in case of trouble."
"We will," Markos promised.
Hermes disappeared into the crowd. Brody glanced around.
"Should we find more food?" he said.
"All right," Markos agreed. "I think there's a platter of bread over there."
The two of them walked over and helped themselves.
Nearby, two mortal boys around their age were deep in conversation.
"I'm glad I'm not Heracles," said the first boy, a skinny youth with bulging eyes.
"I heard all the gods are plotting against him."
His friend laughed. "You, a champion in the Olympic Games? Never!"
The first boy shoved him. "I could beat you in any footrace, that's for sure!"
"Oh yes? I might make you prove that, my friend," the second boy said with a sneer.
Brody grinned. Listening to the two boys boast to each other reminded him of being in the locker room with his friends from the football team.
His smile faded as he remembered how far away he was from that familiar scene.
"Look, Hera just arrived," Markos said, elbowing Brody.
The queen of the gods stepped to the center of the room with her champion beside her.
"Welcome, one and all," Hera said loudly. Everyone stopped talking to listen.
"I know we are all looking forward to the Olympic Games, which begin the day after tomorrow."
Her sharp gaze wandered to Zeus, who was listening with everyone else.
"In the meantime please enjoy the food, drink, and entertainment."
She clapped her hands, and several musicians and dancers hurried in.
Most of the musicians were men, but one was a pretty girl holding a flute.
Some of the dancers were female as well.
"Uh-oh, don't tell Julia there are girls here," Brody joked.
"She's already mad about not being invited to the banquet."
"Perhaps she should have volunteered to be part of tonight's entertainment," Markos joked in return.
"Does she, perhaps, have a talent for the lyre? Or for dancing?"
Brody smiled, but he didn't laugh. He couldn't help feeling a little guilty that Julia hadn't been allowed to attend the banquet.
It didn't seem fair that she couldn't come just because she was a girl.
Still, there was nothing he could do about it, so he took another big bite of his food and prepared to enjoy the show.
Julia was feeling cranky. Ever since the boys had left for the banquet, Markos' mother and sister had kept Julia busy.
They'd all cooked and eaten a quick dinner, then gone to work cleaning and tidying the entire house.
"I wonder what Brody is doing right now," Julia thought as she scrubbed another cooking pot.
"Whatever it is, I bet it's more fun than this."
"Oh dear," Markos' mother said, interrupting Julia's grumpy thoughts.
"We are nearly out of water. One of us had better fetch more from the fountain in the agora."
"I'll do it," Julia said before the other girl could respond. "I'm finished cleaning this thing anyway."
She set the pot aside, and then she grabbed one of the large decorated jars used for collecting water from the public fountain.
She hurried out of the house, glad for any kind of distraction from boring housework.
It was a clear evening with a pleasant breeze, and it felt good to be outside.
Julia took her time walking toward the agora.
She was in no hurry to get back to her chores.
Hearing the faint sound of music, she paused and peered down a side street.
At the far end stood the Temple of Hera.
"I bet that music is coming from the banquet," Julia murmured.
She couldn't resist turning onto the street and walking past the first few houses.
The music got louder, and soon Julia could also hear the sounds of laughing, talking, and singing.
The noise was coming from a building close to the temple.
She stopped in front of the building, the largest home on the street.
Several guards stood near the front door.
The youngest guard eyed Julia suspiciously, but Julia ignored him.
"I'd love to slip inside the building," she thought, "and get a look at the celebration."
Plus, she couldn't help feeling a little worried about Brody, and also about Heracles.
Would the other gods try to play their usual dangerous pranks at the banquet?
"You!" the young guard snapped. "What do you want here? This is a private party."
Julia opened her mouth to answer. Before she could get out any words, the door burst open and a slim, pale goddess came out.
Julia didn't recognize her. The guards immediately bowed deeply.
"We trust you are enjoying the evening, Lethe," the oldest guard said politely.
"Lethe," Julia thought. "I thought that was the name of a river.
Actually, I'm pretty sure it's a river in Hades.
I guess it's the name of a goddess too."
Lethe ignored the guards. She had a dreamy expression on her face as she drifted toward the street.
"You, young dancer," Lethe said when she spotted Julia. "Did you see me inside?"
"What?" Julia said, startled. "Inside? Uh, no."
"Good." Lethe turned her dreamy smile in the direction of the building.
"I wish I could stay at the banquet longer.
But Hera feared that the other gods might guess our plans."
"Your . . . your plans?" Julia swallowed nervously. "What plans?"
"I cannot reveal them to you, young dancer," Lethe replied, her smile widening.
"It's really Hera's plan anyway. All I had to do was deliver a very special drink to the banquet.
It's Hera's job to ensure that some of her champion's competitors take a nice, long sip . . ." Her laugh made Julia shiver.
"Wait," Julia said. "What kind of drink? Which competitors?"
"I'm afraid I cannot answer your questions," Lethe replied dreamily.
"Good night, young dancer." She looked past Julia and started for the street again.
Julia was alarmed by what she'd heard.
"Wait!" she exclaimed, and she reached out to stop the goddess.
As soon as she touched Lethe's arm, Julia's body went limp and her mind went blank.
Suddenly she couldn't remember who or where she was, or anything else.
Then Lethe pulled away, and Julia's memories returned in a rush.
She staggered backward, clutching her water jar tightly and gulping for air.
What had just happened? Julia stared at the goddess.
"Now I remember the river Lethe," she thought.
"It's the river of forgetfulness and oblivion.
Only the dead are meant to drink its waters."
She turned to look at the house.
Were Hera and Lethe working together to poison Heracles?
"No," Julia murmured aloud.
Hera wanted Heracles alive and well until the Games began so that she could force Zeus to send his champion to Tartarus.
Julia was certain of that.
That meant Lethe's poison drink was meant for someone else.
"Maybe Hera wants to kill, or harm, all the other athletes so her champion will be the one to defeat Heracles," Julia thought.
She shuddered. That definitely sounded like something Hera would do.
"Brody!" Julia whispered. She had to warn him!
She rushed up to the entrance. "Halt," one of the guards said. "Invited guests only."
"But my friend is in there," Julia said. "I have to talk to him. Please? I just need to go in for a second."
The youngest guard laughed. "I'd love to hear what Hera would say if we let a mortal girl into the banquet," he said.
The other guards chuckled.
"Go away, little girl," one of them said.
"It doesn't look right for you to be hanging around in the street."
But another guard, a slender, shifty-eyed man, was staring at Julia's water jar.
"That's quite a fancy hydria," he said.
"Is it yours? I'd trade my finest goat for a jar like that."
Julia gritted her teeth. She was in no mood to talk about water jars and goats.
If she didn't figure out a way to get into the banquet right now, Brody could be in big trouble!
"I have to do something!" she thought, feeling desperate. "But what?"
"This is great." Brody burped and reached for another roasted chicken leg. "The banquet food is really good."
Markos nodded, but he didn't answer. His mouth was full of olives.
The two of them had found a spot on one of the sofas.
They were lounging on some comfortable pillows and tasting every type of food the servants brought them.
"Brody, Markos!" a familiar voice called.
Glancing up from his food, Brody saw Heracles coming toward them with a big smile on his face.
Iphicles was right behind his brother, looking bored.
"Hi," Brody greeted them. He waved a hand at the sofa. "Want to hang out with us?"
"Hang out?" Heracles looked confused, but he sat down with Brody and Markos.
"It's nice to see some friendly faces here." He chuckled.
"Everyone else seems to view me as the enemy."
"I suppose that's mostly Zeus' fault," Iphicles said.
He shot a look at Zeus, who was halfway across the room talking with some other gods.
Just then Hera stepped to the center of the room and called for attention.
"I trust you're all having a good time," she said.
"Yeah!" Brody yelled out. Dionysus raised his goblet and whooped loudly.
A few of the other guests cheered.
"Good, good." Hera's sharp eyes swept the room. "I'd like to propose a toast.
My servants will bring out fresh drinks for everyone, but don't taste them yet. First, I wish to say a few words."
"A few?" Zeus called out. "I've never known you to be brief, wife."
Hera ignored him. "I merely wish to say I look forward to the coming contest.
It's a chance for our mortal champions to take part in a glorious tradition, displaying both their skills and their good sportsmanship . . ."
There was more after that, but Brody stopped paying attention.
Instead he focused on choosing the ripest grapes and figs from the tray a servant had left for him and his companions.
Most of the other party guests didn't seem to be listening either.
Markos was watching the servants distribute fresh goblets while Iphicles picked his teeth.
Artemis was sitting on the next section of the sofa, stroking her dogs and crooning to them.
Nearby, Dionysus was shoving bread and fruit into his mouth.
Zeus was lounging on a sofa across the room, his head resting on one hand.
Brody wondered if the king of the gods was taking a nap while his wife spoke.
However, Heracles seemed to be paying attention to what Hera was saying.
So did Athena, who nodded and smiled every time Hera mentioned sportsmanship or fair play.
"Your drink, sir." A servant pressed a cup into Brody's hand.
"Thanks, dude." Brody was thirsty after all that food.
He made a move to lift the cup to his lips, but the servant stopped him with a hand on the arm.
"Begging your pardon, sir," the servant murmured.
"The queen of the gods wishes for everyone to drink only when she gives the word."
"Oh, right." Brody had forgotten that Hera was making some kind of big toast.
The servant handed another cup to Heracles, who nodded his thanks.
"Do you have a beverage for me?" Markos asked.
"Uh . . ." The servant looked him over. "I do not, but perhaps that servant does."
He gestured to another man, who was also carrying a tray of drinks.
"That was kind of rude," Brody said after the first servant moved on.
"That guy had plenty of goblets left.
I wonder why he wouldn't give you one."
Markos shrugged. "Never mind. The other servant is coming this way."
Sure enough, the second servant soon arrived and handed drinks to Markos and Iphicles.
Meanwhile Brody sniffed his cup. "Wow, what is this stuff?" he asked. "It smells awesome!"
Markos sniffed his own cup. "I don't smell anything unusual," he muttered.
Brody licked his lips. "Well, mine smells great!"
He looked at Hera, who was still addressing the crowd.
He hoped she’d finish soon. If he had to wait much longer to taste his amazing-smelling drink, he'd go crazy!
At last Hera seemed to run out of things to say.
"All right, I suppose that's enough from me," she said.
"Hear, hear!" Zeus cheered.
Hera shot him a sour look. "Does everyone have a fresh drink?"
The crowd held up their goblets, and Hera's thin lips twisted into an odd smile.
"Excellent!" She snapped her fingers, and a servant hurried over and handed her a goblet.
Hera lifted it into the air to make a toast. "To the spirit of sportsmanship!"
"Hear, hear!" Athena exclaimed, sounding much more sincere than Zeus had.
"Drink up, my friends!" Hera said.
Brody lifted his cup, eager to do just that.
"Cheers, everybody." The cup was about to touch his lips—
"Stop!"
A boy Brody had never seen before dodged through the crowd and knocked the cup out of Brody's hand!
"Hey!" Brody exclaimed in annoyance.
The liquid inside the cup splashed all over the cushions and floor.
One of Artemis' hunting dogs trotted over and licked at the spilled drink.
The boy didn't stop moving. Leaping toward Heracles, the stranger knocked Heracles' cup away as well.
"What do you think you're doing?" Brody grabbed the boy's arm, spinning him closer.
To his amazement, he found himself staring into a pair of fierce, familiar eyes.
"It's me, you dummy!" Julia hissed, yanking her new, short hair lower over her forehead.
"But what—why . . .?" Brody stammered.
Just then there was a fresh shout of alarm.
"Aah!" Iphicles was staring at Artemis' dog, the one that had been lapping up Brody's spilled drink.
The creature was swaying unsteadily and whining with confusion.
Then it fell over and lay still.
"My baby!" Artemis leaped toward the dog. "He's been poisoned!"
"Poisoned?" several voices murmured. All around the room, gods snatched the goblets out of their champions' hands.
"Whew . . . ." Julia let out a long breath. That had been a close call!
Then she noticed Hera glaring at her and stalking closer.
Did Hera recognize Julia in her disguise? Julia hoped not.
She looked around for an escape route, but she was surrounded by gods and people. She couldn't even see the door.
Artemis was muttering over her dog and waving her hand in circles over its head.
After a moment the animal's tail twitched, and a few seconds later it sat up and whimpered.
"Poor baby," Artemis said, rubbing its sleek head.
She shot an angry look at Hera. "You're lucky I was able to revive him!
I'm sure I'm not the only one who is growing weary of your ridiculous tricks and magical poisons."
Hera ignored her. Her steely gaze was still on Julia.
Julia gulped. "I've got to get out of here," she whispered to Brody and the others.
Brody looked too stunned to respond, and Julia thought that Markos and Iphicles had not yet figured out her identity.
But Heracles nodded. "I'll distract Hera," he whispered. "You go that way."
He pointed, and Julia finally spotted a doorway nearby.
She barely had time to nod before Heracles leaped forward to intercept Hera.
"Beloved queen of the gods," he exclaimed loudly.
"I cannot imagine who dared to tamper with the drinks at your gathering!"
"You can't?" Ares called out with a snort. "Because I can!"
Hera whirled around to glare at Ares. "Silence!" she snapped.
Meanwhile Julia darted toward the door that Heracles had indicated.
It led into a storage room. A few servants glanced at Julia as she raced across the storage room and finally out the back door.
Once she was safely outside, Julia collapsed against the back wall of the house, shaking with relief.
"Wow, that really was close," she murmured.
She still could hardly believe her plan had succeeded.
When the guard had commented again about her water jar, she'd had the idea to bribe him.
She'd lured him away from his post, and then offered to trade the jar for his clothes.
After trading her girl's chiton for the guard's chiton, she'd asked to borrow his knife.
She'd paused only for a second before chopping off a lot of her hair.
The guard loved his new water jar so much, he agreed to keep quiet while Julia sneaked into the house with a group of servants carrying in more food.
Once she was inside, Julia had followed the party sounds to the right room, only to find Brody with the cup already to his lips . . .
Julia shuddered, remembering that awful moment.
She'd arrived in the nick of time.
"What would I do if something happened to Brody?" she thought suddenly. "I'd probably never get home."
But that wasn't the only reason she was glad Brody was okay.
It wasn't even the most important reason.
Brody was actually starting to feel like . . . a friend.
It was a weird thought. But Julia didn't have much time to ponder it.
The door flew open, and Brody and Markos rushed out.
"Julia!" Markos exclaimed. "Is that really you?"
"It's me." Julia touched her short hair.
"This was the only way I could think of to get inside and warn you about the poison."
"But how did you find out about that?" Brody asked.
Julia told them about running into Lethe.
Just as she finished telling the story, the door opened again.
This time it was Heracles and Iphicles.
"Good, you're still here!" Heracles said. "Julia, I wish to thank you for saving my life—again."
"And mine too," Brody added. "What you did, Julia, was really cool."
Iphicles glanced at the open door, looking nervous.
"We should go back in, brother," he said to Heracles. "Zeus will be looking for you."
"I suppose you're right." Heracles smiled at Julia and then bowed. "Again, many thanks to you."
"You're welcome." Julia watched Heracles hurry back inside, followed by his brother.
"Heracles is actually a pretty cool guy, isn't he?" Brody said.
"Indeed," Markos agreed. "It's too bad he'll likely end up in Tartarus."
"Don't say that," Julia said quickly. "Zeus will be at the Games, protecting him."
"You've seen how easily the gods get distracted," Markos said quietly.
"Zeus could take his eyes off Heracles, and the other gods will seize the opportunity."
"Yeah," Brody agreed. "Heracles is in real danger."
Julia knew the boys were right. "So what can we do? We need to help him if we can."
"There's just one way to keep Heracles out of Tartarus.
We need to make sure he wins everything." Brody took a deep breath.
"Even if that means not doing my best."
Julia was surprised. Brody was competitive—he hated to lose.
"You'd do that, Brody?" she asked. "But that's very risky.
If you don't win, Hermes might not let us leave—especially if he suspects you lost on purpose."
"Oh no, you don't!" Hermes' angry voice rang out. "You're not losing anything, mortal!"
Julia slumped against the wall. She and the boys had been so busy talking, they hadn't noticed Hermes standing in the doorway.
"I came out here to make sure you were not injured by Hera's trickery," Hermes went on.
His expression was dark and stormy. "And what do I hear but my own champion threatening to humiliate me at the Games!"
"No, it's not like that," Brody protested. "Listen, dude—"
Hermes cut him off. "No, you listen to me.
You will not betray me again, do you understand?
Because if you don't do your very best in every contest, you and your friends will soon be joining Heracles in Tartarus!"
Hermes stormed back into the banquet room.
"Oops," Brody said. "I guess my plan to lose during the Games isn't going to work."
He felt terrible. He'd wanted to find a way to help Heracles.
Instead Brody had just made things worse for everyone.
"What are we going to do now?" Julia asked.
Markos shook his head. "I don't know. Because if Brody proves to Hermes that he's doing his best by winning one or more events—"
"Then Heracles will end up in Tartarus," Julia finished grimly.
"There's still just one obvious solution," she added. "Heracles has to win everything."
"But Julia," Markos started to argue, "if Hermes thinks Brody isn't doing his best—"
"Hermes won't think that," Julia said. "Not if we can stop the other gods from sabotaging Heracles.
If Heracles gets to compete fairly, without any interference from the gods, nobody will be surprised if he wins every event."
"Hey!" Brody protested. "I might win something!"
Then he thought for a second, remembering some of the amazing things he'd seen Heracles do.
"Actually, never mind. I guess you're right."
"So if Brody comes in second in some of the games, Hermes will believe he's doing his best," Julia went on.
"That way Heracles will be safe from Tartarus, and Hermes probably won't even care if we go back through the rift right away."
"What if Zeus decides to kill me or make me his slave?" Brody said.
"That was part of the deal, remember?"
"Don't worry too much about that," Markos said. "I think Julia is right.
If Heracles wins all the events in the Games, Zeus will be busy bragging and strutting around.
He won't pay any attention to you."
"We need to talk to Heracles and Iphicles," Julia said.
"We have to tell them what's going on and ask Iphicles to help us." Then she looked at Markos.
"For now, I have another problem—I have to find another water jar so I can bring home some water."
Julia and Markos headed toward the fountain. Brody followed them, feeling uneasy.
What if Hermes decided Brody hadn't tried hard enough?
What if the messenger god refused to let them leave?
And how were they supposed to stop the other gods from interfering with Heracles during the Games?
Finally Brody decided to stop worrying about all that stuff.
Julia and Markos were smart—they'd figure everything out.
Brody just had to hold up his end of the deal.
That meant getting some sleep so he could train hard tomorrow!
"Your boxing technique could still use some work, boy," Hermes said the next morning. "Let's find you a sparring partner."
Brody glanced around the gymnasium. Almost all the gods he'd ever seen were there today, along with their champions.
Heracles was nearby, tossing a javelin under Zeus' watchful eye.
"Heracles doesn't look too busy," Brody said. "Should I ask him to spar with me?"
Hermes smiled with approval. "Trying to show me you're sorry by boxing with the toughest competitor out there, eh? I like it.
Go ahead—I'll be right there. I just need to discuss something with Caerus."
Brody hurried over to Zeus and bowed.
"Uh, hi, sir. I was wondering if your champion would spar with me for a while."
Zeus looked amused. "You're Hermes' champion, aren't you, my boy?" he said in his booming voice.
"You can certainly spar with my champion.
Perhaps it's good to experience some humiliation before the Games begin!"
"Yeah. I mean no!" Brody said, flustered for a moment. "Thanks, Zeus."
Soon Brody and Heracles were circling each other, taking jabs now and then.
Brody was pretty sure that Heracles was going easy on him, since only a couple of Heracles' punches hit their marks.
Zeus was watching them, so Brody didn't dare to speak to Heracles for a while.
Finally, though, Athena called to Zeus. The king of the gods went over to talk to her.
"Listen," Brody hissed at Heracles. "I need to tell you something."
As quickly as he could, he whispered everything he knew about the gods' plots against Heracles. Heracles listened, looking worried.
"I know the gods don't play fair, of course," he said when Brody finished.
"And I know that as Zeus' champion, I am a favorite target of the gods.
But I didn't realize it would be this bad."
Brody nodded and dodged a jab. "All the gods are after you," he said.
"Well, except for Zeus, of course. And maybe Athena. But we want to help you."
Now Heracles looked surprised. "How?" he asked.
Brody couldn't resist taking advantage of his opponent's distraction to land a punch on Heracles' shoulder.
The muscles there felt as hard as rocks, and Heracles hardly seemed to notice the punch.
"We have a plan," Brody said. "Well, Julia does. And she's good at that sort of thing."
Once again he spoke quickly, explaining what Julia had in mind.
"You and Julia have been good to me," Heracles said.
"I wish to do whatever I can to help you return to your own time."
One corner of his mouth twitched into a smile.
"And of course I wish to keep myself out of Tartarus." His smile faded.
"Plus, I have to think of my brother."
Brody nodded. "We're hoping Iphicles will help us too.
Julia and Markos are supposed to be talking to him right now."
"I'm sure he will help." Heracles still looked anxious.
"I worry about what could happen to him if I end up disgraced."
"What do you mean?" Brody asked, ducking to avoid another jab.
Heracles sighed. "Iphicles is a fine person," he said.
"But he can be a bit . . . gruff at times. And the gods take offense so easily."
He shook his head, replacing his worried expression with a determined one.
"In any case, my thanks to you and your friends, Brody.
I am with you. Just tell me what you need me to do."
"There he is!" Julia pointed to the long jump area.
Iphicles was standing with some others who were watching as Apollo's champion and Poseidon's champion took turns.
Every time one of the athletes beat the other's score, most of the onlookers cheered.
But Iphicles barely seemed to be paying attention.
"He looks restless," Markos said. "That's good. It shouldn't be difficult to convince him to talk with us."
Julia hurried over to Iphicles. "Can you come with us?
There's something very important we need to talk about."
Iphicles looked surprised, but he nodded. "What is it?"
"Just come on. We don't want anyone else to hear."
Julia led the way to a quiet corner behind a pile of armor used for the hoplitodromos race.
On the way she glanced around for Brody.
She didn't see him, but she hoped he'd found an excuse to talk to Heracles.
"What's going on?" Iphicles asked as he followed Julia and Markos behind the armor.
"A lot, actually." Julia turned to face him. "It has to do with your brother . . ."
She went on to remind him that every god in Olympia was planning to try to sabotage Heracles at the Games.
"So your brother is in great danger," Markos added.
"We think we can save him from Tartarus, but we'll need your help."
Julia held her breath. She was sure he would want to help his brother.
But Iphicles seemed quiet and brooding most of the time.
What if he didn't believe what they'd told him? What if he didn't trust them?
But to Julia's surprise, Iphicles nodded immediately.
"I'll help however I can," he said. "Do you have a plan?"
"Yes," Julia said. "We're still working out some of the details.
But basically, the three of us need to figure out everything the gods have planned for Heracles at the Games."
"And then make sure that the gods don't succeed," Markos finished.
Iphicles slowly nodded. "The gods aren't exactly secretive about their plans," he said.
"I've heard many of them plotting and scheming myself, even though everyone must know I'm Heracles' brother."
"Yes, we're counting on their lack of secrecy," Markos said.
"We've already figured out what a few of them are planning."
He and Julia filled Iphicles in on what they'd learned from the gods. When they finished, Iphicles nodded again.
"All right," he said. "We should split up and eavesdrop on the rest of the gods right now.
We can meet later to figure out how to foil their plans."
"Perfect." Julia smiled at him. She was already feeling more optimistic about the Games.
"Brody is supposed to be telling Heracles about all this right now.
Let's go find them and make sure that happened."
At last it was the day of the Games.
"Are you ready to become an Olympic champion, my boy?"
Hermes called out as he strode across Markos' courtyard.
Brody grinned. "I'm as ready as I'll ever be!"
Julia rolled her eyes, but she was smiling.
She followed as Hermes, Brody, and Markos stepped out of the courtyard.
The whole city felt alive with excitement today.
Cheers rang out from every side. Citizens of Olympia lined the streets leading to the stadium.
"Wow," Brody said. "Check out all my fans!"
He puffed out his chest and strutted along.
Soon they were passing beneath the stone archway leading into the stadium.
The place was already crowded, with mortals sitting in seats made of mud bricks and on the grassy hillsides overlooking the track.
The gods were seated close to the track on golden chairs.
Food and drink vendors were selling their wares , the smells of roasted nuts and fish drifting over the scene.
Looking around, Julia wondered how they would ever be able to find seats.
She also noticed that most of the spectators were boys and men.
Markos had told her that married women like his mother were not allowed to watch the Games.
"I'm glad that tradition will change later," she thought. It was so unfair to women.
"Go and warm up with the other athletes," Hermes told Brody, gesturing toward the track.
"I'll come to advise you once I've found your companion a place to sit with the other gods' mortal guests."
He patted Markos on the shoulder, and then he glanced at Julia.
"Good luck finding a spot to view the events, girl."
"What?" Julia exclaimed.
"Aw, come on," Brody said. "Can't she stay with Markos?"
Hermes smiled at him. "If my champion requests it? I suppose she can."
"Thanks," Julia told Brody. "Good luck."
"You too," Brody said.
He jogged off to join the other athletes, who were warming up on the track.
Julia hurried after Markos and Hermes. Hermes waved them toward some empty seats behind where the gods were sitting.
Then he went and took his own seat right up front among the other gods.
All of them seemed to be there: Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Ares, along with some wind deities and a group of females with leaves in their hair.
Julia guessed they were wood nymphs. Zeus was the only god she didn't see.
"Where's Heracles?" Julia whispered, peering at the athletes warming up. "Do you see him yet?"
Markos pointed. "He just came in. Look, here comes his brother."
Julia saw Iphicles heading toward them. As he sat down beside Julia, he gave her and Markos a meaningful look.
Then Zeus strode in. "Greetings, citizens of Olympia and beyond!" he said, his voice silencing the ruckus immediately.
Julia shivered as the king of the gods lifted a large, flaming torch and then spoke again: "Let the Olympic Games begin!"
Brody puffed out his chest as the crowd cheered. This was it.
He was about to compete in the Olympic Games with all the best athletes in ancient Greece!
The athletes gathered in front of the gods.
Brody glanced at Heracles, who stood beside him. Heracles looked calm and ready.
A minor god named Agon stepped forward.
"Let the Olympic Games officially begin!" he called. "We shall start as usual with—"
"Hold on, Agon!" Zeus suddenly interrupted him.
"I've decided that there will be a change in the order of events today.
We shall begin with the chariot race."
"What?" Ares frowned. "Why?"
"Why not?" Zeus answered with a shrug.
"If your athletes are prepared, they will easily adjust to the change."
Brody felt a sudden pang of worry.
"Did you know about this?" he whispered to Heracles.
"No," Heracles said. "But I'm not surprised by it.
Zeus knows all the other gods want to sabotage me.
He's probably trying to foil their pranks by changing the order of events."
"Yeah," Brody replied. "I just wish we were following the right order."
"These Games will probably be unlike any other contest you've known, Brody," Heracles went on.
"We can expect a lot of mischief and interference from the gods today."
"Isn't that called cheating?" asked Brody.
Heracles shook his head. "No. It's just part of the Games."
Brody shot a look at Ares. The war god had reacted pretty strongly to Zeus' announcement.
Did that mean he had something planned?
By now everyone was hurrying through the exit.
Brody followed the crowd to the hippodrome, where servants were holding teams of horses.
"Over here, Brody," Hermes called.
Brody hurried toward the god and climbed into his chariot.
The horses pulling the chariot snorted and pawed at the ground.
Iphicles was helping Heracles, because Zeus seemed too busy bragging again to pay much attention to his champion.
But as soon as Heracles was in his chariot, Iphicles left his brother and hurried over to Brody.
Hermes was fussing with the horses' bridles and didn't seem to notice when Iphicles approached.
"Don't pull on the reins too much," Iphicles told Brody quietly.
"Try to fall in behind one of the faster teams and just let your horses chase the other chariot.
That way you'll only have to steer at the end of the race, when you're trying to get to the front."
"Thanks," Brody said with a nod. He remembered hearing that Iphicles was good with horses, so he trusted Iphicles' advice.
Hermes led the team of horses to the starting line.
"Champions, get ready!" Agon yelled.
A trumpet blared, and then all the horses sprang forward at once.
Brody's team was so eager that they almost pulled the reins out of his hands.
Poseidon's champion was in the lead, followed by Heracles' team.
Remembering Iphicles' tip, Brody pulled on one rein to steer his horses over behind those two teams. Then he loosened his grip again.
Brody's horses surged forward, chasing Heracles' chariot.
All Brody had to do was stand there.
"This is easy," he thought. He just needed to come in second or third place.
That would keep Heracles safe, and probably satisfy Hermes.
Just then a loud gasp rose from the crowd.
Brody looked up. "Uh-oh," he muttered.
A pack of wild boars had appeared out of nowhere!
The huge, shaggy beasts were running onto the track, heading straight toward Heracles' horses!
The horses snorted with fear and started to bolt to one side.
Heracles calmly lifted his long whip and cracked it at the boars.
The boars squealed and changed course, veering off into the crowd.
People screamed and scattered as the huge animals stampeded.
Brody turned his attention back to his own horses.
They were quickly falling behind Heracles' team.
The boars had probably spooked Heracles' horses, Brody realized.
They looked terrified now and were racing for their lives.
They swiftly passed Poseidon's team, and then, seconds later, they crossed the finish line.
Zeus beamed with pride. "Well done, my champion!" he thundered.
Poseidon's team finished second and Brody came in third.
As Brody halted his team, Iphicles jumped out to grab one of the horses by its bridle.
"Thanks, dude," Brody said breathlessly. He looked out at the spectators.
By now the boars had disappeared. Julia and Markos waved from their seats, and Brody waved back.
Then he looked over at the gods, wondering if Hermes was pleased by the results of the race.
But Hermes wasn't even looking Brody's way.
Instead he was watching Zeus strut around with his champion.
Only Athena walked over to congratulate Zeus.
The rest of the gods looked disgruntled, especially Hera.
She was scowling at Heracles so darkly that Brody shivered.
Finally Hermes noticed Brody and headed over.
"Nice driving, my boy," the god said.
"If Ares hadn't distracted your team with that silly boar prank, you might have won or come in second."
"Thanks," Brody said. "Do you know which event is next?"
Hermes shot Zeus an annoyed look. "Well, if Zeus doesn't decide to change the order again, the pentathlon will be next.
You'll need to watch out for Hephaestus' champion in the wrestling, especially his powerful body hold.
And of course, Ares' mortal is quite good at the discus . . ."
Hermes went on to give Brody advice on all five parts of the pentathlon.
Brody listened carefully and then nodded. "Okay, got it. But what about Heracles? I don't think I can beat him."
Hermes smirked. "Don't worry about him. From what I've heard, he won't be a factor."
Glancing at Heracles, Brody shivered again.
Brody had figured it was his job to compete in the Games, and it was mainly Julia's job to figure out the gods' pranks and stop them.
But Hermes' expression suddenly made Brody nervous.
He hoped Heracles was prepared for whatever was coming next.
"Back to the stadium, champions!" Zeus called out. "It's time for the pentathlon!"
Julia knew that the pentathlon was one of the hardest events of the Games.
It consisted of five separate events: the long jump, javelin throw, discus throw, a short footrace, and wrestling.
Zeus mixed up the order again, and announced that the first event would be the footrace.
Julia felt nervous as she watched Brody join the other runners.
The gods would surely be trying all kinds of pranks.
Iphicles sat down next to Julia and Markos.
"Is Heracles ready for this?" Julia asked him.
"He'll have to pay close attention to what's going on, or he'll be in big trouble."
"He's ready," Iphicles assured her. "You warned him well about Hades' plans for the footrace, right?"
Julia nodded as the runners took off.
All around the stadium people and gods shouted, "Go!"
Soon Heracles was in the lead, with Brody and several others close behind him.
"There!" Markos shouted, pointing.
Julia gasped. The ground had just split open, creating a huge chasm right in front of the runners!
Heracles was ready—this was the exact prank that Julia had warned him about after the banquet!
He leaped over the chasm and landed safely on the other side.
So did Brody, since he'd been watching for the chasm to appear too.
But two or three of the other racers weren't as fortunate.
Apollo's champion couldn't stop in time, and he hurtled down into the chasm with a terrified cry.
Another runner tried to stop, but he skidded over the edge, and was barely clinging on to the walls of the pit.
Most of the others were a little farther behind and were able to stop in time.
They stood now at the edge of the chasm, watching helplessly as Heracles and Brody finished the race. Heracles won by several strides.
"Whew," Julia said. "They did it!" But she didn't feel completely relieved—was that runner in the pit okay?
She glanced at the gods. Apollo was striding toward Hades, shouting and shaking his fist.
Clearly he'd guessed who was responsible for the chasm that had taken his champion out of the race.
Hades wasn't paying much attention to Apollo.
He was watching as Zeus rushed over to congratulate Heracles.
"Hades doesn't look very mad that Heracles foiled his plot," Julia commented.
Markos nodded. "Hades is more reasonable than some of the other gods.
He's probably disappointed that Heracles won, but also impressed by how quickly Heracles reacted."
"It helped that Heracles had some advance warning," Iphicles said.
"Well, I don't think Hera is as reasonable as Hades." Julia nodded toward the queen of the gods.
Hera was grinding her teeth and looking furious. Julia shuddered.
She tried not to imagine what Hera had in store for Heracles now that two gods had failed to stop him from winning.
"What if Hera finds out that Brody and I are helping Heracles win?" Julia thought. This was a very scary thought too.
Abruptly, Julia turned to Iphicles.
"Our plan is ready, right?" she asked him. "You've set up the, uh . . ."
She looked around, making sure nobody nearby was listening. "The escape plan?" she whispered.
"Don't worry," Iphicles said. "I told you I'd take care of that, didn't I?
Look. I think the official is getting ready to start the long jump."
Julia turned to watch the long jump.
She waited anxiously for Heracles and Brody to compete.
At last Zeus gestured toward Heracles. "All right, my champion," he called out.
"Show them how it's supposed to be done!"
Heracles ran up to the short board marking the starting point.
Just as he leaped into the air, flames shot up at the other end of the track.
Julia gasped. Even though they'd known about Hephaestus' prank ahead of time, it was still frightening to see Heracles leaping right into a fire!
Heracles' feet brushed the flames as he jumped.
But to Julia's relief, he landed well beyond the fire.
"What?" Hera cried, her face twisting into an expression of bitter fury. "Impossible!"
But almost everyone else in the stadium was cheering for Heracles.
"What an awesome jump!" Julia cried.
"That's the way, my boy!" Zeus crowed as the flames died away. "No one can beat that jump!"
Nobody did beat it. Brody ended up coming in second, though his jump was not even close to Heracles'.
"So far so good," Julia said as people bustled around, setting up the course for the discus throw.
"I just hope we can keep Heracles safe for the rest of today's events."
"And tomorrow's too," Markos reminded her.
Julia nodded but didn't say anything. The first athlete was stepping forward to begin the discus event.
This time Heracles went last. When he began to spin, preparing to release the discus, Julia glanced quickly at Hermes.
Would Hermes go through with his plan?
She looked back at the track, where suddenly the discus changed shape and color.
"We were right about Hermes!" Markos whispered.
Heracles found himself clinging to an enormous tortoise.
Hesitating slightly, he glanced toward Julia and the others.
Then he flung the tortoise down the course.
Julia held her breath, hoping Markos' guess about what Hermes would do next was right.
The creature's short legs wiggled helplessly as it flew through the air.
A split second before it crashed to the ground, Hermes let out a cry—and suddenly the tortoise turned back into a discus.
Julia let out her breath. "Thank goodness," she told Markos.
"You said Hermes has a soft spot for tortoises, and that he wouldn't let one get hurt. I'm glad you were right!"
Iphicles peered intently at the track. Several gods had rushed out to examine the spot where the discus had landed.
"That tortoise looked awfully heavy," Iphicles said.
"What if my brother has finally lost an event?"
Julia nervously bit her lip.
A second later Agon finally held up his hand. "The victor is Heracles!"
"Man, I'm starving." Brody popped a few grapes into his mouth.
"I wish the gods would give us more food," he complained to Heracles.
The gods were feasting on roasted meats, fish, cheese, and vegetables.
Even the mortals in the crowd had plenty of food, thanks to the vendors wandering around.
A few minutes earlier, after the end of the discus event, Zeus had called for a lunch break.
Brody could see Julia, Markos, and Iphicles enjoying a platter of cheese and olives.
Delicious scents drifted over the track, making Brody even hungrier.
Heracles was chewing on a fig. "Eating light snacks is best," he told Brody.
"If you're full, you can't perform well in the Games."
Brody shrugged, still wishing he had a nice, juicy cheeseburger—or at least some of those sausages Dionysus was enjoying.
"So which event comes next in the pentathlon?" he asked.
"The javelin throw," Heracles replied.
"And what pranks are planned for that?" Brody asked.
"None," Heracles said. "At least none that we know about.
Julia, Markos, and Iphicles heard no one plotting against me in this event."
Brody shrugged. "So maybe the gods will give you a break when it's your turn to throw the javelin." He picked up another grape.
"I doubt it," Heracles replied grimly. "I suppose I'll have to be ready for anything."
"Yeah." Brody tossed the grape into his mouth.
"By the way, I'm sorry for throwing my discus so far. I almost beat you!"
Heracles shot him a surprised look. "You have no need to apologize for that, my friend," he said.
"I didn't realize the tortoise would be so heavy," Brody went on.
"You would have thrown a real discus much farther."
"This is still a competition, Brody," Heracles said, looking serious.
"I'm willing to accept your help in avoiding the gods' mischief.
But I still want to win on my own merits."
Brody nodded. "Yeah. I get it." He knew just how Heracles felt.
He loved to win football games, but winning wouldn't be fun if the other team wasn't doing its best.
Soon the lunch break ended, and the Games resumed.
Zeus announced the start of the javelin event.
"Ares' champion will go first," he declared. Then he smirked.
"Although there's not much point in anyone throwing the javelin, is there?
It's pretty clear already who is going to win every event."
A few gods groaned.
"Don't get cocky, Zeus," Ares called out with a frown.
"Anything can happen in the Olympic Games, and we're not even halfway through!"
A smile curled across Zeus' face. "As you wish, Ares," he said.
"I merely wanted to spare your champions the embarrassment of losing."
Hera scowled. "That's enough, husband," she snapped.
"I came to see the Games, not to listen to your constant bragging."
"It's not bragging if it's true, dear wife." Zeus smirked again.
When Brody's turn came, he threw the javelin as far as he could.
Brody knew at once that it was a good throw, and he instantly heard Hermes cheering and applauding.
Agon stepped forward to retrieve the javelin and mark its landing spot.
"Sorry, Hermes," Demeter said with a smug expression.
"It appears that your champion has failed to beat my champion's mark."
Brody gulped, remembering Hermes' warning about sending Brody to Tartarus.
Would Hermes think that Brody hadn't done his best?
So far Brody had come in second or third in all the events. Was that good enough?
"It has to be," he thought. "Even Hermes must realize that nobody can beat Heracles at any feat of speed or strength.
At least I hope he realizes that."
Brody forgot about Hermes when Heracles stepped up for his turn.
"Good luck, buddy," Brody whispered as he moved aside.
Heracles nodded, but his focus was on the javelin he'd just picked up. He hoisted it to his shoulder.
Suddenly Brody saw the javelin shimmer—and then move in Heracles' hand!
"Heracles! Look out!" he cried.
But Heracles had already felt the change.
The javelin had turned into an enormous hissing serpent!
Ares had played this prank on Brody.
Brody should have predicted that Ares would try it now on Heracles!
Meanwhile Heracles acted fast.
He grabbed the serpent behind its head so it couldn't bite him, and swiftly tied the whole creature into a huge knot.
Then he flung it along the course with all his might.
The crowd roared as the knotted serpent flew through the air.
It untied itself in midair—and then turned back into a javelin just before landing.
Brody let out a sigh of relief. "Snakes," he muttered to himself.
"Why is it always snakes with these guys?"
Agon hurried over. "Oh my!" he exclaimed.
"Heracles has thrown the javelin nearly twice as far as any of the other competitors!"
Cheers rang out from all over the stadium.
Zeus strutted onto the course, waving to the crowd.
"Behold the greatest mortal athlete Greece has ever seen!"
Heracles took a bow and then quickly joined Brody, who was standing nearby with the other athletes.
"Ares was definitely behind that snake prank," Brody whispered. "He seems to like snakes."
"It's possible." Heracles glanced out at the crowd.
"However, Dionysus is frowning, which is unlike him.
My guess is that he was behind this latest prank.
He has a fondness for serpents as well." He paused and thought for a moment.
"Actually, many of the gods like snakes. There's Ares, Demeter, Apollo—"
"Okay, okay," Brody broke in. "Anyway, you'd better get ready, Heracles.
Wrestling comes next, and we know Artemis is planning to make trouble."
Heracles nodded and flexed his powerful muscles.
"Yes. I am quite ready for what is to come."
"Brody is amazing!" Markos exclaimed, leaning forward in his seat. "He's become a really good wrestler."
Julia nodded. Brody was wrestling with Demeter's champion.
"He's pretty good at all of the events," she admitted.
Then she glanced at Heracles, who was standing on the sideline with the other athletes.
"He's definitely not as good as Heracles, though."
"Nobody is as good as Heracles," Markos replied.
He looked around and then lowered his voice.
"But that's no surprise. After all, Heracles is half god."
"Yes," Iphicles muttered. "And if the other gods knew the truth about him, they'd—"
"But they don't know the truth," Julia reminded him quickly.
"And we'd better hope they never find out—for Heracles' sake."
"Right," Markos agreed.
Julia glanced uneasily toward Hera, who was seated in her golden chair with the other gods.
