Did Hera already know that Heracles was Zeus' son?
Was that why she hated Heracles so much?
A roar went up from the crowd as Brody threw down his opponent again and won.
Agon stepped forward and declared him the winner of the round.
Next Heracles stepped up, along with Athena's champion.
The two of them shook hands before getting into position.
"We got lucky with Heracles' opponent," Julia said.
"He's Athena's champion, and Athena is the only god who's playing fair."
"But that won't stop the other gods from interfering." Markos looked glum.
"I know," Julia said. She watched as the match began.
Heracles quickly overpowered the other athlete.
Just as Heracles was about to toss him again, Julia saw Artemis step up to the sidelines and point her bow.
"Here it comes!" Julia thought. "Be ready, Heracles!"
Suddenly Athena's champion changed shape, growing larger and becoming very hairy and muscular.
A second later Heracles was wrestling a huge bear!
The bear roared and slashed at Heracles with its sharp claws.
Heracles had already ducked low, dodging the bear's swipes in the nick of time.
Athena's eyes flashed with anger. "What is this foolishness?" she cried, striding toward Artemis.
"How dare you tamper with my champion? Outrageous!"
She pointed her spear, and the bear instantly changed back into her mortal champion.
"Wh-what happened?" the athlete gasped.
"Never mind." Athena glared at Artemis, who smirked in return.
"Take a moment to recover. Then the match will continue."
"Yes, yes," Zeus said mildly. "Enough of this nonsense."
"Huh . . . ," thought Julia. "That was a pretty dangerous prank!" she said to Markos.
"But Zeus doesn't sound very mad. He sounds amused instead."
"He probably is," Markos said. "The Games are always like this, Julia.
The gods constantly play pranks and make mischief.
Zeus doesn't really care because Heracles just keeps winning."
"Everyone is already acting as if my brother is the greatest champion of all time," Iphicles muttered.
"He is a great athlete," Markos said.
Julia was surprised by Iphicles' comment. Maybe he got a little jealous of Heracles sometimes, she thought.
But Iphicles had to be really worried about Heracles.
After all, the more people praised Heracles, the more the gods—especially Hera—were eager to defeat him.
Soon the match resumed. It wasn't long before Heracles was declared the winner.
A short while later, he was also declared the winner of the pentathlon as a whole.
"And thus my champion remains undefeated," Zeus exclaimed, clapping Heracles on the back.
"And he will remain that way tomorrow as well. Mark my words!"
There was plenty of grumbling from the other gods.
But none of them said anything directly, except for Athena, who congratulated Zeus and Heracles.
Markos jumped to his feet. "Come on," he said to Julia.
"Let's go find Brody and walk him home."
She pointed to Iphicles, who'd gone over to try to talk to his brother.
But Zeus had whisked away Heracles so fast, Iphicles just stood there alone, looking annoyed and a little lost.
Julia felt sorry for him. "Why don't we see if Iphicles wants to come?" she suggested.
"Good idea," Markos agreed. "Perhaps he will stay for dinner."
Later that night Julia had trouble falling asleep.
She kept thinking about the next day's events.
Had she and her friends figured out all the pranks that were planned against Heracles?
Would they be able to continue to stop them?
Iphicles had assured her that his plan to get them home was foolproof.
But what if Hermes caught them? Or something else went wrong?
They couldn't afford to make any mistakes.
Julia tossed and turned and then finally got up.
She went to the window and stared up at the moon for a while, thinking about her family and friends back home.
Did they miss her? Had her parents been freaking out?
Suddenly something below caught Julia's eye. To her surprise two shadowy figures were huddled together.
Julia squinted at the figures. "The shorter one looks like Iphicles," she thought. "What's he doing out there?"
The taller figure, who was facing away from her, wore a long robe and a hood. Still, Julia could tell it was a god.
"It's definitely not Zeus," she thought. "He or she is too slim.
It's not Hades or Poseidon either. But it could be almost any of the others."
She watched as the god, or goddess, leaned closer to Iphicles.
The two of them appeared to talk quietly for a moment.
Then they parted ways and hurried off in opposite directions, disappearing into the night.
"That was kind of weird," Julia murmured aloud.
Maybe she'd ask Iphicles about his moonlit meeting tomorrow.
She yawned and realized that she finally felt a little bit tired.
A few minutes later, she climbed back into bed and soon fell asleep, dreaming about serpents and bears—and home.
The next morning Brody felt good. He was ready to start competing again.
"We're halfway there," he told Heracles, who was stretching beside him.
All the athletes were on the track preparing for the first event of the day, the short footrace known as the stadion.
Most of the gods were already seated in their golden chairs, and spectators filled the rest of the stadium.
Brody spotted Julia and Markos. However, Iphicles was nowhere to be seen.
Brody knew why—Heracles' brother was already in position, waiting to foil the gods' next prank.
Suddenly Brody noticed someone else among the spectators.
"Dude!" he exclaimed, poking Heracles in the shoulder.
"Is that Apollo's champion over there? The guy who fell into the pit yesterday? I didn't expect to see him again!"
Heracles nodded. "I was wondering about him too. But Zeus says he'll be fine.
He injured his arm and bumped his head, but he's recovering well."
"Cool." Brody was relieved.
Just then Agon called for the stadion to begin.
The runners lined up at the starting line.
Brody ended up between Heracles and Ares' champion.
"Well, what do you think?" Ares' champion asked Brody in a low tone.
He shot a glance at Heracles. "Will Zeus' mighty hero make us all look like fools again today?"
"Probably," Brody said. He slapped the other athlete on the back.
"Winning isn't everything, bro. Just do your best."
Ares' champion gave him a strange look. Brody understood why.
Before coming to ancient Greece, Brody never would have said something like that.
In fact, his favorite saying back home was "Winning isn't everything—it's the only thing."
A famous football coach had said that, and Brody had believed it.
But here in ancient Greece, the circumstances were completely different.
For the first time ever, Brody wasn't focused only on winning.
Agon lifted an arm, interrupting Brody's thoughts.
"Champions, get ready!" Agon shouted. Then a trumpet blew and the race began.
Brody took off. Pumping his arms, he ran as fast as he could alongside the others.
Suddenly the stadium was plunged into complete darkness.
"Whoa!" Brody cried. "Who turned out the lights?"
A runner bumped into Brody and almost knocked him over.
But Brody stayed on his feet, staring ahead. He'd been expecting this prank.
He just hadn't imagined that the stadium could get quite this dark.
He couldn't even see his hand in front of his face!
A second later a light flared ahead on the track.
It was Iphicles holding a torch. He tossed it to Heracles as the athlete raced past.
Heracles caught the torch easily as he ran by.
Brody grinned and took off after him, using the light of the torch to stay on the course.
But then he stumbled over a fallen runner and went down with a loud "oof!"
He jumped to his feet and started running again.
By now most of the other runners had caught on as well and were racing after Heracles.
But the race was short, and they'd already lost too much ground.
Heracles won easily, with Brody coming in near the back of the pack.
"Uh-oh," he thought. "I hope Hermes didn't see that!"
Luckily Hermes hadn't seen it. Nobody had been able to see anything except Heracles crossing the finish line first.
As soon as the race was over, the light returned.
Brody saw Zeus grin at a dark-haired goddess. "Nice try, Nyx!" he called.
"However, it will take more than the powers of the goddess of the night to stop my champion!"
Agon stared in dismay at the athletes milling around the track.
"Clearly Heracles won," he murmured. "But we'll have to call it a tie for second place.
There's no way of determining the rest of the order, and there's no time to redo the race."
"Fine." Zeus clapped Heracles on the back.
"First place is the only place that matters."
A few of the other gods grumbled, but no one complained very loudly about the decision.
Brody was relieved when Hermes flashed him a pleased smile.
Then it was time for the next race, a longer one known as the diaulos.
"This is your best event, isn't it?" Heracles took his place beside Brody at the starting line.
"Yeah." Brody grinned. "I'm pretty good at this distance. Maybe even better than you."
Heracles grinned back. "We shall see."
The trumpet blared again and the runners took off.
Heracles and Brody immediately took the lead. Brody shot a look at Heracles.
Could he actually beat him at this race?
Out of the corner of his eye, Brody saw Poseidon stand up.
The sea god slammed his trident into the ground.
Shock waves made the entire stadium rumble as if from an earthquake.
"What's happening?" a runner cried out from somewhere behind Brody.
Markos had overheard Poseidon telling Artemis about this prank, so again Brody and Heracles were ready.
They slowed down a little to catch their balance on the heaving track.
"Whoa," Brody said, stretching his arms out as the ground heaved again beneath his feet.
"I feel like I'm surfing, not running!"
"Don't stop," Heracles said. "Come on!"
He ran on, jumping over the worst of the moving lumps of ground.
Brody did the same, making the turn at the other end of the stadium.
Most of the other runners had stopped, even though their gods were yelling at them to keep going.
But Brody caught a glimpse of one runner coming up behind them. It was Drakon, Poseidon's champion.
"Oh no, you don't, dude," Brody said as Drakon tried to pass him.
Brody put on another burst of speed. So did Heracles.
The two of them crossed the finish line a second later.
Heracles was just two steps in front of Brody, and Drakon came in behind them, a distant third.
Brody grinned, thrilled that he'd beaten Poseidon's speedy champion and nearly outrun Heracles.
"Winning isn't everything," he thought. "But sometimes it sure feels great!"
From her seat in the stadium, Julia watched Poseidon stride over to Zeus.
"Congratulations, brother," Poseidon said in his deep voice. "It seems your champion remains undefeated."
"Indeed." Zeus puffed out his chest and grinned.
"And he'll stay that way—mark my words."
Hera narrowed her eyes. "We shall see, husband," she said.
Her voice was cold and angry. "The Games aren't over yet."
"That's right." Demeter was standing nearby with a mysterious smile on her face.
She stroked the sheaf of wheat she was holding.
"Beware, Zeus. Anything can happen in the next few events."
Julia kept her eyes on Demeter for a moment. The dolichos was the next event.
It was the longest footrace, taking runners out of the stadium and through the surrounding hills.
Then, sticking to the plan that she and the others had made last night, Julia got up.
She picked up the sack at her feet and headed for an exit.
She was careful to slip behind the gods so they wouldn't spot her carrying something.
She especially didn't want Hermes to notice her.
"Julia."
Suddenly feeling a hand on her arm, Julia froze. But it was only Iphicles.
"Are you sure you want to do this?" he whispered, casting a look at the gods. "Maybe I should go instead. It's safer."
"Thanks, Iphicles, but no." Julia shook her head. "Zeus might notice you're gone."
Iphicles grimaced. "That's unlikely. Must I remind you that Zeus notices almost nothing except my brother?"
"True," Julia said. "But we should play it safe.
And we all agreed last night that no one would notice if I left the Games."
Iphicles still looked concerned.
"I'll be fine," Julia added in a whisper. She lifted the sack slightly.
"Don't worry, I can do this. I'm just glad we realized in time that Demeter had changed her original plan.
I thought she was going to make the wheat sticky."
Julia suddenly remembered how she'd seen Iphicles the night before in the moonlight.
"Oh, and speaking of last night, I saw you and . . ." Just then Hermes glanced over at the two of them.
"Never mind," Julia said quickly. "I have to get out of here!"
Iphicles nodded and Julia continued on toward the exit.
As soon as she was outside the stadium, she felt a little safer.
She glanced at the marked track, which wound its way through the city and into the hills.
Julia started jogging along the track. The sack was heavy, and Julia wasn't used to running in sandals.
Within a few minutes, she was out of breath and had a stitch in her side.
"How does Brody do it?" she muttered, shifting the sack to her other side.
Luckily she hadn't bumped into anyone yet.
She knew she looked strange carrying a mysterious bundle.
Soon Julia stopped, leaned over, and rested her hands on her knees to catch her breath.
But she didn't dare stop for long. The runners would be coming soon.
And if Julia hadn't reached the right spot by then, Heracles would have little chance of finishing the race.
So she picked up the sack and started jogging again, ignoring her racing heart and sweaty forehead.
She ran out of town and up a series of hills.
Finally she spotted a hill with a crooked tree near the top. She was almost there now.
Moments later Julia crested the hill and smiled with relief.
Spread out before her at the foot of the hill was a broad, flat meadow of short grass.
This meadow was where she needed to be.
Finally she could rest and wait for the runners to reach her.
She ran down to the meadow and scouted the area for a hiding place.
Spotting a clump of tall weeds, she flopped to the ground behind it.
She reached into the sack for the object inside.
As she pulled it out, she heard pounding footsteps coming from above, on the hill. The runners were already here!
Julia leaped to her feet. She could see that Heracles was in the lead, just as she'd expected.
He came sprinting down the hill and slowed slightly when he reached the meadow.
As he glanced around, Julia stepped into view. Heracles smiled when he saw her.
He kept coming, running across the short grass.
But the grass didn't stay short for long; as soon as Heracles' foot touched it, the grass started growing.
It grew taller and taller, quickly turning the golden color of mature wheat.
Within seconds the wheat was nearly as tall as Heracles himself.
"Heracles!" Julia cried, barely able to see the runners through the still-growing wheat.
"I've got it!" She plunged forward, clutching the sack.
Inside was a curved sickle, which Markos had assured her was all that Heracles would need to combat Demeter's new prank.
Julia could barely see a thing through the tall wheat, though she heard confused cries from the arriving runners.
Then she heard footsteps behind her. Spinning around, she saw Demeter's champion sprinting toward the edge of the meadow.
"Obviously Demeter warned him about what was coming," Julia thought.
The athlete was running away from the rapidly growing wheat.
She called Heracles' name again.
"Julia!" He finally heard her. "I'm over here!"
"Coming!" Julia pushed forward and saw Heracles again.
She handed him the sickle, and he nodded his thanks.
Then he turned and slashed at the wheat, quickly clearing himself a path through it. Brody was right behind Heracles.
"Good job, Julia," Brody called as he ran after Heracles, following the path the hero had cleared. "We did it again!"
"Yeah!" Julia watched until the boys were out of sight.
Then she found her way back to the hill and returned to the stadium.
She arrived out of breath and exhausted. But she arrived in time to see Zeus still celebrating Heracles' latest victory.
"Congratulations, dude," Brody said to Heracles. "You've won every event so far."
"Thank you." Heracles looked solemn.
"But I won't relax until the final event is complete—and you and Julia are safely through the time passage."
"Yeah. Me neither," Brody agreed. "I'm definitely ready to go home."
The athletes had just completed the boxing event.
There had been more pranks from the gods, of course, but Heracles had handled them without much trouble.
Now all that was left was the final race—the hoplitodromos.
Brody wished Heracles luck and headed over to his armor. Hermes and Markos were waiting there.
"You've performed well today, my boy," Hermes said cheerfully. "I'm proud of you!"
"You are?" Brody was relieved. He'd been pretty sure that Hermes was pleased with his performance, but it was still good to hear it.
Especially since Brody had come in second or third in most of the events.
"Of course!" Hermes chuckled. "You can't be blamed for failing to defeat the mighty Heracles.
He's quite amazing, isn't he? I'm almost tempted to cheer for him myself in this final event."
Brody scowled as he put on his armor.
He was a little annoyed by Hermes' remark.
After all, Brody was Hermes' champion, not Heracles. Didn't Hermes believe in Brody?
"Heracles is very dominant," Markos said politely.
"Of course . . ." Hermes seemed to be thinking aloud.
"If Zeus' champion sweeps the Games, then Zeus will be impossible to deal with." He shot a look at Brody.
"But if something happens to Heracles in this final race . . ." He winked mischievously.
"Well, I suppose in that case, they'd have to award the olive crown to you, my champion!"
"Oh." Brody hadn't thought about it that way.
It would be fun to win, but he needed to make sure that Heracles came in first.
Hermes' words alarmed Brody.
"There's no reason to worry," he told himself. "Julia is a genius."
She had figured out what Aphrodite had planned for Heracles during the hoplitodromos.
She'd also figured out a plan to help Heracles avoid the prank.
"So there's no danger," Brody thought. "It's almost time to go home."
"Hold still, Brody," Markos said. "I'll help you put on your shin guards."
Hermes watched as Markos fixed the guards to Brody's legs and then handed the helmet to Brody.
"You've performed well too, my boy," Hermes told Markos.
"Your loyalty and hard work are a credit to your family."
"Thank you, Hermes," Markos said with a bow.
"It has been an honor to serve you."
"Yes, I know," Hermes said. "Still, I wish there were a way to thank you.
Perhaps I should declare your entire family to be henceforth under my patronage and protection."
Markos' eyes widened. "You would do that?"
Athena happened to be walking by at that moment.
She stopped and raised an eyebrow at Hermes.
"I would like to hear your answer too, Hermes," she said.
"You shouldn't promise such protection to mortals unless you mean to follow through with it."
"Of course I mean to follow through with it." Hermes looked annoyed.
"I don't need a warning from you, Athena."
Athena shrugged. "Perhaps you do. It's not as if your word has always been good."
"Well, my word is good this time!" Hermes declared with a frown.
"From this day forward, upon my word, the family of Nikolaos shall be under my protection.
May I be thrown out of Mount Olympus if I break this vow."
"It's official then." Athena looked approving. "Good luck to your champion in the hoplitodromos, Hermes."
She moved on. Hermes still looked annoyed, but Markos looked awed.
"This is incredible!" he whispered to Brody.
"Hermes won't dare break his vow to protect my family—not with Athena as a witness!"
Before Brody could answer, Hermes handed him his shield.
"Get ready, boy," he said. "And stay away from Heracles.
Hera might be planning some trouble, and I don't want you caught up in it."
"Okay," Brody said. He hurried toward the starting line.
Halfway there, he realized what Hermes had said.
"Huh?" Brody thought. "We're expecting a prank from Aphrodite during this event, not Hera."
Brody glanced around, suddenly in a panic. Where were Julia and Markos?
Finally he spotted Iphicles in the crowd and waved him over.
"What is it, Brody?" Iphicles seemed distracted.
"I must leave soon to prepare your escape."
"I know," Brody said. "But I just heard something weird about Hera . . ."
He told Iphicles what Hermes had said.
"I'll get word to my brother," Iphicles said. "I'm sure he'll figure something out."
"Thanks, dude," Brody said, relieved. "See you after the race!"
He rushed on to the starting line.
"Go!" Agon shouted a few minutes later.
Brody took off, clanking along the track in his heavy armor.
As usual Heracles was already in the lead.
Suddenly there was a clamor of chirping.
A huge flock of sparrows swooped toward Heracles and mobbed him.
Then Heracles' muscular arm emerged from the cloud of birds, tossing a large handful of grain onto the track.
The birds eagerly dived for the grain.
"That was easy!" Brody thought gleefully as Heracles raced on.
Heracles had now foiled Aphrodite. And since Iphicles had promised to warn Heracles about—
Just then Hera stepped forward. She waved her hand—and a sea of pomegranates rolled across the track, right in front of Heracles!
"Ahh!" Heracles cried as his foot hit one of the fruits.
His heavy armor made it hard to balance, and he almost fell. More pomegranates were rolling toward him!
Brody knew that Heracles couldn't see the fruit clearly because of his helmet.
But he had an idea. "Hold on, dude!" he yelled.
Brody ripped off his helmet and tossed it aside, along with his shield.
Hermes would be furious when he saw Brody disqualifying himself.
But that didn't matter anymore. All that mattered was making sure their plan worked.
Julia stood with Markos near the exit to the stadium.
She gasped along with everyone else when Hera tossed the pomegranates onto the track.
"Uh-oh," she murmured.
Then she saw Brody running to help guide Heracles around the rolling fruits, and she let out a sigh of relief.
"I guess that's one prank we didn't hear about," she said to Markos.
He looked relieved too. "Hera is more secretive than most of the gods," he said.
"It's lucky for Heracles that Brody thought quickly."
"It sure is," Julia agreed. "Lucky for us too."
Before today the idea of Brody's thinking quickly would have made her laugh.
But not anymore. She had learned that Brody wasn't dumb at all.
She glanced back at the track, checking to see if it was time for her to put the plan in motion.
Thanks to Brody, Heracles was off again, running slowly but steadily in his armor.
The other athletes were just about to reach the pomegranates—it was time for Julia to go.
"Thanks again for all your help," Julia said to Markos.
"I'll miss you when we go home. I know Brody will miss you too."
She was glad Markos had told her about Hermes' oath of protection.
Now she wouldn't have to worry about Markos or his family after she and Brody left ancient Greece.
Hermes had sworn to protect them, and Athena would make sure he kept that promise.
Markos looked a little embarrassed. "I'll miss both of you as well," he said shyly.
"I never expected to become friends with a girl." He shrugged.
"Then again, you're not like most girls, Julia."
Julia decided to take that as a compliment.
"Thanks," she said with a smile. "I'd better get moving now."
Markos nodded. "I'll distract Hermes if needed. But I'm guessing it won't be necessary.
Everyone will be focused on Heracles as soon as he wins this final event."
Julia smiled again, certain that Markos was right. "Good luck, Markos," she whispered.
"Same to you," Markos whispered back. "Good-bye, Julia."
Julia tightened her hold on a cloth bundle as she hurried outside the stadium.
Not far away Iphicles was waiting for her in a chariot.
The chariot was pulled by a pair of horses—just as they'd planned.
Iphicles waved her over. "Ready?" he asked.
"The hoplitodromos is a very short race, and it's probably nearly over.
I suppose my brother is about to triumph yet again?"
"Yes, but no thanks to Hera," Julia said.
"She played a nasty prank, which slowed everything down.
Just give me a second to change clothes, Iphicles, and I'll be ready."
She pulled her jeans out of the bundle she was carrying and slipped them on under her chiton.
Iphicles turned away politely as Julia finished changing.
Then she jumped aboard the chariot. "Let's get in the stadium and finish this, Iphicles. I'm ready to go home!"
Iphicles nodded and flicked the reins, and the horses trotted into the stadium.
Julia looked toward the finish line. Heracles was still on the track, running as fast as he could in the heavy armor.
Brody had picked up his armor, and was running again, many strides behind Heracles.
Julia still felt nervous, but so far everything was going according to her plan.
All they had to do was wait for Brody to finish the race.
While everyone mobbed Heracles, Iphicles would drive Julia and Brody out of the stadium and up to the Temple of Caerus.
Brody and Julia would be through the passage before anyone in Greece even noticed they were gone.
"This has to work," Julia thought, crossing her fingers. "It has to!"
Iphicles steered the chariot to a spot just past the finish line.
A second later Heracles raced past them. Brody came next.
He veered off the track and leaped into the chariot.
"Let's go!" he cried breathlessly.
Iphicles started to turn the chariot toward an exit.
Julia glanced back, hoping to catch a glimpse of Heracles' moment of glory.
That would definitely be something to remember once she was back in her own time.
How many kids could say they'd met—and helped—the mighty Heracles?
But when Julia saw what was happening on the track, she let out a loud gasp. "Oh no! What's Hera doing?"
The queen of the gods had approached Heracles, her face twisted with anger.
She pointed her lotus-tipped staff directly at the champion. "I've had enough of this nonsense!"
Suddenly a pit opened right beneath Heracles.
He fell in, but he managed to grab onto the edge, scrabbling at the dirt as smoke poured out from below.
The horses were galloping toward the exit. "No!" Julia yelled.
"Iphicles, turn back! We have to help Heracles!"
Iphicles seemed to hesitate for a second before whipping the horses into a sharp turn.
The chariot careened toward Heracles, who was still clinging to the edge of the pit.
"Hold on, dude!" Brody hollered at him. "Here we come!"
Julia held her breath as Brody leaned out and reached for Heracles.
Brody grabbed the other athlete and held him tightly.
Heracles hung off the edge of the chariot as it raced on.
Julia could see him gritting his teeth with pain as his legs dragged on the ground.
Brody grunted with effort. "Dude, you're heavy!" he exclaimed. "Especially with that armor on."
"Just hang on to Brody!" Julia urged Heracles.
She reached down to help, grabbing Heracles by the wrist.
Brody was right—Heracles was really heavy.
But together the two of them finally managed to pull Heracles onto the chariot.
"Thank you!" Heracles let out his breath. "I owe you two my life—yet again."
"Get us out of here," Julia told Iphicles. "Hurry!"
She glanced back at Hera. Zeus was storming toward the goddess. "How dare you, Hera!" he thundered.
"Never mind that, you idiot!" Hera gnashed her teeth and pointed at the chariot as it sped toward the exit. "Somebody stop them!"
Brody peeled off the rest of his armor as the horses galloped toward the Temple of Caerus.
"Did you bring our regular clothes?" he asked Julia.
Then he blinked, realizing she'd already changed.
She handed over his clothes. "Hurry," she said, glancing back over her shoulder.
"It won't take long for the gods to catch up to us."
"Only if they figure out where you're going," Heracles said.
"Do you think they will?" Brody asked.
Julia shrugged. "Hermes or Caerus will certainly figure it out. But will they tell Zeus and Hera?"
"I doubt it," Heracles said. "Hermes and Caerus won't wish to help Zeus or Hera under the circumstances."
Brody hoped Heracles was right.
Soon Iphicles pulled sharply on the reins, and the chariot skidded to a stop at the bottom of the temple's steps.
"Thanks for the ride," Julia called as she and Brody climbed out.
She looked at Heracles."Is it safe for you two to return to the Games?"
"I think you'll be fine once we're gone," Brody said.
"Zeus will protect you from Hera, Heracles.
And he probably wants to crown you with that olive wreath!"
"The festivities can wait." Heracles climbed out too.
"I want to make sure you two get home safely.
How will you get past the temple guard?"
"We'll be fine," Brody said.
"I insist," Heracles said firmly. "Come on, Iphicles."
"If you say so, brother." Iphicles got out of the chariot and tied the horses to a tree.
There was no guard outside the temple.
"Good!" Brody said. "Modern times, here we come!"
He charged through the temple's outer room and through the entrance to the inner room. The passage was still open.
"Whew!" Brody exclaimed. "Hurry up, Julia. We don't want to—"
A sudden flash of bright light interrupted him.
Brody shaded his eyes and coughed at the smoke that suddenly filled the chamber.
When the smoke cleared, Hera stood between Brody and the rift.
"Oh, good," she said with a sneer. "I was hoping I wasn't too late to see you off, mortals."
Julia ran in with Heracles and his brother.
"Hera, leave them alone!" Heracles called. "They've done nothing."
Hera ignored him. "Come here, mortal," she said, reaching for Iphicles and pulling him toward her.
Brody expected Iphicles to struggle to free himself.
But Iphicles just stood there as Hera stroked his hair.
"You have my thanks, mortal boy," the goddess purred.
"Without your information I might not have learned all of your friends' secrets until it was too late."
"Huh?" Brody said, not understanding what she meant.
But Julia was scowling. "I hate to tell you this, Brody," she exclaimed, "but Iphicles betrayed us!"
"Don't flatter yourself," Iphicles snapped. "It wasn't you two I was after." He glared at Heracles.
Now Brody was starting to follow along.
"Wait . . . you betrayed your own brother, Iphicles?" he blurted out. "That's low!"
Hera chuckled. "It's all a matter of perspective, mortal.
I consider Iphicles a hero. He informed me about where I might have a moment alone with my husband's mortal champion.
I couldn't rely on the other gods to destroy Heracles."
Brody shuddered. Once again Hera had put extra emphasis on the word "mortal."
Brody guessed that meant she knew that Heracles was half god.
Julia was still glaring at Iphicles. "How could you do this?" she said. "Heracles is your own brother."
Iphicles shrugged. "It was easy for me to do it.
I've been hearing about the wonderful Alcides for my whole life.
What about me? Nobody ever pays the slightest attention to me."
"That's no reason to betray him to Hera!" Brody retorted.
Heracles hadn't said a word yet. He stared at his brother with hurt in his eyes. Then his expression darkened.
"If you had a problem with me, brother, you should have said so," he said.
"Now you've put our friends in danger."
"They're your friends, Heracles, not mine," Iphicles said. "I don't have any friends."
"Say good-bye to them, Heracles," Hera spoke up.
"Well, unless you wish me to send them to somewhere like Tartarus along with you."
Brody's heart pounded. He didn't want to go to Tartarus!
He didn't want Heracles to go there either.
"Wait a minute!" Julia blurted out. "You can't send Heracles to Tartarus."
Sparks shot out of Hera's eyes as she glared at Julia.
"Who are you to tell me what I can or cannot do?"
"You made a bet," Julia said, her voice shaking.
"According to the bet, you were only allowed to send Heracles to Tartarus if he lost at least one event at the Games. And he won them all."
Brody was impressed. Julia was standing up to Hera—and Hera was scary!
Hera stared down at Julia. "You're right, my fellow gods were not able to stop Zeus' mighty hero in the Games.
Unfortunately, that means he's safe from Tartarus."
"Whew!" Brody thought.
But Hera wasn't finished. "That doesn't mean he's completely safe, however." She sneered.
"I can toss him somewhere much worse than Tartarus—like into the terrible future world beyond this rift."
She pointed a long, thin finger at the time passage.
Brody gasped. "But if you throw him through there, the rift will close!" he blurted out.
"Yes, that's what my young mortal friend tells me." Hera patted Iphicles again.
"It means that I won't be bothered by the mighty Heracles ever again." She let out a terrible cackle.
"And he will surely suffer in that new place—because he'll know that his mortal friends are trapped here in Olympia forever!"
"No!" Heracles cried. He leaped forward and grabbed at Hera.
But the goddess was too quick for him.
Tilting her staff forward, she shot out a bolt of energy.
It struck Heracles in the chest and sent him hurtling backward.
Heracles flew through the rift, and it closed with a snap!
